title: COBOL (ISO/IEC 1989:2023)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 54/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 54/100
Core Coupling Analysis: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) is a compiled, English-like language that has dominated business, finance, and mainframe systems since 1960. Its most coupling-relevant feature is the strict four-division structure — Identification, Environment, Data, and Procedure — which genuinely separates data definition from program logic. The Data Division declares data hierarchically via level-numbers and the PICTURE clause. But COBOL’s coupling profile is weak: typing is weak and static (numeric data converts silently between representations; alphanumeric data can be placed in any item that holds strings), the standard specifies no large library (43 statements, 87 functions, one class), and PERFORM provides no parameter passing or call stack. Pre-COBOL-85, a procedure could access and modify any data item — access restriction was impossible. GO TO promotes spaghetti code, and COBOL programs are infamous for being monolithic and hard to modularize. Exceptions are handled by declaratives and may not terminate the program. The result is a language whose local readability masks pervasive global coupling.
Platform & Ecosystem: COBOL remains among the most widely deployed languages: Gartner reported over 200 billion lines in 1997, and COBOL still runs background processes for most credit/debit-card swipes. The 2023 standard (ISO/IEC 1989:2023) added asynchronous messaging, transaction processing, and other modern features, and GnuCOBOL (a standalone open-source compiler, distinct from GCC) implements it. However, the ecosystem is legacy and vendor-fragmented (IBM, Micro Focus, GnuCOBOL), evolution is glacial, and the skills base is shrinking due to retirements (a problem highlighted during the COVID-era unemployment-systems crisis). It is superb for its niche — high-volume batch and transaction processing on mainframes — but poor for nearly everything else. The learning curve is steep in practice because of verbosity and over 300 reserved words.

title: Python (3.14)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ Dynamic typing: All coupling at runtime
✅ Duck typing radical: If it quacks, it’s a duck—maximum runtime decoupling
✅ match/case structural pattern matching (3.10+): Exhaustive dispatch on data structures, like Rust/Swift
✅ | union type syntax (3.10+): str | int cleaner than Union[str, int]
⚠️ Type hints (PEP 484) help: Gradual typing, but not enforced by the runtime; mypy/pyright provide enforcement at build time
⚠️ Protocols (PEP 544): Structural typing like Go, but runtime only

Object Construction:

⚠️ __init__ can have side effects: Constructors couple to initialization
✅ Dataclasses decouple: Auto-generated methods; kw_only, slots options improve control
⚠️ Multiple inheritance: Diamond problem; MRO (Method Resolution Order) couples resolution to inheritance order
✅ @override decorator (3.12): Catches broken overrides at check time

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Reference counting + GC: Immediate deallocation for most objects
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ Reference cycles need GC: Cycle detector runs periodically
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Cycle collection can pause
❌ __del__ timing non-deterministic: Finalizers unreliable for resource cleanup
✅ Context managers for resources: with statement provides deterministic cleanup
❌ Global references common: Module-level variables extend lifetimes

Error Handling:

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking in signatures
✅ Exception groups + except* (3.11+): Can handle multiple concurrent exceptions without losing information
❌ Broad exception catching couples: except Exception catches too much
⚠️ Result types possible: Libraries exist but not idiomatic

Concurrency:

✅ Free-threaded Python (3.14, officially supported): GIL removed as opt-in — threads can use multiple cores. Single-threaded performance overhead ~5-10%.
⚠️ GIL still default: Free-threaded mode is opt-in via --disable-gil build or python3.14t
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions
⚠️ Multiprocessing decouples: Separate processes, but manual (less necessary with free-threaded mode)
⚠️ Free-threaded mode is new: Ecosystem still adapting; many C extensions need GIL

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Global mutable state common: Module-level variables couple
❌ Monkey patching couples: Can modify anything at runtime
❌ Import side effects: Module execution couples to import
❌ Mutable default arguments: def f(x=[]) couples calls together
❌ None everywhere: Couples to absence checking

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Dynamic Typing vs. Maintainability: All coupling invisible until runtime, couples correctness to testing — mitigated by mypy/pyright in CI
Free-threaded Mode vs. Ecosystem Readiness: GIL removal is real but opt-in; many libraries haven’t adapted
Monkey Patching: Can modify stdlib/libraries at runtime, couples code to load order
Mutable Default Arguments: def f(x=[]) shares state across calls, couples invocations
Import Side Effects: Modules execute on import, couples import order to behavior
Duck Typing vs. Protocols: No interface enforcement couples to runtime type checking — statically checked by type checkers

title: Groovy (5.x)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 53/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 80/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Groovy is a Java-compatible, multi-paradigm language for the JVM that can be both dynamically and statically typed. Its dual typing is the central coupling issue: dynamic typing (the def keyword) defers coupling detection to runtime, while optional static compilation and static type checking (Groovy 2+) provide compile-time detection and near-Java performance. Closures act like method pointers, decoupling callbacks from calling code. Traits (interfaces carrying default implementations and state) support behavior composition without inheritance coupling. The safe-navigation operator ?. reduces null-checking coupling. However, prototype extension via ExpandoMetaClass and Objective-C-style categories enable metaprogramming that can create hidden, action-at-a-distance coupling at runtime. GroovyBeans auto-generate getters/setters, reducing construction boilerplate. Much of Groovy’s power lies in AST transformations (compile-time metaprogramming), which add flexibility without runtime penalty but couple code to compile-time semantics. Groovy’s syntax omitting parentheses and dots enables DSLs that decouple surface syntax from meaning. The JVM ecosystem and tools such as Gradle and Jenkins pipelines make Groovy widely used for scripting and build automation.
Platform & Ecosystem: Groovy has a strong, well-established ecosystem as an Apache top-level project. It is central to Gradle (build automation) and Jenkins Pipeline (CI), and powers Grails web development. Performance is moderate in dynamic mode (JVM, dynamic dispatch) but approaches Java with static compilation. The learning curve is gentle for Java developers, since most valid Java is valid Groovy. The syntax is concise and Java-compatible. Testing is excellent via Spock and JUnit. Security is reasonable, though dynamic typing and metaprogramming (ExpandoMetaClass) can create type-confusion and hidden-coupling risk. The language has no fixed release cadence; Groovy 5.x (2025) improves performance and JDK 17+ support.

title: Transact-SQL (SQL Server)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 65/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 69/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is the procedural extension to SQL used by Microsoft SQL Server and SAP Adaptive Server Enterprise. Like PL/SQL, it couples application logic directly to the database engine. Stored procedures provide modularity and can return status values and output parameters. TRY...CATCH gives structured exception handling. Local variables (declared with DECLARE @name) default to NULL, and NULL handling pervades the language. Triggers create implicit coupling by firing on data changes. T-SQL is fundamentally distinct from PL/SQL despite superficial similarity — porting between them requires non-trivial work, because of feature differences and of deeper differences in how Oracle and SQL Server handle concurrency and locking. There is no general type system beyond SQL data types; everything is data-centric.
Platform & Ecosystem: Transact-SQL is deeply embedded in the Microsoft enterprise data stack (SQL Server, Azure SQL) and in SAP ASE, giving it a large, mature ecosystem. Microsoft and SAP maintain separate documentation. Evolution follows the SQL Server release cadence, which is regular and active. It is strongly vendor-locked to the Microsoft/SAP database world. The learning curve is moderate for SQL developers, and tooling (SSMS, Azure Data Studio) is good. Security is reasonable with parameterized queries, but string-built dynamic SQL and legacy cursor patterns carry injection and coupling risk. Its niche is transactional and analytical logic that must live inside SQL Server or SAP ASE.

This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 51/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 54/100
Core Coupling Analysis: SAS is a proprietary data-analysis and AI platform whose language has a genuinely distinctive feature: the strict separation between the DATA step (which retrieves and manipulates data) and PROC steps (which analyze and report on it) — a genuine separation of data-handling concerns from analysis concerns. Beyond that, SAS is weak on coupling separation: data is organized into datasets (tables of observations and variables) rather than general typed values, there is no general-purpose type system or modules beyond macros, and there are no structured exceptions. Macros (pieces of code or variables coded once and referenced for repetitive tasks) can create macro-expansion coupling. Platform & Ecosystem: SAS was the leading advanced-analytics platform for decades — the largest market-share holder in advanced analytics (35.4% in 2013) and widely used in finance, insurance, government, healthcare, and clinical trials (the FDA historically required NDA submissions in the SAS XPORT transport format, since largely superseded by CDISC standards). However, it faces strong competition from R and Python, which are cheaper and open source. SAS is proprietary and expensive (subscription-based), and the language has evolved slowly; SAS Viya (2016) modernized the architecture and added cloud and open-source interop (R, Python, Jupyter) without positioning as a replacement for SAS 9.4. The learning curve is steep, the DATA-step syntax is idiosyncratic, and the ecosystem is large but closed. It remains powerful for regulated statistical work but is increasingly a legacy choice.

title: PL/SQL (Oracle)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 46/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 61/100
Core Coupling Analysis: PL/SQL (Procedural Language for SQL) is Oracle’s procedural extension for SQL, modeled on Ada and Pascal. Its best coupling feature is the package, which separates a specification (the interface: types, variables, constants, exceptions, cursors, subprograms) from an optional body (the implementation), enabling encapsulation and function overloading. Blocks with DECLARE/BEGIN/EXCEPTION/END provide structured error handling, and user-defined and predefined exceptions make failure explicit. Its coupling weaknesses are those of its domain: everything is coupled to the Oracle database engine, variables default to NULL, and triggers create implicit coupling by firing automatically in response to data changes. Dynamic SQL (via EXECUTE IMMEDIATE or DBMS_SQL) couples code to string-built queries and carries injection risk. Package variables have session scope, which can create hidden shared state. It is not a general-purpose language; it only makes sense inside an Oracle database.
Platform & Ecosystem: PL/SQL is ubiquitous in Oracle enterprise systems and has been since Oracle 6 (stored procedures since 7), so the ecosystem and tooling are mature. It implements the ISO SQL/PSM standard and is also available in TimesTen and IBM Db2. Evolution is tied to Oracle’s release cadence. It is strongly coupled to Oracle and porting to other databases (e.g., SQL Server’s Transact-SQL) is non-trivial because of differences in features and in concurrency and locking models. The learning curve is moderate for developers who know SQL and a Pascal-like language. Security is reasonable with proper bind variables, but dynamic SQL is a classic SQL-injection surface.

title: Design
text:
Software design is the broad concern of how software is structured. Architecture is a part of design — the decisions that are hard to change — but not all design is architecture.
This section organizes software design into:

Architecture — the part of design concerned with module boundaries and system-level structure.
Languages — the design of, and analysis of, programming languages.
Principles — design principles and their analysis.

The change-management account of module structure that underlies the design analysis is published in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].




References

[1] Y. Loth, “The independent variation principle.” Zenodo, Jun. 2026. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.20794332.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
Onion architecture places a domain model at the centre and wraps it in rings. Around the model sit the application’s other layers; around those sit the infrastructure, the user interface, and the tests. One rule governs every dependency: it points inward. Code may depend on layers closer to the centre, and never on layers further out. The database is external; persistence is reached through interfaces the core defines and an implementation at the rim supplies [1].
Palermo presents onion openly as a named pattern — a set of object-oriented techniques and conventions gathered and named so that they can be communicated [1]. So the question is not whether onion admits to being a design. It does. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut? The argument below is self-contained for onion. The shared machinery — representation, the partition, the shape-versus-rule boundary — is developed on the hexagonal page.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Onion nests a domain model inside a centripetal stability ordering of rings.
The domain model is genuinely stable and the infrastructure volatile; the gradient is monotonic.
The gradient inverts (a volatile model) or is non-monotonic (a stability valley); the model’s state and its mapping are split.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
2 The claim
The domain model is the innermost ring, and Palermo says it “is only coupled to itself.” The next ring holds the interfaces the core needs — repository interfaces, for example — while their implementations live at the rim. The rim is “reserved for things that change often”: infrastructure, the user interface, tests. It is isolated from the core.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 3 Onion justifies the ring order by change frequency
text:
3 Onion justifies the ring order by change frequency
The rule that fixes the ring order is the inward dependency rule. Its justification, though, is stated in terms of change: isolating the volatile rim protects the core from churn. That is a claim about how often things change.
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) does not rank change drivers by frequency. Frequency orders work; it does not fix a boundary. A boundary is fixed by which change activates which elements, not by how often [2]. So onion’s stated axis — changes often versus changes rarely — is a proxy. It can coincide with the partition. It does not determine it.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as a domain model at the centre, a repository-interface ring around it, and infrastructure at the rim. Analysis names rules, entities, processes, events, decisions, responsibilities, and policies. The ring scheme is not among those forms. The rings appear when a designer lays out code; they are an object-oriented encoding. Palermo says so directly: the architecture is “unashamedly biased toward object-oriented programming, and it puts objects before all others.” That is an encoding choice, and the designer makes it. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 5 The domain model is not coupled only to itself
text:
5 The domain model is not coupled only to itself
The strongest of onion’s claims is that the domain model is coupled only to itself. That is a claim about the direction of reference: the model imports nothing from an outer layer. Onion exists to isolate change, so the coupling at issue here is change coupling. Under the framework’s reading, if recording a new domain fact is taken as one change driver covering the field, the column, and the wire field, then the model’s state and its mapping carry the same change-driver assignment.
Onion puts the model at the centre and its mapping at the rim. The ring boundary therefore runs through one Γ-equivalence class. It separates the entity type from its mapping and splits that class — a Unit Completeness failure. It is exactly the failure the model-at-the-centre claim is meant to prevent. The model is not quiescent: under the framework’s reading, it is coupled to the very mechanics the rings were meant to isolate.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 6 What onion embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What onion embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The inward dependency rule is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Onion’s blanket rule points every dependency inward, whether or not the domain orders them that way. Where they align, the rule adds no structure; where they do not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The rings are a claim about the cut. The domain-model kernel, the repository-interface ring, the domain-service and application-service division: none of these is in the analysis.

A representation is unavoidable: some structure must carry the knowledge. What is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A ring is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the ring groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if its boundary splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a ring that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality. Onion’s rings are that deviation. The repository interface is the clearest case: Palermo places it in the core because the model needs to be saved, but the need to persist is an infrastructure fact, and the interface that expresses it is a code artifact. The core does not gain knowledge from holding it; it gains a dependency on a shape the domain never named.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of onion, arrives at the partition and not at the rings. The rings are not a structure a developer arrives at on their own: the impulse to keep business rules out of the database is common, but the ring scheme is a taught pattern.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Onion fails wherever a ring straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the persisted entity, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s. When the encoding is read as knowledge, the chosen structure goes in as if the domain had asked for it, and the domain never did.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [2]. Judged by that standard, onion’s rings are correct where no class straddles them and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For a persisted entity, they are not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Onion Architecture
section: 9 When onion is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When onion is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [3]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So onion answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Onion does no harm only where its rings coincide with that decomposition. Where they do not, every change crosses a boundary the domain did not set: a class split across rings scatters one change, and a ring that groups non-equivalent elements couples what the domain keeps apart.
Two caveats bound the claim.

The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost. The partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states; the pure, disjoint change-driver case is unconditional [4]. Whether the metric matches real economic cost is an empirical question. Palermo’s advice — onion is “not appropriate for small websites” and suits “long-lived business applications” [1] — is a statement about where that cost matters. The placement result does not depend on it: Γ-equivalence is correct placement for every modelled concern, whatever the cost coefficients.
The theory does not discover the rule. It defines what cohesion is; identifying the domain conditions that matter and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [3]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.

Beneficial, here, means only that onion does no harm: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own; the partition does the work, and onion packages it. Outside the band, onion is harmful wherever its rings do not coincide with the partition.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties, each attached to a different object: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [3].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter the condition. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Onion can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in onion checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the ring diagram looks the same.
Onion is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
11 Verdict
Onion is a chosen encoding, and its rings are invented concepts wherever they do not coincide with the partition. It is not a domain-mandated decomposition.

Its rings embody the domain’s knowledge only where they coincide with the partition; elsewhere they invent structure the domain did not mandate.
Its “domain model coupled only to itself” claim is false for the persisted entity: under the framework’s reading, the state and its mapping are one class, and the ring boundary splits it.
Its organising heuristic — changes often versus changes rarely — is a frequency proxy, not the change-driver structure.
It does no harm only where its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful wherever they do not. Even in the good case, onion adds no decomposition value, and placement is not faithful embodiment.

When read as a prescription rather than read from the domain, onion supplies no domain knowledge and no domain-grounded reason to choose it.

title: Onion Architecture
text:
12 Summary

Onion directs all coupling toward a domain-model centre and rings the rest around it. Its stated axis is change frequency.
IVP does not rank change drivers by frequency; frequency orders work, not boundaries. The frequency axis is a proxy.
The rings — model kernel, repository-interface ring, service layers, infrastructure rim — appear in no analysis artifact. They are concepts the designer adds; Palermo presents them as a named pattern of conventions.
The domain model is not coupled only to itself: under the framework’s reading, a persisted entity’s state and mapping carry the same change-driver assignment, so the ring boundary splits one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Where the rings coincide with the partition, onion adds nothing; where they do not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: onion’s rings are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Onion does no harm only where its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where they do not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them, correct under all at once. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare hexagonal architecture, which reaches the same conclusion by a different route.

title: Architecture
text:
Architecture is the part of software design concerned with module boundaries and the decisions that are hard to change — the system’s skeleton. Architecture is a subset of design; not all design is architecture.
The change-management criterion for module boundaries that distinguishes architecture from lower-level design is developed in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1]. The criterion is the missing piece two design notions openly defer to. Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule, assessed as a purity-completeness pair per rule, so a cohesion judgment is only as definite as the rule behind it [2]. Coupling is access to a shared resource, and telling couplings a domain artifact mandates (essential) from the rest (accidental) needs a criterion grounded in the domain; without one, module boundaries are arbitrary [3]. The change-driver partition closes both gaps at once: grouping by the full change-driver set is the common refinement of the modularisation principles, so one partition answers to all of them together [2].

title: Architecture
text:
1 What architecture is
The usual answers describe the occupation, not the discipline. One says architecture is what architects do — an activity. Another says it is “the important stuff, whatever that is” [4] — a judgment, not a criterion. A third says it is the set of decisions that are hard to change — a cost correlate that misfires exactly where a criterion is needed. None of the three can say, for a concrete design question, whether the question is architectural at all.
The change criterion completes the significance answer instead of leaving it a shrug: “important” becomes definite once it is read as whatever materially shapes how the system varies under change. Significance is then a fact about the domain, not a consensus of experts.
One criterion does the classifying: derivability.

A question the design must answer is architectural exactly when the domain’s causal knowledge bears on the answer by restricting which answers the system may take.

The domain’s causal knowledge is the knowledge required to realize the system’s purpose within the obligations its governing artifacts impose — regulations, contracts, specifications, service-level commitments. Two separations carry the weight:

Domain obligations are facts about the domain. The architect has no authority over them; the architect’s derivation is a fallible estimate of them.
Machine and cost knowledge are not second sources of authority. They enter the derivation only through the obligations that depend on them: a latency SLA in the platform contract, not a taste for speed, forces the cache; a seven-year retention statute, not caution, forces the durable store.

The architecture of a system is then the set of its answers to architectural questions, together with their admissible sets. Given jointly satisfiable obligations, the criterion classifies each answer:

Derivable core — the obligations admit exactly one answer. The design transcribes it; no selection occurs, because a decision is a selection from two or more admissible answers, and a singleton leaves nothing to select.
Feasible region — the obligations admit several answers. Judgment operates here, and must be presented as judgment: reasoned, challengeable, never dressed up as necessity.
Provisional — the available knowledge does not settle the admissible set. The gap is a defect to repair, not a preference to push through quietly.
Infeasible — the obligations cannot be jointly satisfied. No realizable design exists, and the remedy is a governing act on the artifacts, not a design choice.

A payment system runs all four classes in one place. The acquiring contract requires settlement deduplication, and a seven-year tax statute makes that storage durable: derivable core, no design debate left. Confirmation by push or by polling admits several admissible answers: feasible region, and the choice is recorded as judgment. Whether capture must close within seven days is settled by no artifact at hand: provisional, a gap to repair. A new erasure duty within thirty days collides with the seven-year retention statute: infeasible, and resolved above the design when the statute prevails.
Checkability has a stated scope: the governing artifacts must be identifiable, the obligations expressed in them, and the knowledge required to realize the purpose within them available. Within that scope a third party can decide whether the derivation holds, given only the artifacts and the recorded material. Checkable does not mean true — a claim can be checkable and false — but it means the argument never rests on the architect’s private word.

title: Architecture
text:
2 The architect enables everyone else
Architecture is instrumental. It is a means to delivery, not an end in itself, and it is judged by whether it enables the delivery system around it to function. This is the central claim of the account:
Enablement. Every role the product’s obligations require — product managers, builders, testers, sponsors — must be able to do the job those obligations make necessary: with satisfying quality, in time, and in budget.
Three consequences follow:

Enablement is a property of the whole delivery system, and the architect is answerable for it even though many hands achieve it. Which roles are necessary is itself derived: a role is necessary exactly when some obligation makes its work necessary. Both errors are derivation defects — omitting a role some obligation requires leaves work that must be done with no one accountable for it; inventing a role no obligation supports smuggles a preference into the delivery system under the name of architecture.
The accountability is held by a single role. This is an organizational commitment, not something the criterion derives. The organization decides what fills the role — one individual architect, a team, or a committee whose members share the architecture tasks. Whoever fills it is answerable for the whole of enablement.
The duty is dischargeable. One accountability, four duties: derive (identify the causal domain knowledge and extract the design from it), document (express the one derivation so each role can act on it), validate (check the built system against the recorded derivation), and re-examine (re-derive when the knowledge moves).

Why the role must exist at all has a structural answer. Apply the change criterion recursively to the organisation itself: modules sit in deployment units, deployment units in organisational domains, and at each level the units below become elements with their own change-driver structure. A team that applies the criterion flawlessly inside its own modules is blind to the level where its whole module is one element among many. Cross-team and cross-system drivers therefore have no owner at the team level. The failure looks mundane. A module set one team owns is legitimate: all coordination is internal. The day a second team takes authority over half of it, nothing in the domain changes, but internal coordination silently becomes inter-team coordination — interface contracts, synchronised releases, shared pipeline ownership. No team can see the misalignment from inside. The role exists to hold what no team can see: a system whose change drivers cross team or system boundaries needs an architect — not a decision-maker, but the reader and steward of the drivers no single team can see.
The role account also corrects Fowler’s aphorism that an architect’s value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions made [4]. That metric can only describe what a good architect avoids. The value is three positive readings: identify the change drivers; decide when a hard constraint — security isolation, regulatory separation, deployment topology, a real-time budget — should dominate the change-cost axis; and choose the tools whose constructs let the domain knowledge be embodied faithfully. The rest is read off the domain, not decided.
Enablement is not the satisfaction of every local preference. A tester’s wish to bypass an audit trail is a local preference when the domain forces the trail; the correct answer is no, together with a way for the tester to do the real job — verifying behaviour — within the constraint. Only a blockage the architecture produced, or could have removed at a cost the domain permits, counts against the architecture.
Two tests make the claim operational rather than aspirational:

The documentation test. Documentation is one derivation expressed per audience, not a set of artifacts: milestones for product management, testable quality attributes for testers, contracts for builders, risk posture for the sponsor. Each role must be able to act on its view without interviewing the architect; under-documentation fails one way, and a view no required role consumes fails the other.
The validation test. When something fails, the process must be able to attribute the failure to the derivation and not only to the builders. A validation process that can only ever blame the builders is quality theater: it performs assurance while protecting the one thing that most needs to be challengeable.

The failure test turns the definition into three checkable predicates, each with an observable condition:

Blocking an artifact-derived job. A role cannot do the job its governing artifacts require because of a decision the causal knowledge does not admit.
Incoherent combinations. Every choice is admissible alone, but combinations fail — either behaviourally (no single behaviour of the system can exhibit two answers together, such as synchronous fraud review against a one-second latency SLA) or in delivery (a decision taken to satisfy one role defeats the required job of another, such as an hourly data-funnel rebuild that blocks the daily regression run).
Validation that attributes every failure to the builders. There is no recorded derivation to check the build against, or no step in the process that can blame the derivation.

Refusal follows the same pattern. The architect may refuse a demand that contradicts the derivable core, but only by showing why — citing the obligation the demand violates and the artifact that imposes it. An architect who cannot show why a demand violates the domain’s obligations has no authority to refuse it.
Re-examination closes the loop. The knowledge moves — an obligation is amended, a latency ceiling shifts, pricing changes — and every derivation built on it is in question. An architecture correctly derived from yesterday’s knowledge is today a derivation from a false premise, and it fails exactly as if it had been wrong from the start.

title: Architecture
text:
3 Architecture is derived, not designed
The account sharpens into a partition criterion, and the consequence is stark:

A decision is architectural exactly when its answer constrains the assignment of elements to modules — the partition of the system into modules — and therefore, wherever module and team boundaries align, which future change-work falls to which team. A decision the causal knowledge forces but that determines only itself — which database is named, which integer width is used — is derived but not architectural.
The class diagram is recovered, not designed. The classes, the coupling, the cohesion, and even the kind of relationship between two classes — parameter, association, or event — are transcribed from the domain’s temporal and identity semantics. Where the shape varies across developers, the variation traces to a convention the language underdetermines, not to a choice over the structure of knowledge.
Modularisation is derived too: the objective it serves is itself domain knowledge, read from the domain’s economics, and the cost-minimising partition is read off the forcing conditions. That the partition minimising change propagation minimises lifetime maintenance cost is a proved result, not a preference [5]; the optimal modularization is derivable from coupling [6], and the partition it produces is the change-driver partition [1] — the common refinement of the modularisation principles, so one decomposition answers to all of them at once [2].
Most apparent trade-offs dissolve once demands carry numbers and scopes. The irreducible remainder is resolved by a business commitment made above the system, not by the architect: the architect surfaces the conflict with its prices attached, and stops.

Within the design there is no choice: only the value choice above the system and the reading beneath it remain. The value choice has a number attached and is made above the design — committing to one card scheme’s fees over another’s, or accepting a 200 ms p99 to halve infrastructure cost. Everything else is arithmetic, and arithmetic does not have taste.

title: Architecture
text:
4 Styles assume; the domain decides
Read as hypotheses about which parts change for different reasons, the styles get a uniform diagnosis. Each style fixes a structural proxy — rings, layers, slices — and succeeds where the proxy tracks the domain’s actual variation. Where it does not, the style fails silently: nothing in the diagram tells you the assumption broke.
The shared prescription behind the core-protecting styles — that business logic can always be made independent of infrastructure — does not always hold. Achievability is a structural property of the domain. Where the domain’s drivers require infrastructure-level knowledge, no reformulation of the domain eliminates that knowledge, enforcing the style forces a falsified model, and abstraction that removes load-bearing drivers is domain substitution, not purification. A pricing module whose rounding rules a tax statute fixes shows the substitution: route the statute’s rounding into an infrastructure adapter, and the adapter now embodies domain knowledge wherever the diagram places it. What counts as infrastructure is relative, too — a payment processor is infrastructure to a client system, and a first-class, regulation-driven domain to its own operators. The practical test is driver completeness: after the abstraction, are all original drivers still represented and independently testable?
Clean Architecture decomposes into a partition criterion (group by ring role) plus a dependency-direction constraint. The partition criterion diverges from the optimal partition whenever ring role does not track the change drivers [1], and stability by ring position corrupts the stability ordering, because genuine stability is a property of an element’s governing authorities, not its ring membership. The conclusion is not to apply the rings more carefully, but to apply the change-driver partition directly and invert dependencies only where the domain grants substitutability.
Boundary ownership has its own grammar: who controls an interface specification, who implements it, and who uses it. Of the ownership configurations that grammar allows, three are stable — bilateral control, provider-driven control, shared governance; four degenerate to simpler forms; two are structurally contradictory.
Architecture Styles examines the styles one at a time: Hexagonal Architecture, Onion Architecture, Clean Architecture, Layered Architecture, and Vertical Slice Architecture. Each asks whether the style embodies the domain’s knowledge or invents structure the domain never mandated.

title: Architecture
section: 5 Splitting services trades a coupling space, it does not shrink one
text:
5 Splitting services trades a coupling space, it does not shrink one
The monolith-to-services split has a reputation for reducing coupling, and a habit of disappointing it. The analysis:

Coupling is access to a shared resource, and it does not depend on where the elements run [3]. A split therefore cannot remove coupling in general; what it does is replace one kind of coupling space with another.
The co-location family — shared mutable state, implicit initialisation order, cache and configuration bleed, concurrency, shared transactions — is unbounded, bespoke to each system, largely written nowhere, and therefore unmanageable.
The remote-deployment family a boundary installs is short, fixed, and manifest by construction: latency, availability and partial failure, serialisation and versioning, delivery and ordering, consistency, transport security, discovery, and boundary observability. It is handled largely by organisational discipline — timeouts, retries, idempotency, contract tests, service-level objectives — with a small named residue of genuine technical complexity, consistency above all.
Coupling grounded in what two sides share, not where they run, survives any seam. The coupling paper names it essential: a domain artifact — a statute, a contract, a standard — requires the elements to share the resource, so no deployment can remove it [3]. Where a seam strands such a genuinely-shared resource across the boundary, the split adds the fixed remote set on top of the surviving domain-imposed coupling [7]: the distributed monolith, which is not a botched decoupling but the predictable cost of a seam that ignores the shared-resource structure. The canonical case is two services and one database: the seam splits the code, but both sides still write the same orders table, so every schema change now crosses the very boundary the split was meant to remove.
Because one side’s coupling is invisible and never priced while the other’s is tangible and fully counted, the choice cannot rest on a cost estimate. It rests on the preconditions: whether a favourable seam exists, whether what crosses it is thin, and whether the organisation can bear the fixed remote set.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
Clean Architecture puts enterprise rules at the centre and rings the rest around them. The rings are Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks and Drivers. One rule governs every dependency: source-code dependencies point inward, and only inward. The centre holds the highest-level policy; the rim holds the mechanisms — the web, the database, the frameworks [1].
Martin presents Clean Architecture as a synthesis: it gathers the concentric-ring family — hexagonal, onion, and others — under one rule and one picture [1]. So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It does. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for onion architecture and hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Clean Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Clean nests a role partition (Entities, Use Cases, Adapters, Frameworks) inside a stability ordering: depend toward the stable core.
The domain has one capability, the core is genuinely stable, and providers are substitutable — role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability.
Role does not track the change driver (the use-case ring aggregates independent capabilities); ring position does not track real stability (a volatile domain core, a concrete-but-inert framework); or the client depends on a provider’s specifics.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
2 The claim
Clean draws four rings. At the centre sit Entities, the enterprise-wide business rules. Around them sit Use Cases, the application-specific rules. Around those sit Interface Adapters, which convert data between the use cases and the outside. At the rim sit Frameworks and Drivers: the web, the database, the devices. Martin’s rule is that source-code dependencies point only inward. An inner ring knows nothing of an outer one.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 3 Clean is a role partition plus a stability ordering
text:
3 Clean is a role partition plus a stability ordering
Clean is the composition of two ingredients. The first is a partition criterion: group every element into one of four rings by its role in the application flow. The second is a dependency-direction constraint: enforce the Stable Dependencies Principle across ring boundaries — depend toward the stable core.
The stability ordering rests on Martin’s metrics. Instability is I(P)=Ce(P)/(Ca(P)+Ce(P))I(P) = C_e(P) / (C_a(P) + C_e(P)), the ratio of efferent to total coupling: I=0I = 0 is maximally stable (many depend on it, it imports nothing); I=1I = 1 is maximally volatile. Abstractness is A(P)A(P), the fraction of abstract types. The Main Sequence A+I=1A + I = 1 is the optimal locus; the entity ring sits near I=0I = 0, the framework ring near I=1I = 1 [1].
The stability here is structural self-containment on the import graph, not actual change frequency. An element counts as “stable” because nothing imports force it to change, not because an external authority changes rarely. Clean’s axis therefore couples a role partition to a structural stability ordering, and asserts that ring position determines stability for every element, whatever actually governs it.
IVP groups by which change activates an element. Role and ring-position stability are proxies for that. They can coincide with the partition — in a domain where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability. They do not determine it [2].

title: Clean Architecture
section: 4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The rings are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks. Analysis names rules, entities, processes, events, decisions, responsibilities, and policies. “Entity” and “use case” are domain-near; the ring stratification is not. The rings appear when a designer lays out code; they are an encoding. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 5 Entities are not coupled only to themselves
text:
5 Entities are not coupled only to themselves
Clean’s strongest claim is that Entities — the centre — are the most stable rules, encapsulating the most general business rules, and that outer rings depend on them and never the reverse. That is a claim about the direction of reference. Clean exists to isolate change, so the coupling at issue here is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, if recording a new domain fact is taken as one change driver covering the field, the column, and the wire field, then an entity’s state and its mapping carry the same change-driver assignment. Clean puts the entity at the centre and its mapping in an outer ring. The ring boundary therefore runs through one Γ-equivalence class. It separates the entity type from its mapping and splits that class — a Unit Completeness failure. It is exactly the failure the entity-at-the-centre claim is meant to prevent. The entity is not quiescent: under the framework’s reading, it is coupled to the very mechanics the rings were meant to isolate.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 6 What Clean embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What Clean embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The Dependency Rule is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Clean’s blanket rule points every dependency inward, whether or not the domain orders them that way. Where they align, the rule adds no structure; where they do not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The rings are a claim about the cut. Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, Frameworks and Drivers: the stratification is not in the analysis.

A representation is unavoidable. What is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A ring is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the ring groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if its boundary splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a ring that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality. Clean’s rings are that deviation, most sharply in the Use Case and Interface Adapter rings: the split between “application rules” and “adapters” is a code distinction the domain does not name.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of Clean, arrives at the partition and not at the rings. The rings are not a structure a developer arrives at on their own: the impulse to keep business rules out of the database is common, but the four-ring scheme is a taught pattern.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Clean fails wherever a ring straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the persisted entity, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [2]. Judged by that standard, Clean’s rings are correct where no class straddles them and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For a persisted entity, they are not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Clean Architecture
section: 9 When Clean is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When Clean is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [3]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So Clean answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Clean does no harm only where its rings coincide with that decomposition — that is, where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability. That is the single-capability, substitutable-provider domain Clean was calibrated against: one capability, a genuinely stable core, genuinely interchangeable providers. There, role happens to track the change driver and ring position happens to track stability.
Outside that domain, Clean is harmful in three ways. Role does not track the change driver: the use-case ring aggregates independent capabilities, and every capability’s changes propagate through it. Ring position does not track real stability: a domain core that is volatile, or a framework that is concrete but inert, inverts or flattens the assumed gradient, and the Dependency Rule then points dependencies toward the most volatile elements. And the inversion is unconditional: where the client’s correctness depends on a provider’s specifics, the abstraction the pattern demands is fabricated — it claims a substitutability the domain does not grant.
Two caveats bound the claim. The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost: the partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states, unconditional only in the pure, disjoint change-driver case [4]; whether the metric matches real economic cost is empirical. And the theory does not discover the rule: identifying the domain conditions and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [3]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.
Beneficial, here, means only that Clean does no harm: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own. Outside the band, Clean is harmful wherever its rings do not coincide with the partition.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [3].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Clean can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in Clean checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the ring diagram looks the same.
Clean is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its rings coincide with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
11 Verdict
Clean Architecture is a chosen encoding, and its rings are invented concepts wherever they do not coincide with the partition. It is not a domain-mandated decomposition.

Its rings embody the domain’s knowledge only where they coincide with the partition — the single-capability, substitutable-provider case; elsewhere they invent structure the domain did not mandate.
Its stability ordering is structural self-containment, not real stability: ring position is asserted to determine stability for every element, whatever actually governs it.
Its entity-at-the-centre claim is false for the persisted entity: under the framework’s reading, the state and its mapping are one class, and the ring boundary splits it.
It does no harm only where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability; it is harmful wherever they do not. Even in the good case, Clean adds no decomposition value, and placement is not faithful embodiment.

When read as a prescription rather than read from the domain, Clean supplies no domain knowledge and no domain-grounded reason to choose it.

title: Clean Architecture
text:
12 Summary

Clean Architecture rings Entities, Use Cases, Interface Adapters, and Frameworks around a centre, with all dependencies pointing inward. It is a role partition plus a stability ordering.
The stability ordering uses Martin’s metrics — instability, abstractness, the Main Sequence — which measure structural self-containment on the import graph, not real change frequency.
The rings — entity, use-case, adapter, framework — appear in no analysis artifact; the use-case/adapter split is a code distinction the domain does not name.
Entities are not coupled only to themselves: under the framework’s reading, a persisted entity’s state and mapping carry the same change-driver assignment, so the ring boundary splits one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Clean does no harm only where its rings coincide with the partition — where role tracks the change driver and ring position tracks real stability; it is harmful where they do not.
The strongest defensible claim: Clean’s rings are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare onion architecture and hexagonal architecture, which reach the same conclusion by different routes.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Almost every design pattern/principle can be used as a completeness-check on domain knowledge.
When you’re reaching for a pattern, ask “does the domain knowledge mandate the coupling this pattern would add or remove?” If you can’t answer, you’ve found a knowledge gap. If you can, the knowledge prescribes the structure directly — the pattern adds nothing the domain hadn’t already decided.
Each family of patterns sharpens that question in its own way. Where a family frames it differently, its framing opens above that family’s posts.
Pick a post on the left. It opens on the right.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Abstract Factory Pattern

GoF Intent: “Provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The set of concrete types that must vary together (the “product family”) is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when you’re in context X, you use implementations A₁, B₁, C₁; in context Y, you use A₂, B₂, C₂” — and that these groupings are cohesive units in the domain (e.g., a regulatory regime, a hardware platform, a deployment tier) — then an Abstract Factory is just embodying that knowledge. The factory interface is the domain’s own abstraction; the concrete factories are its real partitions.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates product-family coherence but the language offers no native construct to express “these N types co-vary.” The Abstract Factory is a technical artifact that closes the gap — it prevents each client from individually selecting concrete types, which would scatter the family-binding knowledge across the system and create accidental coupling (every client must know which concrete A goes with which concrete B).








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of product families. The concrete types vary independently. Forcing them into an Abstract Factory imposes a grouping the domain doesn’t recognize — it bundles change-drivers that are actually independent, creating a single point of modification for unrelated changes. That’s the cohesion-reducing move.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the concrete-type groupings as a thing?

If yes → applicable. The Abstract Factory is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code inventing knowledge the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#GoF #EIP #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #Domain #Knowledge #DesignPrinciples #Java #C# #SoftwareArchitecture #OOP #FP



References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Strategy Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The existence of multiple algorithms for the same operation is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “this operation admits variants A, B, C, and there is a domain rule that selects among them,” then Strategy is just embodying that knowledge. The strategy interface is the domain’s own abstraction (the what); the concrete strategies are its real alternatives (the how).






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates algorithmic substitutability — it recognizes that the operation meaningfully differs across contexts, and a domain rule dictates which variant applies. The Strategy pattern closes the gap: it prevents each caller from embedding variant-selection logic inline, which would scatter the selection rule across the system and create accidental coupling (every caller must re-encode which variant to use under which conditions). The pattern collects each variant behind a shared interface; the selection rule lives wherever the strategy reference is assigned.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no notion of multiple algorithms for this operation. The “variants” are a decomposition artifact, not a domain partition — the developer split one algorithm into pieces for readability or reuse and wrapped them in a strategy interface as organizational glue. This imposes a grouping the domain doesn’t recognize: it bundles what the domain treats as one thing into an interface-plus-implementations structure, adding ceremony that signals a richness of variation that isn’t there. If the variants also pull in different data dependencies, Strategy scatters data-acquisition logic across implementations that must each independently discover their inputs.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize multiple algorithms for this operation as a real thing?

If yes → applicable. Strategy is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code inventing variation the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.





References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Observer Pattern

GoF Intent: “Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.” [1]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that “a change in A constitutes a domain event that B, C, and D must know about” is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that certain state transitions are meaningful events to other entities — that the event is a first-class domain concept — then Observer is just embodying that knowledge. The subject interface is the domain’s own event source; the observer interface is the domain’s own event consumer.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain state changes constitute events with multiple consumers, and the set of consumers is open-ended. Observer closes the gap — it prevents the event source from encoding the full list of consumers and their reaction logic inline, which would bundle every downstream concern into a single class and couple the event source to each consumer’s change-drivers.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “event” is not a domain event — nothing in the domain recognizes the state transition as meaningful in itself. B must recompute when A changes not because the domain treats A’s transition as an event, but because the developer chose to cache or denormalize. Observer used for technical consistency (UI model-view synchronization, the GoF’s canonical example) is valid engineering. The cohesion risk is when notification cascades for technical reasons (cache invalidation, denormalization-update chains) are presented as domain event propagation, inventing event semantics the domain model never had.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain model this state transition as an event even if the system weren’t software?

If yes → applicable. Observer is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s the code manufacturing events the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

References
[1] E. Gamma, R. Helm, R. Johnson, and J. Vlissides, Design patterns: Elements of reusable object-oriented software. Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Dispose Pattern

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a resource has a bounded lifetime — that acquiring it and releasing it are two ends of a single domain transaction — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “this resource must be acquired before use and released after, and the interval between acquisition and release is a meaningful domain scope (a session, a connection, a lock window),” then Dispose is just embodying that knowledge. The disposal interface is the domain’s own “bounded lifetime” contract; the using block is the domain’s own scoping rule made mechanical.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a resource has a deterministic end-of-life tied to a domain scope. Dispose closes the gap — it prevents each caller from manually pairing acquire and release calls, which would scatter the lifetime knowledge across the system. Every call site would need to know both the acquisition protocol and the release protocol, coupling unrelated code to resource lifecycle details it shouldn’t own.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “resource” is not a domain resource — it’s a memory-management artifact. The developer wraps a plain object in IDisposable because the GC won’t finalize it soon enough, not because the domain mandates a bounded lifetime. Dispose here addresses a runtime behavior, not domain knowledge. Infrastructure resources — file handles, database connections, network sockets — have bounded lifetimes by OS nature, and Dispose is correct for them even when the domain is silent. The inapplicable case: domain objects with no resource semantics beyond memory, where disposal introduces lifecycle coupling the domain never defined.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain model this resource as having a defined end-of-life — or is the resource inherently finite by the nature of the computing environment?

If yes → applicable. Dispose catches up to domain knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. But the resource is infrastructure (files, sockets, connections) or the domain is resource-constrained (embedded/real-time), it remains valid — the bounded lifetime comes from the environment. If purely a GC workaround, the pattern adds lifecycle coupling the domain didn’t require.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.
