[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Recipient List Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message to a list of dynamically specified recipients?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message has a domain-determined list of recipients — where the list itself is a domain artifact, not a configuration file — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a customs declaration must go to the importing country’s customs authority, the exporting country’s customs authority, the carrier, and the importer of record; a trade confirmation goes to both counterparties’ settlement desks,” then Recipient List is just embodying that knowledge. The list of recipients is the domain’s own distribution rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a single message be delivered to a specific, domain-determined set of recipients — and those recipients are each domain actors, not technical mirroring targets. Recipient List closes the gap: it isolates the distribution logic so the sender doesn’t embed a hardcoded list of downstream systems, which would couple the sender to the topology of the integration landscape. Without it, adding a new regulatory recipient means modifying the sender’s code — making the sender change with the regulatory environment even though its domain logic (produce the trade confirmation) hasn’t changed.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The recipient list is an availability tactic — send to primary and backup instances, or fan-out to multiple replicas. The domain doesn’t recognize “instance 1” and “instance 2” as distinct recipients; it recognizes one recipient (the order-processing system) — the fact that it runs on two machines is an implementation detail. Recipient List here masks infrastructure redundancy as domain distribution, creating coupling between the sender and deployment topology. A domain expert would say “just send it to order-processing — how many machines that runs on is not my concern.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert, given only knowledge of the business process, produce the same list of recipients without knowing how the system is deployed?

If yes → applicable. Recipient List is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s deployment topology leaking into domain logic.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #RecipientList #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Splitter Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can we process a message if it contains multiple elements, each of which may have to be processed in a different way?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a composite message is domain-recognized as containing independently processable parts, and that the decomposition rule is a domain rule, is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an insurance claim package contains a claim form, a police report, medical records, and repair estimates — each processed by a different team,” then Splitter is just embodying that knowledge. The decomposition rule is the domain’s own partitioning; each sub-message is a domain-recognized unit of work.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a composite message be decomposed into independent parts that travel different paths — and the decomposition corresponds to a domain-recognized partition. Splitter closes the gap: it prevents each downstream processor from re-extracting its own piece, which would couple each processor to the composite message format and scatter extraction logic across the system. Without it, the medical-records processor must know how to locate its section within the full claim package — structure knowledge that belongs in one place (the splitter), not in every downstream handler.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The composite message is a technical envelope — a batch of messages bundled for transport efficiency — and the domain sees the individual messages as the real units of work that were always separate. Splitter here just unwraps a transport artifact. Worse: if the original messages were produced independently at different times, splitting them doesn’t re-establish their original arrival order or context, and a later aggregator may produce results that arrived in a different sequence than they were produced.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the composite as a single thing that contains multiple independently meaningful things — like an “order” containing “line items” — rather than as a bunch of messages in a box?

If yes → applicable. Splitter is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s unwrapping a transport artifact and calling it domain decomposition.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #Splitter #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Aggregator Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we combine the results of individual, but related messages so that they can be processed as a whole?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that multiple independent messages together form a domain-recognized whole — and that the domain specifies when the whole is complete — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a trade is complete only when we have both the execution report from the exchange and the allocation from the trader; a purchase order is fully processed when all its line items have been fulfilled from their respective warehouses,” then Aggregator is just embodying that knowledge. The completion condition is the domain’s own completeness rule; the aggregated result is the domain’s own composite state.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a result is the composition of multiple independent sub-results — and the domain itself defines when “enough sub-results have arrived” (by count, by timeout, by content, by domain predicate). Aggregator closes the gap: it prevents each downstream consumer from tracking partial state and re-implementing the completion check, which would scatter the aggregation logic across every consumer. Without it, the trade-settlement system must know when both the execution report and the allocation have arrived — knowledge that belongs at the aggregation point, not at every settlement subsystem.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “aggregation” is a technical re-assembly of parts that were split for transport — the splitter split by count, the aggregator reassembles by count, with no domain knowledge involved. The completion condition is “got all three pieces” rather than a domain predicate like “we have both the execution report and the allocation.” Aggregator here becomes a stateless reassembly mechanism that adds latency and a stateful waiting point for no domain reason.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain define the completeness condition — and would a domain expert state it in domain terms (“we need both the execution report and the allocation”) rather than as a count (“all three parts arrived”)?

If yes → applicable. Aggregator is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s re-gluing what was unnecessarily split.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #Aggregator #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Scatter-Gather Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do you maintain the overall message flow when a message needs to be sent to multiple recipients, each of which may send a reply?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a single request requires answers from multiple domain sources, and that the best answer is a domain-defined composition of those answers, is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “to price a shipment, you need quotes from carrier A, carrier B, and carrier C, then you select the lowest; to approve a loan, you need a credit-score check, an income-verification check, and a fraud check — all must pass,” then Scatter-Gather is just embodying that knowledge. The recipients are the domain’s own information sources; the aggregation rule (lowest, all-pass, majority) is the domain’s own decision procedure.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a fan-out to multiple domain actors whose results must be combined by a domain rule — and the rule itself (not just the data) is domain knowledge. Scatter-Gather closes the gap: it prevents the requester from invoking each source sequentially, collecting results, and combining them inline — which would couple the requester to the list of sources, their invocation patterns, and the combination rule. Without it, adding a fourth carrier means modifying the pricing module’s internal loop.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “scatter” is a technical fan-out for performance — send the same query to all three replicas and take the fastest response. The domain doesn’t recognize replica voting; it recognizes one source (the product catalog), and the fact that it has copies is irrelevant. Scatter-Gather here masks a latency-hedge as a domain composition, introducing a gather step whose “aggregation rule” is “first one back” — a rule with no domain meaning. A domain expert would say “you’re asking the same question to three copies of the same book and taking whichever page turns first.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert, asked “how do you decide the answer?” produce the same aggregation rule that the Scatter-Gather uses — without mentioning system architecture?

If yes → applicable. Scatter-Gather is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a race condition dressed as a decision procedure.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #ScatterGather #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Routing Slip Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message consecutively through a series of processing steps when the sequence of steps is not known at design-time and may vary for each message?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message must visit a sequence of processors, and that the sequence itself is a domain process that changes based on domain rules, is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a purchase order above $10,000 goes: budget check → compliance review → director approval → procurement; a purchase order below $10,000 goes: compliance review → procurement — and for international orders, add export-control review after compliance,” then Routing Slip is just embodying that knowledge. The slip is the domain’s own process definition; each step is a domain actor in a domain sequence.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a variable multi-step process whose steps are domain operations — and the step sequence depends on domain conditions (order value, jurisdiction, product category). Routing Slip closes the gap: it prevents the process logic from being embedded in a central process manager that must know every step for every variation, which would couple all process variants together. Without it, the process manager becomes a god object that grows with every regulatory change.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The routing slip encodes a technical pipeline, not a domain process: “validate the message, transform the format, enrich with reference data, persist, notify.” The domain doesn’t recognize these as distinct business steps — it sees “process the order.” Routing Slip here wraps a technical ETL pipeline in the vocabulary of a business process, adding domain-coded step names (compliance, approval) to steps that are really validation, transformation, and persistence.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert, given a specific scenario (e.g., “an international order above $10,000”), list the steps in the correct sequence without consulting anyone technical?

If yes → applicable. Routing Slip is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The “process” is a technical pipeline with domain window-dressing.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #RoutingSlip #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Process Manager Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we route a message through multiple processing steps when the required steps may not be known at design-time and may not be sequential?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a long-running multi-step process has a domain-defined state machine — where states, transitions, and compensating actions are all domain concepts — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a trade lifecycle is: initiated → allocated → affirmed → confirmed → settled; an insurance claim lifecycle is: filed → assessed → approved/rejected → paid; and each state transition has domain preconditions and domain rollback procedures,” then Process Manager embodies that knowledge. The state machine is the domain’s own lifecycle; each transition is a domain event; compensating actions are the domain’s own reversal procedures.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a long-running process whose intermediate states are domain-recognized states — and the domain itself specifies what can happen from each state and what undoes a failed transition. Process Manager closes the gap: prevents the process logic from being scattered across the message handlers that implement each step, where each handler must independently decide whether the step is valid given the current state and what to do if it fails.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “process” is a saga — a technical transaction-coordination mechanism that chains service calls with compensating actions to simulate distributed atomicity. The domain doesn’t recognize compensating actions like “refund the payment” as a business process; it recognizes “the payment was refunded” as an independent event. Process Manager here becomes a distributed-transaction coordinator that hides failure-handling code behind state-machine syntax. A domain expert would say “the payment shouldn’t have been taken in the first place if the rest of the process couldn’t complete — fix the order of operations.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a name for each intermediate state, and can a domain expert draw the state machine from memory — states, transitions, and what goes wrong at each transition — using only business vocabulary?

If yes → applicable. Process Manager is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a distributed-transaction coordinator wearing a state-machine costume.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Message Broker Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can you decouple the destination of a message from the sender and maintain central control over the flow of messages?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the systems in a domain are decoupled — that system A should not know about system B, that the topology is a domain property not a deployment detail — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the order-entry system produces orders; the warehouse system consumes orders; the revenue-recognition system consumes fulfilled orders — and none of them should know about each other because they’re separate bounded contexts with different ownership and release cadences,” then Message Broker embodies that knowledge. The broker is the domain’s decentralized hub; the channels are the domain’s communication paths.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that components communicate without direct knowledge of each other — because they evolve independently, are owned by different teams, or sit in different bounded contexts. Message Broker closes the gap: prevents each producer from maintaining a registry of consumers and each consumer from knowing the producer’s endpoint, which would couple the entire ecosystem together. Without it, changing the warehouse system’s endpoint means modifying the order-entry system — coupling two systems that the domain says should be independent.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The systems are in the same bounded context and the “decoupling” is architectural dogma — “we always put a broker between things” — when no external constraint mandates it. A broker between services sharing the same team, repository, domain model, and release cadence turns a function call into a message round-trip with serialization and new failure modes. The knowledge gap is adopting a decoupling structure without a constraint that demands decoupling.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize the two sides of the broker as genuinely separate things — different bounded contexts, different owners, different evolution cadences — or are they one logical system that you split across two services?

If yes → applicable. Message Broker is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s adding a network boundary where the domain already had a module boundary.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Content Enricher Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do we communicate with another system if the message originator does not have all the required data items available?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message arrives with incomplete information and that the missing information has a domain-designated source is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “an order message carries a customer ID, but the warehouse needs the shipping address — which is owned by the customer profile service,” then Content Enricher is just embodying that knowledge. The missing field is domain information that belongs to a different domain authority; the enricher is the domain’s own information-completion step.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain information belongs to a specific domain authority — and the downstream consumer legitimately needs that information but shouldn’t own the authority to produce it. Content Enricher closes the gap: it prevents the consumer from calling the authority directly, which would couple the consumer to the authority’s interface and create a runtime dependency that the domain didn’t intend. Without it, the warehouse system must know how to call the customer profile service — coupling the warehouse to customer-profile concerns, when its domain job is “ship to this address,” not “look up addresses.”








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “missing” information is not missing from a domain perspective — the downstream consumer doesn’t need it, but the developer thinks it’s “nice to have” or is preemptively enriching for a future use case. Or the information belongs to the producer and should have been in the original message — the producer was lazy and Content Enricher is doing the producer’s job post hoc. A domain expert would say “if orders always ship to the customer’s default address, why doesn’t the order-entry system put the address on the order to begin with?”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the missing piece of information belong to a different domain authority than the producer — and does the consumer legitimately need it to do its job?

If yes → applicable. Content Enricher is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s either gold-plating or compensating for a producer that skimped on its domain responsibility.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Content Filter Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do you simplify dealing with a large message, when you are interested only in a few data items?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a downstream component should receive only a subset of the fields in a message — and that the subset is defined by the component’s domain responsibility, not by technical parsimony — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the compliance-audit system only needs the trade ID, counterparty, and amount — not the full trade message with settlement instructions, broker details, and execution venue; the customer notification system only needs the order number, status, and tracking link — not the internal warehouse-routing fields,” then Content Filter embodies that knowledge. The field subset is the consumer’s domain interface; the dropped fields are information the consumer has no domain authority to see.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a downstream component’s interface is a proper subset of the upstream message for domain scope, regulation, or bounded-context boundary reasons. Content Filter closes the gap: prevents the consumer from receiving fields it shouldn’t know about, which would couple the consumer to upstream message schemas it has no domain interest in.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The filter is adopted without a constraint that mandates which fields to drop — “we strip the big fields to fit the consumer’s buffer” — when no external condition dictates the subset. Buffer size is a genuine constraint, but it tells you how many bytes to drop, not which fields to drop. When the filter is chosen by byte count rather than by constraint-driven relevance, the filter predicate changes with buffer sizes — coupling integration logic to a metric that doesn’t identify the fields.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you justify each dropped field with a domain reason — “the consumer has no authority to see this,” “this field belongs to a different bounded context,” “this field is not in the consumer’s ubiquitous language”?

If yes → applicable. Content Filter is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (regulation, authority boundary, bounded-context scope) selects the field subset.
If no → inapplicable. You’re trimming fields without a constraint that identifies which ones to drop.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Normalizer Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do you process messages that are semantically equivalent, but arrive in a different format?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Multiple systems expressing the same domain concept in different formats, with a canonical representation as the domain’s own definition, is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “system A represents currency as USD, system B as 840, system C as $ — but the domain recognizes ISO 4217 alpha codes as authoritative,” then Normalizer embodies that knowledge. The canonical format is the domain’s own type; the conversion rules are the domain’s own translation from local dialects to the canonical form.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the same concept is expressed in multiple formats across systems — and the domain itself has chosen a canonical representation (from a standard, a regulation, or a domain agreement). Normalizer closes the gap: prevents each consumer from implementing N format conversions, which would scatter translation logic across every downstream system and couple each consumer to every upstream format variant. Without it, adding a fourth system that represents currency as “US Dollars” means modifying every consumer to handle the new variant — even though the consumer’s domain concern is “process the amount,” not “parse currency codes.”








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “canonical” format is a team preference — “I like YYYY-MM-DD, so I’ll convert everything to YYYY-MM-DD” — when no external constraint (ISO standard, regulatory mandate, industry convention) prescribes the canonical form. If all three source systems already agree on MM/DD/YYYY and no standard requires otherwise, normalization adds translation steps without a constraint demanding them. When an ISO standard or regulatory mandate IS the constraint, the normalizer is the structure that constraint prescribes.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the canonical format drawn from a domain authority (ISO standard, regulatory mandate, industry agreement) rather than from a team’s local preference?

If yes → applicable. Normalizer is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (ISO standard, regulatory mandate, industry agreement) prescribes the canonical form.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a preference layer without a constraint to ground the canonical choice.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Canonical Data Model Pattern
text:
Case study: Canonical Data Model Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can you minimize dependencies when integrating applications that use different data formats?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an enterprise has a shared vocabulary for a concept that transcends any single system — and that this vocabulary is maintained as a domain artifact by domain governance, not by individual development teams — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a Customer has a stable definition across order-entry, billing, support, and marketing — though each system uses a different subset of Customer attributes,” then Canonical Data Model embodies that knowledge. The CDM is the domain’s own enterprise-wide type system; message transformations are mappings from local vocabularies to the shared vocabulary.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a shared concept that crosses bounded contexts — maintained by domain governance. Canonical Data Model closes the gap: prevents each pair of systems from defining point-to-point translations, which grows an N×N translation mesh where every system must know every other system’s format.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The CDM is a developer-driven abstraction — an attempt to unify concepts that the domain keeps distinct. “We’ll model everything as a generic Entity with properties” or “we’ll create one uber-Customer that satisfies every system.” This forces reconcilable-but-different concepts into one model: the billing system’s Customer (which cares about payment methods) and the support system’s Customer (which cares about ticket history) are forced into a single type with optional fields for both. The CDM becomes a lowest-common-denominator that satisfies no one, or a superset that burdens every system with fields it doesn’t recognize. A domain expert would say “billing-Customer and support-Customer are different things — why pretend they’re the same type?”








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the canonical model maintained by a domain-governance function (data-governance board, enterprise architecture, industry consortium) — and does each concept in the model map to a concept that domain experts across systems recognize as “the same thing”?

If yes → applicable. Canonical Data Model is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a forced unification of concepts the domain keeps separate.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Claim Check Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can we reduce the data volume of message sent across the system without sacrificing information content?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message carries a reference to bulk data rather than the data itself — and that the reference system is the domain’s own data store, not a workaround for messaging infrastructure — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the order message carries an order ID, and the full order detail (line items, pricing, tax calculation) is retrievable from the order-management system; the claim message carries a claim number, and the supporting documents (police report, photos, estimates) live in the document-management system,” then Claim Check embodies that knowledge. The claim-check key is the domain’s own identifier; the data store is the domain’s own system of record; the retrieval step is the domain’s own information-access pattern.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the bulk data belongs to a system of record — and the message carries the identifier because the downstream consumer should fetch the data from the authoritative source, not receive a potentially stale copy. Claim Check closes the gap: it prevents the messaging infrastructure from becoming a data-replication mechanism, where every message carries a full snapshot that drifts from the source.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The claim check is adopted without a constraint that mandates it — “we always store large payloads externally” — when no external condition (broker limit, data-authority boundary, message-size regulation) forces the indirection. The structure is a pattern-choice, not a constraint-response: the system adds a retrieval step and external storage dependency with no forcing condition. When the constraint does exist, Claim Check is the constraint-driven structure.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the referenced data belong to a different system of record than the one that produced the message — and would the consumer fetch it from that system even if the message could carry it inline?

If yes → applicable. Claim Check is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (data authority, broker limit, regulation) mandates the indirection.
If no → inapplicable. You’re adding a retrieval step your domain doesn’t need.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Command Message Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can messaging be used to invoke a procedure in another application?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message represents an instruction — “do this” — is a message-semantics choice with domain consequences. If your domain model already crystallizes that “do X” and “X happened” are distinct domain actions — the domain recognizes that commands can be rejected and events record what already occurred — then Command Message is just embodying that knowledge. The command is the domain’s own imperative; the command’s receiver is the domain’s own designated executor; the command’s validation rules are the domain’s own preconditions.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain interactions are instructions directed at a specific actor — and the domain itself distinguishes “do X” from “X happened.” Command Message closes the gap: it prevents commands from being conflated with events. Without it, a “CustomerUpdated” message might be a command (please update the customer) or an event (the customer was updated) — and consumers must guess. The difference is fundamental: a command can be rejected; an event cannot. Conflating them loses the rejection semantics.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “command” is really an event with a bossy name — “PlaceOrder” is just a past-tense event (“OrderPlaced”) that someone named in the imperative because they prefer the grammar. The domain doesn’t distinguish commands from events; it only has notifications. Command Message here introduces false intent semantics: a “command” that cannot be rejected, targets an implicit receiver, and carries no acknowledgment mechanism is not a command — it’s an event with an imperative name. A domain expert would say “whether you call it ‘PlaceOrder’ or ‘OrderPlaced,’ the order gets placed — the verb tense doesn’t change the behavior.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize rejection of this message as a meaningful outcome — “no, I will not do this” — and does the domain specify what happens after rejection?

If yes → applicable. Command Message is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s an event with a commanding tone.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #CommandMessage #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Document Message Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can messaging be used to transfer data between applications?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message carries a self-contained unit of data that the receiver interprets — where the meaning is in the data, not in the sending — is a message-intent choice with domain consequences. If your domain model crystallizes that “a purchase order is a document — it carries the order details, and the receiving system decides what to do with it,” then Document Message embodies that knowledge. The document is the domain’s own information unit; the receiver’s autonomy in interpreting it is the domain’s own separation of concerns between sender and receiver.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that data units are self-describing and that the receiver has domain autonomy in how it processes them — the sender produces a document, but does not prescribe the processing logic. Document Message closes the gap: it prevents the sender from embedding processing instructions (like a command) in what should be a data unit, which would couple the receiver’s behavior to the sender’s intent. Without it, every sender also becomes a process designer — embedding “and then do this with it” in the message — which scatters processing logic across the senders rather than keeping it where it belongs (in the receiver’s domain).








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “document” is really a command in data clothing — “here is the order, and by the way, you must process it within 24 hours because the SLA field says so.” The domain distinguishes between the data (the order) and the instruction (process it). Conflating them puts processing instructions in the document body, coupling the receiver to the sender’s preferred processing rules — a coupling the domain separates. A domain expert would say “the order says what was ordered; the SLA is a separate agreement with the fulfillment team — don’t put the SLA on the order.”








TipThe faithfulness test



If you gave this message to two different domain actors, would they each process it differently based on their own domain rules — and would both interpretations be valid?

If yes → applicable. Document Message is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. You’re sending a command and calling it a document.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Event Message Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can messaging be used to transmit events from one application to another?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that something happened — and that the system boundary determines whether a message is a fact or an instruction — is domain knowledge when the domain itself distinguishes the two. If your domain model crystallizes that “‘OrderPlaced’ is an event — it records that an order was created; no receiver can reject an event, because it already happened,” then Event Message embodies that knowledge. The event is the domain’s own fact; the event’s immutability is the domain’s own recognition that the past cannot be changed.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain information is a record of what happened — a fact that downstream actors can react to but not reject. Event Message closes the gap: prevents events from being confused with commands, which would allow a receiver to “reject” something that already happened — creating a split reality where the upstream system recorded the event as having occurred but the downstream system refused to acknowledge it. Without it, the system drifts into inconsistency: the order was placed according to order-entry, but the warehouse never saw it because the “event” was rejected. An event cannot be rejected; it can only be ignored or mishandled — and the domain must decide which is acceptable.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “event” is really a command with a past-tense name — “CustomerUpdated” as a polite way to say “update the customer.” The domain distinguishes “the customer was updated” (event) from “please update the customer” (command). Calling a command an event hides the fact that the receiver has agency: it can reject the update. Event Message here creates a false sense of inevitability — “CustomerUpdated” implies the update happened, but the receiving system may disagree. A domain expert would say “don’t tell me the customer was updated if you’re asking me to update them — those are different things.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat this message as an established fact — something that cannot be refused because it already happened?

If yes → applicable. Event Message is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. You’ve named a command as an event.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #EventMessage #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Cohesion

[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Request-Reply Pattern

EIP Intent: “When an application sends a message, how can it get a response from the receiver?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a message requires a response — and that the domain specifies what the response must contain and when it must arrive — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “when a payment gateway is asked to authorize a transaction, it must respond with an approval code or a decline reason within 30 seconds; when a pricing engine is queried for a quote, it must respond with a price or an error before the caller times out,” then Request-Reply is just embodying that knowledge. The request is the domain’s own query; the reply is the domain’s own answer; the timeout is the domain’s own SLA.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a query requires a timely answer — and the answer is domain information that the caller genuinely needs to proceed. Request-Reply closes the gap: it prevents the caller from assuming a fire-and-forget pattern when the domain demands acknowledgment, or from hand-rolling correlation logic when the constraint (a domain SLA) mandates a request-reply channel. Without it, the caller sends a request and waits — but the waiting logic is ad-hoc, the timeout is arbitrary, and the correlation is hand-rolled.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain does not require a response — the caller can proceed without it, or the reply is informational only. Request-Reply here introduces blocking where the domain tolerates asynchrony: every request waits for a reply, turning an asynchronous domain process into one that depends on a timely response. Worse, when the reply fails to arrive (timeout, network partition), the caller must decide whether to retry — and if the original request was processed but the reply was lost, retrying creates a duplicate. A domain expert would say “I don’t need to wait for the answer — just let me know when it’s ready.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the caller genuinely need the response to proceed with its domain work — where not receiving a response is a domain failure, not just an annoyance?

If yes → applicable. Request-Reply is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. You’re adding a blocking dependency where the domain tolerates asynchrony.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #RequestReply #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Correlation Identifier Pattern

EIP Intent: “How does a requestor that has received a reply know which request this is the reply for?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that independent messages belong to the same domain entity — and that the domain itself defines the entity by which messages are grouped — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “an OrderCreated, an OrderShipped, and an OrderDelivered all belong to the same order, identified by the order ID,” then Correlation Identifier embodies that knowledge. The correlation ID is the domain’s own entity identifier; the messages that share it are the domain’s own lifecycle events for that entity.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a sequence of messages relate to the same domain entity — and the entity identifier is a domain concept (order ID, claim number, trade reference), not a technical UUID. Correlation Identifier closes the gap: it prevents each consumer from inferring correlation through heuristics (timestamps, ordering channels, message content), which would scatter correlation logic across the system. Without it, the consumer must guess: “these two messages arrived within 50ms of each other from the same queue, so they’re probably for the same order.”








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The correlation ID is a technical trace identifier — a UUID generated by the messaging infrastructure to link messages for observability, not a domain entity identifier. The domain doesn’t group things by trace ID; it groups them by order ID, customer ID, or claim ID. Correlation Identifier here masks the absence of domain correlation — the system has a trace ID but no domain entity ID, so messages appear correlated for debugging but cannot be grouped for domain processing. A domain expert would say “I need to know which order this shipment belongs to — not which request triggered the message.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the correlation identifier a domain entity ID — something a domain expert would use to look up the entity in their own system of record?

If yes → applicable. Correlation Identifier is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s an observability trace ID that happens to link messages technically but has no domain grouping power.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#EIP #CorrelationIdentifier #EnterpriseIntegrationPatterns #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion



References
[2] G. Hohpe and B. Woolf, Enterprise integration patterns: Designing, building, and deploying messaging solutions. Boston, MA: Addison-Wesley, 2003.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Competing Consumers Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can a messaging client process multiple messages concurrently?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
Work that is domain-interchangeable across workers, where assignment carries no domain significance, is domain knowledge. If your domain crystallizes that “any order processor can handle any order; any worker can resize any image,” then Competing Consumers embodies that knowledge. The pool of consumers is the domain’s own pool of interchangeable workers; the competing-consumers mechanism is the domain’s own work-distribution pattern.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that work units are interchangeable and that the domain doesn’t care which worker handles which unit — only that each unit gets handled. Competing Consumers closes the gap: prevents the system from building a routing mechanism (like Content-Based Router) to assign work to specific consumers, which would introduce a routing rule where the domain says “anyone can do it.” Without it, each consumer polls independently, and the system must implement load-balancing logic — duplicating a work-distribution concern that the messaging infrastructure handles natively.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



Two patterns overlap: when the domain assigns specific work to specific workers — “region-East orders go to East warehouse, region-West orders go to West warehouse” — the distribution rule IS domain knowledge. Competing Consumers as a standalone work-assignment mechanism would let any worker grab any message, overriding the domain’s partition. If you need both domain routing AND horizontal scaling, use Content-Based Router or Recipient List for the partition, then Competing Consumers within each partition. Throughput requirements and domain routing are both constraints external to the code; the structure must satisfy both. The knowledge gap is using competing consumers when a domain partition exists but hasn’t been identified.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain truly not care which worker handles which message — or does the domain recognize a partition (by region, by product type, by priority tier)?

If yes → applicable. Competing Consumers is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. The domain recognizes a partition — route by the domain partition first, then scale within each partition.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Idempotent Receiver Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can a message receiver deal with duplicate messages?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that duplicate messages are a domain reality — and that the domain itself defines what “the same message” means — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a trade-execution message is uniquely identified by its trade reference; receiving the same trade reference twice means ‘you already executed this trade — do nothing,’” then Idempotent Receiver embodies that knowledge. The deduplication key is the domain’s own identity concept; the idempotent behavior is the domain’s own rule for handling repetitions.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that operations have domain identities — and that repeating an operation with the same identity is a domain no-op, not a duplicate action. Idempotent Receiver closes the gap: prevents the system from relying on at-most-once delivery guarantees from the messaging infrastructure, which would couple domain correctness to transport-level promises that the domain shouldn’t depend on. A network retry should not become a double payment — the domain, not the transport, should guarantee that payment ID X is processed exactly once.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The receiver uses a technical deduplication key (message UUID, queue sequence number) rather than a domain identity — the idempotency check is “have I seen this UUID?” not “has this domain operation been performed?” The same order placed via two different message UUIDs (double-click) creates domain duplicates. Idempotent Receiver catches transport duplicates but misses the ones that actually matter. A domain expert would say “I don’t care if the message was sent twice; I care if the order was placed twice.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the deduplication key a domain identity — something a domain expert would use to determine whether an operation has already been performed — rather than a technical message identifier?

If yes → applicable. Idempotent Receiver is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. You’re deduplicating at the wrong level — catching transport retries but missing the semantic duplicates the domain actually cares about.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Wire Tap Pattern

EIP Intent: “How do you inspect messages that travel on a point-to-point channel?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that observing messages is a domain requirement — for audit, compliance, or monitoring purposes that the domain itself specifies — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “every trade message must be copied to the audit system for regulatory record-keeping; every payment message must be copied to the fraud-detection system for real-time screening; every customer-interaction message must be copied to the analytics system for business intelligence,” then Wire Tap embodies that knowledge. The tap point is the domain’s own observation point; the tap destination is the domain’s own monitoring actor; the tap’s read-only semantics reflect the domain requirement that observation must not alter the observed flow.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that messages be observed without interfering with the primary flow — and the observer is a domain actor (audit, compliance, fraud, analytics) with a domain reason to see the traffic. Wire Tap closes the gap: prevents the primary flow from being modified to explicitly send copies to every observer, which would couple the message producers and consumers to every downstream monitoring concern.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The wire tap is adopted without a constraint that mandates a permanent tap — “let’s tap this queue so we can see what messages are flowing” — when no external condition (regulatory audit requirement, compliance mandate, monitoring SLA) requires a permanent copy. When the constraint does exist, Wire Tap is the constraint-driven structure. The knowledge gap is leaving a debugging tap in place when no constraint requires continued observation.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a permanent, named consumer of the tapped messages (audit system, compliance archive, fraud-detection engine) — and would disabling the tap violate a regulatory or business requirement?

If yes → applicable. Wire Tap is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (regulation, compliance mandate, operational SLA) requires permanent observation.
If no → inapplicable. The tap is scaffolding with no remaining constraint — it should be removed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Message History Pattern

EIP Intent: “How can we effectively analyze and debug the flow of messages in a loosely coupled system?” [2]


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the path a message took through the system is domain-relevant — for audit, debugging, or traceability purposes that the domain itself specifies — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a trade message must record every system it passed through, because regulators require a complete audit trail; a claim message must record every processing step, because the claims department needs to reconstruct the adjudication path for disputed claims,” then Message History embodies that knowledge. The history is the domain’s own audit trail; the recorded steps are the domain’s own processing stations; the history’s integrity is the domain’s own requirement for tamper-proof provenance.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that message provenance be recorded — for regulatory compliance, operational troubleshooting, or domain auditability. Message History closes the gap: prevents each component from logging its participation independently, which would scatter provenance across N application logs with N formats, creating an audit trail that cannot be reconstructed without log-aggregation infrastructure.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The message history records infrastructure transitions rather than domain steps — “message entered broker at 12:00:01, passed through XML parser at 12:00:02” — when no constraint identifies which transitions must be recorded. Operational observability is a legitimate constraint, but middleware hops are infrastructure transitions. The knowledge gap is knowing you need to record history without knowing which transitions the constraint identifies.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert, shown the message history, be able to reconstruct the business process the message went through — identifying each step by its domain name (not its component name)?

If yes → applicable. Message History is the code catching up — a constraint external to the code (regulation, audit requirement, operational SLA) identifies which transitions to record.
If no → inapplicable. You’re recording infrastructure events the constraint doesn’t ask for.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Monad Pattern

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Some operations have structured non-value outcomes a domain expert would reason about: “can return nothing,” “can fail with a domain error,” “depends on flowing context,” “must run in an order the world fixes.” In FP this knowledge lives in the underlying type — Maybe, Either, Reader, IO/Task — and the Monad pattern composes these outcomes so downstream computations respect them. (The monadic interface — bind/flatMap — is the generic machinery; the domain carrier is the underlying type.) Effect sequencing is knowledge too: write-before-acknowledge is an audit obligation; acquire-then-release is a resource fact.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognizes structured non-value outcomes — Maybe for “result or nothing,” Either for “domain error,” Reader for “shared context,” IO/Task for “fixed order.” The monad closes the gap: without it, every call site writes its own if-null or if-error branches and hand-rolls the sequencing, scattering failure handling and ordering obligations across code that shouldn’t own them.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The inapplicable case is monadic structure with no knowledge behind the outcome. Wrapping absence the domain treats as presence in Optional improves the type contract but encodes a distinction no expert makes; an unrecognized error or unfixed order does the same. There is no knowledge-free half of this split — if nobody can name the condition or obligation behind the structure, the monad hides the gap instead of closing it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the knowledge behind the structure — the condition for “no result” or “this error,” or the obligation that fixes the order?

If yes → applicable. The underlying type is the code catching up — the monad instance keeps those semantics composed.
If no → inapplicable. The type contract may still improve, but the structure encodes a distinction no condition or obligation asked for.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #FunctionalProgramming #Monad #Maybe #Either #Result #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Functor

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a domain transformation must be lifted into a context — that the operation happens inside a container or effect, and the container’s structure must be preserved — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “every field in this validated form must be transformed to canonical form without discarding validation failures,” then Functor is just embodying that knowledge. The map operation is the domain’s own “transform the contents, preserve the context” rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that transformations respect the container’s semantics: validation errors must propagate, absent values must remain absent, list structure must survive item-wise transformation. Functor closes the gap: it prevents every call site from pattern-matching on the container to extract, transform, and re-wrap — scattering “how to reach inside” knowledge across the system. The structure survives; only the values transit.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “context” is not a domain container — it’s a data-transfer wrapper whose transformation always produces a trivial result. Mapping over a wrapper whose sole purpose is to carry a value through middleware adds an abstraction layer for an operation that could be a direct function call. The functor interface signals “this container has transformation semantics” when the container has none beyond transport. If every map call is immediately followed by extraction, the functor was never doing work the domain needed.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain recognize that the container’s structure is separate from the values it holds — and that preserving the structure through transformations matters?

If yes → applicable. Functor is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The container is wrapping for transport — the functor interface adds an abstraction layer the domain didn’t call for; a direct extraction-then-transform achieves the same effect.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Functor #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Applicative

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that multiple independent computations must combine — and that the combination preserves each computation’s failure independently while gathering all results — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “validating a form means checking name, email, and address independently; all failures must be collected, not just the first one; a valid form requires all three to succeed,” then Applicative is just embodying that knowledge. The apply/zip operation is the domain’s own independent-validation-then-combine rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that multiple computations are independent — their results have no dependency on each other, and the combination is a domain-recognized aggregation. Applicative closes the gap: it prevents each call site from manually sequencing then combining, which would couple unrelated computations together. A form validator that chains name → email → address with flatMap would short-circuit on the first failure; Applicative collects all failures, matching the domain’s own “tell me everything that’s wrong” requirement.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The computations are not independent — they form a sequential pipeline where each step depends on the previous. Using Applicative where computations are dependent imposes a structure the domain doesn’t support: the same domain logic would be more clearly expressed with monadic sequencing (flatMap). The code signals “these operations are independent” when they form a natural pipeline.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert describe these computations as independently checkable — and would collecting ALL failures (not just the first) match the domain’s own reporting requirement?

If yes → applicable. Applicative is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The computations depend on each other, and the parallel structure overstates the domain’s independence.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Applicative #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Fold / Reduce

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a collection must be reduced to a single value — and that the reduction rule is a domain operation — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “total invoice value is the sum of line-item totals; the consolidated risk score aggregates individual exposure assessments; the merged document incorporates all section contributions,” then Fold embodies that knowledge. The accumulator function is the domain’s own combination rule; the initial value is the domain’s own neutral element.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a collection resolves to a single result via a well-defined reduction rule. Fold closes the gap: prevents each call site from writing a loop with mutable state, which would scatter the reduction rule across the system and risk accidental mutation. The reduction rule is isolated — change “sum” to “max” or “weighted average,” and only the accumulator function changes, not every iteration site.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The reduction rule has no domain semantics — it serves infrastructure needs where the result of the fold is invisible to the domain model. Counting elements for a progress bar, hashing a list for cache keys, or summarizing stream length for monitoring: these model infrastructure aggregation. Fold is a dual-use construct: when the accumulator and combination rule are domain-defined (total, aggregate, consolidate), it’s domain modeling; when they serve technical concerns, it’s infrastructure. The test discriminates the instantiation, not fold itself.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain define the combination rule as a business operation — would a domain expert name the reduction (total, aggregate, consolidate, merge)?

If yes → applicable. Fold is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. It’s infrastructure aggregation — valid FP usage, but modeling a technical concern rather than a domain rule.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Lens

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an entity’s internal structure must be navigated and updated through a defined path — not through getters and setters — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a shipment’s destination city is accessed via order → fulfillment → address → city, and updating the city means replacing the address without touching the rest of the order,” then Lens is just embodying that knowledge. The lens is the domain’s own access path; the get/set/modify operations are the domain’s own nested-update rule.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain has deeply nested, immutable data structures, and domain operations target specific nested fields. Lens closes the gap: it prevents every call site from manually destructuring then reconstructing the nested path — which would scatter the structural knowledge (the shape of the order → fulfillment → address chain) across the system. The lens centralizes the access path; when the data structure changes (fulfillment moves to a different nesting level), only the lens changes, not every access site.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The “nested path” is not a domain structure — it’s a wire-format projection. The developer builds lenses for a deeply nested JSON API response whose nesting reflects transport format, not domain semantics. Lenses remain a valid FP tool for nested immutable updates — the distinction is whether the nesting reflects domain semantics or transport format. Adding a lens library for wire-format shapes that change with API versions adds abstraction overhead the domain model doesn’t benefit from.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain expert describe the access path using domain vocabulary — and would changing the nesting break something they care about?

If yes → applicable. Lens is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. It’s navigating API response shape — the nesting is wire-format detail.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Lens #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Currying

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The domain-knowledge lens for currying asks: when does staged parameter supply map onto a domain concept? If your domain model crystallizes that “a tax calculation needs the tax year, the jurisdiction, and the income amount — and these arrive from different domain events,” then Currying captures that knowledge. The partially-applied function represents “everything we know so far, waiting for the last piece.” Unlike structural patterns where the code IS the domain structure, currying is an encoding choice: a Builder expresses the same behavior, though it loses the compositional benefits.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain dictates that parameters are gathered across distinct phases: configuration is set at setup time, context is established at session start, and the operation parameter arrives at invocation. Currying closes the gap: prevents each call site from holding all parameters and passing them together, which would couple the final caller to what should already be resolved. The partially-applied function is a domain artifact — “everything we know so far, waiting for the last piece.”








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The parameters always arrive together — there is no domain stage where partial application is meaningful. Currying a function whose arguments are all available at the same call site signals temporal separation the domain never had. When currying’s value is purely computational (composability, type-class coherence), it’s sound FP practice with no domain connection.








TipThe faithfulness test



Setting aside currying’s type-theoretic and compositional benefits, does the domain ALSO have distinct phases of parameter gathering?

If yes → applicable. Currying is one faithful encoding — computational utility PLUS domain fidelity.
If no → inapplicable. It remains valid for partial application and composability.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Currying #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Immutability

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Immutability is unique: it is an FP baseline, not a pattern chosen from alternatives. Its primary justifications (referential transparency, equational reasoning, thread safety) are computational guarantees, not domain-specific rules. The domain-knowledge question is supplementary: when the domain ALSO mandates immutability, the construct gains additional justification. If your domain model crystallizes that “a ledger entry, once recorded, is never modified; corrections produce a new entry referencing the original,” then Immutability encodes domain knowledge on top of its computational benefits.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



Immutability eliminates shared-mutable-state coupling by construction. When the domain also mandates append-only state (audit trails, event sourcing, ledgers), immutability closes the gap twice: it provides the computational guarantee AND matches the domain’s conceptual model.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The domain has no concept of version history, AND the context is single-threaded with no concurrency concern, AND the data volumes make persistent-structure overhead a real cost. Enforcing immutability here serves neither domain modeling nor thread safety — the persistent data structure adds allocation and indirection for a domain that operates naturally with in-place mutation. A mutable approach is simpler in this narrow case, though the thread-safety and referential-transparency guarantees are sacrificed.








TipThe faithfulness test



In addition to the universal benefits of immutability, does the domain ALSO treat state transitions as append-only — would the domain expert describe updates as “creating a new version” rather than “changing the current one”?

If yes → applicable. Immutability is doubly justified — computational correctness PLUS domain fidelity.
If no → inapplicable. It remains valid for thread safety and referential transparency — FP’s default, not a mistake.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Immutability #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Higher-Order Function

The domain knowledge gap it signals
An operation parameterized by another operation — a rule taking a rule as input — is knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “the discount policy varies by customer tier, and the order total applies whichever policy is in effect,” then Higher-Order Functions embody that knowledge; the function-accepting-function is the domain’s “supply the policy at call time” rule. The lens does not stop at the business layer: retry windows, audit logging, error recovery, and resource limits are knowledge too — failure modes, obligations, the operating environment. The question is never “domain or infrastructure.” It is whether named knowledge stands behind the parameterization.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The knowledge mandates the variation and requires the variant at the call site — a business policy (discount by tier, risk assessment) or an operational fact (retry this often; log it — audit demands it). They close the gap: the variant stops being scattered as if/else or switch branches inside the caller, which would couple the caller to every variant. The caller expresses “apply whatever rule you’re given” — the knowledge’s own delegation.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. HOFs are FP’s mechanism for ALL parameterized behavior. The inapplicable case is parameterization with no knowledge behind it: a caller that accepts a function “just in case” — a variation point no rule, obligation, or failure mode asked for. That coupling hard-codes a decision no knowledge has made.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the knowledge that mandates the variation — the rule, failure mode, or obligation behind it?

If yes → applicable. The HOF is the code catching up — the parameter carries named knowledge to the call site.
If no → inapplicable. The variation point is speculative — coupling added before any knowledge demanded it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #HigherOrderFunction #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Semigroup

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that two values of the same type can be combined — and that the combination is associative and produces another value of that type — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “two risk assessments combine into a composite risk; two budgets sum into a consolidated budget; two permission sets merge into a unified set,” then Semigroup is one encoding of that knowledge. The combine operation captures the domain’s merging rule; associativity means domain order doesn’t change the result. Unlike structural patterns where the code IS the domain structure, the typeclass is an encoding choice: a plain combine function gives the same runtime behavior, but the typeclass adds compile-time guarantees.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that entities of the same type compose into larger entities of the same type, with a closed, associative operation. Semigroup closes the gap: it prevents each call site from implementing its own combination logic, scattering the meaning of “combine these” across the system. One combine captures the domain’s merging rule.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The combination is not domain-meaningful — it’s a data-marshaling convenience. Concatenating strings for logging, merging configuration maps, or combining statistics for a dashboard are infrastructure operations. The semigroup interface signals “these values compose into a meaningful whole” when the combination serves representation or transport, not domain semantics.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert describe the combination as a domain operation — merging, summing, consolidating — and would they agree that the order shouldn’t matter?

If yes → applicable. Semigroup is one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The combination is technical aggregation — a plain function has the same runtime behavior but loses the typeclass’s compile-time guarantees.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Semigroup #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Monoid

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A type with a neutral element and closed associative combination is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “zero is the neutral element for monetary amounts; an empty permission set is the starting point before merging,” then Monoid is one encoding of that knowledge. empty captures the domain’s identity; combine captures its associative merge. Unlike structural patterns where the code IS the domain structure, the typeclass is an encoding choice: a constant ZERO and a plain combine give the same runtime behavior, but the typeclass adds law-based reasoning and generic derivation.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a type has a well-defined neutral element — a real value that does nothing under combination — and an associative combination rule. Monoid closes the gap: empty and combine give the canonical neutral element and merge, so no call site invents its own. This is powerful with Fold — folding a collection produces a domain aggregate with defined semantics for the empty case.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The neutral value is not domain-defined — it’s an implementation convenience. A default configuration, empty logger, or zero-initialized counter are infrastructure neutrals. The monoid interface signals “this type has a mathematically meaningful identity” when the identity exists only to let fold handle empty collections without error. If the domain expert wouldn’t recognize the neutral value as a meaningful concept, the monoid formalizes infrastructure semantics, not domain rules.








TipThe faithfulness test
