Would a domain expert name the neutral element — “zero balance,” “no permissions,” “empty order” — as a concept the domain itself uses?

If yes → applicable. Monoid is one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The neutral value is an implementation convenience — valid for generic programming and folding, but not a domain rule a domain expert would name.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Monoid #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Foldable

What Foldable actually is
Foldable answers one question: can I combine the elements of this thing into one value? The primitive is foldMap :: Monoid m => (a -> m) -> t a -> m. Two facts follow.
First, the fold is a reduction; iteration is only the derived case (toList is itself a foldMap). The result is one value of the monoid you choose — and m = [a] rebuilds the list, so a fold need not lose anything.
Second, the container varies while the element type is fixed. Maybe a and Either e a (Result) are Foldable too: foldMap f Nothing = mempty, foldMap f (Just x) = f x; foldMap f (Left e) = mempty, foldMap f (Right x) = f x. Foldable thus covers 0-or-1 elements too.


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The domain knowledge is the combining rule: which monoid, and which fold. If your domain says “line items total in order of entry,” Foldable just embodies it. The class fixes no order; direction belongs to the chosen fold and monoid, not to Foldable.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a lawful way to combine the structure’s elements into one result. Foldable closes the gap: it keeps each call site from hand-writing a loop with mutable state, coupling the caller to the collection’s shape. When the structure changes (list to tree to stream), the fold is unchanged.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



Implementing Foldable for a structure whose domain meaning resists lawful combination, or whose traversal carries meaning that one collapse destroys. A state-machine graph, a dependency DAG, or a weighted decision tree resists it; a generic fold obscures their traversal semantics.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain define a lawful combination of the structure’s elements into one result, and does one collapse lose no meaning the domain needs?

If yes → applicable. Foldable is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The structure’s semantics are richer than one collapse.
If you cannot answer → unclear. The pattern is not wrong — your domain knowledge is incomplete.




#FP #Foldable #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Traversable

What Traversable actually is
Traversable asks: can I apply an effectful step to every element and rebuild the shape? The primitive is traverse :: Applicative f => (a -> f b) -> t a -> f (t b), mirrored by sequenceA = traverse id.
The effect must be an Applicative. Identity gives back fmap; Maybe is all-or-nothing; Either stops at the first error; Validation accumulates errors. One traverse serves them all.
The shape is preserved while the element type changes: t a becomes t b at the same positions, but one function and one effect must serve every position.


The domain knowledge gap it signals
The domain knowledge is the per-element step and the shape that must survive it. If your domain says “validate every line item and rebuild the order,” Traversable embodies it. Two limits matter: the same step runs at every position, so per-position rules need another tool; and on failure with Either you get the error, not the structure.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates the same effectful step at every position, and the structure must survive it. Traversable closes the gap: call sites stop hand-writing map-collect-rebuild, which scatters the logic and hard-wires one effect. Swap the effect and the traversal is unchanged.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



When positions are not interchangeable. An AST that needs a different effect at different node types, or a sequence whose steps are genuinely different operations rather than one uniform step, is not one traverse. A recursive function fits; forcing one traversal hides the per-position rules.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain apply one uniform effectful step at every position, and must the structure’s shape survive it?

If yes → applicable. Traversable is the code catching up.
If no → inapplicable. The rules vary by position; a uniform traversal misrepresents them.
If you cannot answer → unclear. You have not found the pattern wrong — you have found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Traversable #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Bifunctor

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A type with two independent parameters, each varying for its own reasons, is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a Result type holds either a domain error or a success value, and both sides transform independently: errors map to user-facing messages, values map to domain objects,” then Bifunctor is one encoding of that knowledge. The bimap operation captures the “transform each side independently” rule. Unlike structural patterns where the code IS the domain structure, the typeclass is an encoding choice: mapError and mapValue give the same runtime behavior, but the typeclass adds law-based reasoning and a unified interface.






ImportantWhen it’s applicable (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that a two-sided type has independently transformable sides. Bifunctor closes the gap: it prevents each call site from pattern-matching, extracting, transforming, and re-wrapping both sides individually, scattering “how to reach into each side” knowledge. One bimap transforms both sides; when only one changes, first or second does it.








WarningWhen it’s inapplicable (cohesion-reducing)



The two type parameters are not independent domain concerns — one is a technical annotation. A logging wrapper carrying a logger context alongside a domain value is not a two-sided domain type: the logger side is infrastructure that changes only for technical reasons. The Bifunctor interface signals “both sides are domain-relevant and independently variable” when one side is an implementation detail piggybacking on the type.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain expert describe both sides as independently meaningful — and would they say “yes, transforming an error to a user message and the value to a domain object are two separate domain operations”?

If yes → applicable. Bifunctor is one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. One side is technical annotation — separate functions lose the law-based reasoning and the unified interface.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Bifunctor #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Contravariant
A contravariant type is a consumer: an Ordering[A] (a comparator) compares values instead of producing them. Contravariant maps consumers in reverse: given a way to turn a B into an A, an Ordering[A] becomes an Ordering[B]. On its own that is pure plumbing — any function adapts any consumer, so it says nothing about your domain. The domain knowledge is the coupling: which mapping the consumer uses.

The knowledge gap the pattern signals
Your domain says orders are ranked by their customer. That is a fact about what an Order is: it has a customer, and the ranking uses it. Given Ordering[Customer] and the mapping Order => Customer, contramap yields Ordering[Order] — the domain rule encoded once. If you can’t say why Order => Customer is the right mapping, you have found incomplete domain knowledge, not a missing pattern. Unlike a structural pattern, where the code IS the domain structure, this is an encoding choice — it adds reusable laws and a unified interface, not new domain knowledge.






ImportantApplicable (the mapping is a rule of your domain)



The domain states the mapping as a rule, so call sites never invent it. One contramap keeps that rule in one place — “rank B’s by mapping each to an A” — instead of scattering it across call sites.








WarningInapplicable (the mapping belongs to another domain)



The consumer sits in a different domain — a logger taking strings, a database writer taking SQL, a file sink. Logging and persistence have their own rules; contramapping into them encodes those, not a rule of your domain. Same shape, opposite verdict: a rule of your domain in one case, an adjacent domain’s rule in the other.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would an expert in your domain state the mapping as a rule — “if we rank orders by customer, sorting any collection of orders should use the customer, and change when that rule changes”?

If yes → applicable: the rule is real, and one contramap encodes it.
If no → inapplicable: the mapping belongs to another domain, and the pattern buys nothing your domain did not ask for.
If you can’t answer → you haven’t found the pattern wrong, you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Contravariant #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Profunctor
A profunctor is a function-shaped type with two independently transformable sides: it consumes an input (contravariant) and produces an output (covariant). dimap maps both sides at once: pre-process the input, post-process the output. On its own that is pure plumbing — any function can be adapted, so it says nothing about your domain. The domain knowledge is the coupling: which input and output mappings the pipeline uses.

The knowledge gap the pattern signals
Your domain says validation takes a RawOrderRequest and produces a ValidationResult. That is a fact about what validation is: the input it accepts and the output it returns are domain concepts. When rules change, the input narrows (lmap) and the output enriches (rmap) on the same pipeline. Given those mappings, dimap yields one validation function — the rule encoded once. If you can’t say why those mappings are right, you have found incomplete domain knowledge, not a missing pattern. Unlike a structural pattern, where the code IS the domain structure, this is an encoding choice — it adds laws and coherence, not new domain knowledge.






ImportantApplicable (the mappings are rules of your domain)



The domain treats the pipeline’s input and output as independently variable. One dimap keeps that rule in one place — “prepare what goes in, wrap what comes out” — instead of scattering it across call sites.








WarningInapplicable (the mappings belong to another domain)



The adaptations belong to an adjacent domain — a request parser, a response formatter. Those have their own rules; wrapping a core function in them encodes those, not a rule of your domain. Same shape, opposite verdict: your domain’s rule in one case, an adjacent domain’s rule in the other.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would an expert in your domain state the input mapping (narrowing) and output mapping (enriching) as distinct domain rules that vary independently?

If yes → applicable: the rules are real, and one dimap encodes them.
If no → inapplicable: the mappings belong to another domain, and the pattern buys nothing your domain did not ask for.
If you can’t answer → you haven’t found the pattern wrong, you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Profunctor #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Alternative
Alternative is the FP typeclass behind the <|> operator, read as “try this, else that.”

The gap it signals
That a computation can fail, and that there is a domain-recognized fallback (not just an error), is domain knowledge. If your model says “try the primary payment processor; if it fails, use the secondary; if a config key is missing, use the default,” then Alternative is one encoding of that rule. <|> captures the “try this, else that” part. Unlike structural patterns, where the code is the domain structure, here the operator is a choice: if/else gives the same runtime behavior, but the operator adds law-based reasoning.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates fallback: primary-then-secondary, preferred-then-default. Alternative keeps that rule in one place instead of scattering if/else or try/catch across call sites. For a left-biased instance like Maybe, <|> chains read left-to-right, matching “prefer X, but Y is acceptable.”








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



A fallback that looks purely technical is still a domain decision. “On a 5xx, use a mirror” is a requirement. A parser that tries several grammars states a domain fact — the accepted input formats. The gap is not that these are technical. The gap is that Alternative does not merely record a fallback: it records an order. It fits only when the domain names the alternatives and ranks them. If the domain treats the mirrors as interchangeable, it never ranked them, and <|>’s left bias asserts a preference no one decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Name the alternatives and their order the way a domain expert would — “primary processor, secondary processor,” “preferred carrier, backup carrier.”

If yes → applicable. Alternative is a faithful encoding of a decided rule.
If the alternatives are interchangeable → the operator adds an order the domain never made. Decide the order, or use a construct that does not rank.
If you can’t name them → you haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Alternative #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Algebraic Data Types

The domain knowledge gap it signals
An algebraic data type (ADT) builds a type from other types — a sum (one of these) or a product (all of these together). Whether a domain concept is a sum or a product is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “a Payment is either CreditCard, BankTransfer, or Cash — and a CreditCard payment always has a card number, expiry, and CVV together,” then ADTs embody that knowledge. The sum type is the domain’s own enumeration of cases; the product type is the domain’s own bundled fields. ADTs make illegal states unrepresentable — which is precisely what domain knowledge demands.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates product types (fields always appear together) and sum types (alternatives are mutually exclusive). ADTs prevent representing states the domain says cannot exist — eliminating validation logic that would scatter across the system.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



A sum type asserts its cases are mutually exclusive and complete; a product type asserts its fields always co-occur. The domain may violate both. Categories that overlap — a party is both customer and supplier — cannot be one branch of a sum. Categories the business keeps adding make a closed sum a change magnet. Fields that arrive independently — a middle name, a sometimes-present tax ID — make a product a togetherness nobody decided. That is the finding: the exclusivity or the togetherness is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can the domain expert enumerate the mutually exclusive cases and the co-occurring fields — and would a misplaced field be a domain error?

If yes → applicable. ADTs are the code catching up.
If no → the cases overlap or stay open, or the fields do not always co-occur; the ADT asserts a structure the domain doesn’t have.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #ADT #AlgebraicDataTypes #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Pattern Matching

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Pattern matching selects a branch by the shape (variant) of a value, and the compiler checks that every case is handled. The fact that an operation behaves differently for each variant — and that the set is closed — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a Payment is either CreditCard, BankTransfer, or Cash, and each type has its own processing rules; every payment MUST be processed through one of these paths,” then Pattern Matching is just embodying that knowledge. Each match arm is a domain rule; exhaustiveness checking is the domain’s own “every case must be handled” constraint.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates exhaustive handling over a closed set of variants. Pattern matching closes the gap: the compiler warns about every non-exhaustive match site, matching the domain’s own “these are all the possibilities” rule. Adding a new Payment variant flags every such site until the new case is handled, making domain evolution visible.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The set of variants is open or externally defined — the domain doesn’t know all the cases at compile time. A plugin system, a configuration schema, or a message format from an external service: these have runtime-discovered variants. The open set is knowledge, and so is the default: what happens to an unknown variant is a domain decision. Pattern matching with sealed types fits only when the domain names that default. If the domain has not named it, a catch-all or open-union encoding asserts a fallback no one decided. That is the gap: the unknown-case rule is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain define a closed, knowable set of variants — and would an unhandled variant be a domain error, not acceptable default behavior?

If yes → applicable. Pattern Matching is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The case set is open, and exhaustive matching overstates the domain’s completeness.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #PatternMatching #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Lazy Evaluation

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a value may never be demanded — and that deferring it is a domain decision, not only a performance optimization — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “most requests never open the full report detail; only a few accounts need the risk breakdown; the customer may never submit the form and so never need a premium quote,” then Lazy Evaluation embodies that knowledge. The thunk is the domain’s own “derive only if demanded” contract: the value is computed only when something asks for it.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain treats the derived value as demand-driven — computing it eagerly would do work the domain may never ask for. Lazy Evaluation closes the gap: the value is not computed unless it is demanded. The laziness is a domain rule here, not merely a caching trick.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Even a “purely performance” deferral is a domain decision: someone chose when the value is needed. Lazy evaluation fits only when the domain names that timing — compute on first request, or compute at period close. If the timing is an arbitrary knob the domain never fixed, laziness asserts a demand schedule no one decided. If the domain always demands the value, laziness asserts a suspension no one asked for. That is the gap: the timing is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would the domain expert describe a scenario where this computation genuinely should not happen — not “should happen later,” but “may never happen at all”?

If yes → applicable. Lazy Evaluation is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The timing is an arbitrary knob — the domain has not named when the value is needed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #LazyEvaluation #Thunk #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Trampoline

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A trampoline is a loop that runs recursive steps as plain returns, so deep recursion does not overflow the stack. Stack safety is one axis. The domain question is the other: when the computation has meaningful discrete phases the domain recognizes, the trampoline’s steps are those phases. If your domain model crystallizes that “processing a batch of claims requires progression through validation, assessment, approval, and payout — each step is a domain phase,” then the trampoline’s structure is the domain’s own.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates stepwise execution where each step is a meaningful domain unit — AND the computation is deeply recursive, requiring stack safety. Trampoline closes the gap: its steps are the domain’s phases, and it runs them without overflowing the stack.








WarningWhen the steps are not domain phases (cohesion-neutral)



Stack safety is not knowledge-free: the runtime’s stack bound is a fact about the environment the code runs in, and the trampoline fits it. The inapplicable case is naming each step a domain phase when no rule or state the expert recognizes stands behind it. Then the phase names are invented, not discovered — calling each step a “phase” asserts a domain granularity no one decided. That is the gap: the phase boundaries are unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Beyond the need for stack safety, would the domain expert describe the computation as a sequence of distinct, named domain phases?

If yes → applicable. Trampoline is doubly justified — runtime safety AND domain fidelity.
If no → no phase knowledge. It remains correct for stack safety — a real environment fact, never a mistake.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Trampoline #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Memoization

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Memoization stores a computation’s result under its inputs, so a repeated call reuses it. That a result is determined solely by its inputs — and that caching it is a domain guarantee, not just a performance optimization — is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallizes that “a tax table lookup for a given bracket always returns the same rate; a risk score for a given exposure profile is immutable for the scoring period,” then Memoization is just embodying that knowledge. The cache is the domain’s own “this value, once computed, is stable” guarantee.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates determinism: for a given key, the same inputs always produce the same output. When validity is period-bounded, the period is part of the key. Memoization closes the gap: it avoids redundant recomputation and fixes one value per input set. The cached value becomes the single source of truth — matching the domain’s own “the rate doesn’t change mid-period” constraint.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Even a caching optimization is a domain decision: someone chose to reuse the result, and how long. Memoization fits only when the domain names a stability window. When the output changes for reasons external to its inputs, the window is unfixed; memoizing a database query, a time-dependent computation, or a stateful function then adds staleness risk. The cache asserts a stability the domain never guaranteed. That is the gap: the validity window is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain guarantee that the same inputs always yield the same output — and would a differing result for the same inputs be a domain error?

If yes → applicable. Memoization is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The function’s output is time-dependent or externally mutable, and caching risks domain-incorrect results.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Memoization #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Pure Function

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a domain demands deterministic, side-effect-free computation is domain knowledge. Purity is also the FP default, but the domain’s demand for it is still a choice. The question is whether the domain demands referential transparency. If your domain model crystallizes that “computing a tax liability from income and bracket must yield the same result every time for the same inputs — and must not depend on or modify anything outside those inputs,” then the Pure Function matches the domain’s own determinism constraint. Purity is double-counted: computational correctness AND domain fidelity. Domain-essential effects are handled with effect types, not by violating purity.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that certain computations are deterministic and side-effect-free. Pure Functions close the gap: they prevent the system from introducing hidden dependencies (global state, clock time, random seeds) into computations the domain says should be deterministic. Testing, reasoning, and caching become trivial — consequences of that determinism, not just technical benefits.








WarningWhen the determinism constraint is unstated (cohesion-neutral)



The pattern does no harm here. It also gives no signal. In functional code, purity is the default, so the code reads the same whether or not the domain requires determinism. Two cases collapse into one: “the domain requires this result to stay stable” and “this function is pure by habit.” The code cannot tell them apart. The requirement is real, but it is unwritten. The gap is the missing statement, not a missing constraint.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain impose determinism constraints on certain computations — and would a non-deterministic result (same inputs, different output) be a domain error?

If yes → applicable. The pure function is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → no named constraint. It remains FP’s default — never wrong, but the requirement is unstated.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #PureFunction #ReferentialTransparency #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Recursion Scheme

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A recursion scheme is a reusable function that captures a standard traversal of a recursive data type, such as a fold. When a domain operation is defined over such a type and the recursion pattern is domain-meaningful — not just algorithmic convenience — that is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “an org chart folds to its root to compute headcount,” then a Recursion Scheme encodes that knowledge. The fold captures bottom-up reduction; the unfold captures top-down generation. Unlike structural patterns, where the code is the domain structure, the recursion scheme is an encoding choice. A recursive function or Visitor gives the same behavior, but loses the clean separation of traversal from per-node logic.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



Recursion Schemes close the gap: they separate “how to walk the structure” from “what to do at each node.” When the data type changes, only the per-node function changes; the traversal updates.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The data structure is not domain-recursive — it is a tree-shaped intermediate representation. A JSON AST, parse tree, or object graph recurses structurally. But the shape is still a decision: the domain chose it. A recursion scheme fits only when the domain names the tree as a hierarchy it owns. If the shape is a format detail the domain never named, the scheme formalizes an artifact and couples operations to a shape that changes when the format evolves. That is the gap: the tree’s domain standing is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Is the recursive structure a domain concept — would an expert describe the tree as “an organization of sub-organizations” or “an expression of sub-expressions”?

If yes → applicable. Recursion Schemes are one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The tree is a format detail the domain never named — a recursive function expresses the same traversal without formalizing it.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #RecursionScheme #Catamorphism #Anamorphism #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Continuation

The domain knowledge gap it signals
A continuation is a function that represents “the rest of the computation,” passed in so the caller decides what happens next. That a computation’s next step is a domain decision passed at runtime — that “what happens after” is not fixed — is knowledge. If your domain model crystallizes that “after payment processing, send a confirmation email on success or queue a fraud review on failure,” then Continuations encode that knowledge. CPS captures the domain’s “here’s what to do next” parameterization. Unlike structural patterns where the code is the domain structure, CPS is an encoding choice: a Strategy, a callback, or an event emitter gives the same behavior, but loses CPS’s composable control flow.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the “and then” is itself a domain decision, not a fixed algorithm. Continuations close the gap: they prevent the computation from hardcoding its successor, which would couple the processor to the notification and fraud systems. The continuation is supplied at the call site — the business process determines the next step.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “and then” is always the same — but even a fixed callback is a domain decision: someone chose that the step must happen. The construct fits only when the domain names the next step as a decision point. Passing a logger, a metrics collector, or a response writer as a continuation transforms plumbing into CPS when no rule varies the step. The interface then signals a choice no one makes. That is the gap: the fixed step is unstated, not “merely plumbing.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have multiple, different “what happens next” paths — and would an expert describe the continuation as a business-process decision point?

If yes → applicable. Continuation is one faithful encoding of the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The step never varies — a direct call expresses the same fixed step without passing a continuation.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong — you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#FP #Continuation #CPS #FunctionalProgramming #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Actor Model
An actor is an isolated unit that owns its state and processes arriving messages one at a time.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a domain entity owns its state and reacts to the work that arrives to it is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “this entity processes its work one unit at a time, in isolation, and the only way to influence it is to hand it a new unit of work,” then the Actor Model embodies that knowledge. The heart of an actor is the behaviour: the entity’s own rule for each unit of work. However the code is dressed, this entity owns its state and changes it only in response to what it received.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that each entity is a self-contained unit that owns its state and changes it only in response to the work it is given. Actors close the gap: they stop outside code from reaching in and rewriting that state, which would scatter ownership across every caller. The queue of arriving work is the domain’s own “work is consumed as it arrives” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the domain treats the work as one immediate, ordered step with nothing to protect. The actor still looks technical, but it is a domain decision: someone chose to model this work as an isolated entity with a queue. It fits only when the domain names the state ownership and the queue as requirements. If not, the actor asserts a boundary nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert describe this entity as owning its state and responding to the work it is given — a thing that “handles what arrives, in isolation,” not a thing you reach into and change?

If yes → applicable. The Actor Model is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If no → inapplicable. The construct asserts an ownership boundary the domain never drew. Decide it, or use a plain call that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ActorModel #Concurrency #MessagePassing #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Semaphore / bounded resource
A semaphore is a counter that limits how many tasks may use a shared resource at once.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that only a fixed number of these things may be in use at once is domain knowledge. If your domain model already crystallises that “there are exactly eight loading docks,” “we hold at most fifty concurrent licences,” or “the lot has two hundred spaces,” then the bound is a fact about the world. A semaphore is that fact made executable. The count is the domain’s own “how many can exist at once” rule; the acquire/release discipline is the domain’s own “hold one only while the world lends it” rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a hard ceiling on concurrent use, and exceeding it is a domain error, not just a slowdown. A semaphore closes the gap: it stops the code from treating a limited resource as unlimited, which would let callers exceed a limit the world does not permit. The permit count is the domain’s own capacity; the wait is the domain’s own “queue until one frees” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the bound looks like a performance knob — a connection-pool size, a thread count, a rate limit. But even a capacity limit is a domain decision: someone chose the bound. A semaphore fits only when the domain names the resource as a bounded shared pool. If the number is an arbitrary, freely changeable knob, the domain has not named a bound, and the semaphore asserts a constraint nobody decided. That is the gap — the bound is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert name the limit — “eight docks, fifty licences, two hundred spaces” — as a fact of the business rather than a setting someone picked?

If yes → applicable. The Semaphore is the code catching up to the knowledge; the count is the domain’s own capacity.
If no → inapplicable. The count asserts a bound the domain never set. Name the bound, or use a plain limiter that does not claim one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Semaphore #Concurrency #BoundedResource #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Read-Write Lock

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that many parties may look at the same thing at once, but only one may change it, is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a timetable may be read by every dispatcher while a single edit is in flight,” or “a catalogue may be browsed while one price is corrected,” then the read-write asymmetry is a fact about the world, not a performance guess. A read-write lock is that fact made executable: readers share, writers exclude.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain distinguishes observation from modification, and the two are asymmetrically compatible — many observers may coexist, but a change must be alone. A read-write lock closes the gap: it gives readers concurrent access while keeping the writer exclusive, which is the domain’s own “look freely, change carefully” rule. Using a plain mutual-exclusion lock instead would needlessly serialise observers the domain says may proceed together.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “readers” and “writers” split may look purely technical. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed these operations differ in kind. A read-write lock fits only when the domain names observation and modification as distinct activities. When everything is an update, the domain has not named that distinction, and the second lock state and writer-starvation risk assert a role nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat reading and changing this thing as genuinely different activities — many may look, one may alter — or is that distinction only about performance?

If yes → applicable. The Read-Write Lock is the code catching up to the knowledge; observers and changers are domain roles.
If no → inapplicable. The split asserts an observer role the domain never named. Name the distinction, or use a plain mutex that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ReadWriteLock #Concurrency #SharedState #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Producer–Consumer

The domain knowledge gap it signals
Producer–Consumer is a pattern where one side adds work to a queue and the other takes it off. The fact that work arrives on one rhythm and is handled on another is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “orders arrive whenever customers click, but the kitchen cooks one ticket at a time,” then the queue is not an optimisation — it is the domain’s own buffer between two activities that run at different rates, with the bounded queue as the domain’s own “we can hold only so much waiting work” rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain contains two distinct activities — arrival and handling — that proceed at different rates, and the gap between them is real waiting work. Producer–Consumer closes the gap: it prevents the arrival side from being coupled directly to the handling side, which would force clicks to block on cooking and cooking to be paced by clicks. The queue decouples the rhythms the domain already treats as separate.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the domain sees one immediate, ordered step: the work arrives and is done in the same breath, with no waiting state. A queue still looks technical, but it is a domain decision: someone claimed arrival and handling are separate. Producer–Consumer fits only when the domain names a real waiting state. If not, the queue asserts a waiting room nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain have a real waiting state — work that has arrived but is not yet handled — or is arrival and handling one immediate act?

If yes → applicable. Producer–Consumer is the code catching up to the knowledge; the queue is the domain’s own waiting room.
If no → inapplicable. The queue asserts a waiting state the domain never named. Name it, or use a direct call that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ProducerConsumer #Concurrency #BoundedQueue #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Barrier (phase synchronization)
A barrier makes every participant wait until all have arrived, then releases them together.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a stage cannot begin until all participants have finished the prior stage is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the meeting cannot start until every attendee has arrived,” or “the tally is only valid once every ward has reported,” then the barrier is the domain’s own rendezvous rule made executable.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates a rendezvous: the next step is well-defined only when every participant has completed the current one, and a partial set is meaningless. A barrier closes the gap: it stops fast participants from racing ahead into a stage the domain says is not yet valid, which would let a premature actor act on an incomplete world. The barrier is the domain’s own “wait for all” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “wait for everyone” looks like a technical staging device — a synchronisation point that exists because one task happens to depend on several results. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed the participants form one collective. A barrier fits only when the domain names the group as a real unit and the moment as shared. If the domain has not named a collective, the all-must-arrive rule asserts one nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat the stage as meaningful only when all participants have completed the prior one — is the group itself a domain entity?

If yes → applicable. The Barrier is the code catching up to the knowledge; the rendezvous is the domain’s own rule.
If no → inapplicable. The rendezvous asserts a collective the domain never named. Name it, or use a future or gather that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Barrier #Concurrency #PhaseSynchronization #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Double-Checked Locking / lazy initialization
text:
Case study: Double-Checked Locking / lazy initialization
Double-checked locking tests a flag first, then locks and tests again before it creates the object.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this thing should not come into existence until it is first needed is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a ledger is opened only when the first entry is posted,” or “the archive is materialised only when someone asks for it,” then laziness is the domain’s own “existence begins on demand” rule. Double-checked locking makes that rule executable safely. When the domain has not named when existence begins, that is unwritten knowledge.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain mandates that the object’s lifecycle begins on first use: its creation has a real cost or meaning, and eager creation would assert existence before the domain says it exists. Double-checked locking closes the gap: it keeps creation lazy while avoiding the cost of serialising every access. The laziness is the domain’s own “not until needed” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the laziness looks purely technical — a startup-cost optimisation. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose when the object exists. Double-checked locking fits only when the domain names that moment as meaningful. If creation timing is a free choice the domain never named, the volatile flag and null-check assert a lifecycle rule nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain care when this thing begins to exist — does it recognise a real “not yet” state — or is creation timing purely a performance question?

If yes → applicable. Double-Checked Locking is the code catching up to the knowledge; laziness is the domain’s own lifecycle rule.
If no → inapplicable. The laziness asserts a lifecycle rule the domain never named. Name it, or create eagerly without the memory-model ceremony.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DoubleCheckedLocking #LazyInitialization #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Immutable Snapshot / copy-on-write

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that an observation must reflect a single consistent instant is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a quote is the price at the moment it was issued,” “a bank statement is the balance as of the closing date,” or “a submitted tax return is frozen,” then a snapshot is the domain’s own “this reading is a point in time” rule made executable. Copy-on-write is one encoding: the reader sees a stable version while a writer prepares a new one.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain requires point-in-time consistency: what an observer sees must be one coherent state, not a mixture of before and after. An immutable snapshot closes the gap: it prevents a concurrent reader from observing a half-applied change, which would show the domain a state that never legally existed. The snapshot is the domain’s own “freeze this reading” rule; the writer’s new version is the domain’s own “changes take effect as a new whole” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the snapshot is taken to avoid locks or allocations, so it looks purely technical. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed a reader must see one consistent moment. Copy-on-write fits only when the domain names the instant of observation as meaningful. If the domain has not named it, copying the whole structure adds allocation and garbage pressure for a rule nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain treat this reading as a fact fixed at a moment — a quote, a statement, a frozen submission — rather than a casual glance at whatever is current?

If yes → applicable. Immutable Snapshot is the code catching up to the knowledge; the frozen reading is the domain’s own fact.
If no → inapplicable. The snapshot asserts a frozen instant the domain never named. Name it, or read directly without inventing one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#CopyOnWrite #Snapshot #Immutability #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Saga / compensating action
A saga runs local steps in sequence and, on failure, compensates each completed one.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain knows how to reverse or offset each step is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a booking can be cancelled,” “a shipment can be returned and restocked,” and “a charge can be refunded,” then a saga is the domain’s own set of reverse actions made executable. Each compensating step is a domain rule — the reverse of a domain act — not a technical rollback invented by the transaction machinery.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain comprises several long-running steps across boundaries that cannot be made atomic, and each step has a reversal the business already performs. A saga closes the gap: it prevents a distributed transaction from pretending that the whole process is atomic, which the domain does not permit. The compensations are the domain’s own “how we undo this” rules; the sequence is the domain’s own business process.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “compensation” looks purely technical — a data cleanup to fix a failed write. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed the steps are separately reversible. A saga fits only when the domain names a real reversal for each step. When the steps are atomic within one boundary, the domain has not named a reversal, and the undo path asserts one nobody decided. That is the finding: the knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain perform these reversals in the real world — a cancellation, a refund, a restock — or would the “compensation” be a cleanup only engineers understand?

If yes → applicable. The Saga is the code catching up to the knowledge; compensations are the domain’s own reverse acts.
If no → inapplicable. The saga asserts reverse steps the domain never named. Name them, or keep one transaction that does not invent undo.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Saga #CompensatingTransaction #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Circuit Breaker

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain names a dependency as unavailable is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “when the card processor is down, we take the order on account,” or “when the address service is unavailable, we route to manual review,” then the domain has named the failure state: this dependency is down. A circuit breaker is that state made executable — after repeated failure it trips open and stops the calls. The trip threshold is a chosen bound; the down state it acts on is the domain’s rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain names the condition under which a dependency is unavailable, and it accepts that calls must stop while the dependency is down. A circuit breaker closes the gap: it prevents the code from hammering a failing dependency, and it records the domain’s own down state. The open state is the domain’s own “stop calling” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the domain treats every call as independently worth attempting, with no named state in which the dependency is down. The breaker still looks technical, but it is a domain decision: someone claimed this dependency has a failure state. A circuit breaker fits only when the domain names that state. If the domain has not named it, the trip threshold and open state assert a failure boundary nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain name a state in which this dependency is unavailable — a real down state — or is every call independently worth attempting?

If yes → applicable. The Circuit Breaker is the code catching up to the knowledge; the open state is the domain’s own down state.
If no → inapplicable. The open state asserts a failure boundary the domain never named. Name it, or retry plainly without inventing one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#CircuitBreaker #Resilience #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Scheduler / time-triggered job
A scheduler runs a job at a set time or on a recurring timetable.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that something happens at a particular time is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the books close at end of business on the last working day,” “interest posts on the first of the month,” or “the report runs every Friday before the stand-up,” then the trigger is a domain rule and the cron expression is merely its encoding. The schedule is the domain’s own calendar made executable; the job is the domain’s own “this must happen then” rule.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain attaches meaning to the moment: a deadline, a settlement date, a statutory filing window. A scheduler closes the gap: it prevents the timing from being buried in an operator’s habit or a manual reminder, and it records the domain’s own calendar. The trigger time is the domain’s own fact; the recurring run is the domain’s own recurring obligation.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the “schedule” looks like an operational convenience — a nightly cache warm, a log rotation, a cleanup at 03:00. But it is still a domain decision: someone chose the time. A scheduler fits only when the domain names the moment as meaningful. If the time is a free choice the domain never named, the trigger asserts an obligation nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert say the business requires that this happens at that time — a deadline, a settlement, a statutory date — or is the time just when it is convenient to run?

If yes → applicable. The Scheduler is the code catching up to the knowledge; the trigger is the domain’s own calendar.
If no → inapplicable. The trigger asserts a business date the domain never named. Name it, or run an interval that does not invent one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#Scheduler #Concurrency #TimeTriggered #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
section: Case study: Thread Confinement / thread-local state
text:
Case study: Thread Confinement / thread-local state

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that one worker handles one case from start to finish is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the assigned caseworker owns the case until it closes,” or “one clerk processes one application throughout,” then confinement of the working state to that worker is the domain’s own “this caretaker owns this case” rule made executable. Thread-local state is one encoding: the state belongs to the worker, not to the shared code.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain assigns a case to a single owner for the duration of its handling, and no other party may touch the in-progress work. Thread confinement closes the gap: it prevents the in-progress state from being shared and mutated by unrelated workers, which would let a case be advanced by two clerks at once. The confined state is the domain’s own “one owner while in progress” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



Here the confinement looks like an accident of the runtime — state stashed in a thread-local to avoid passing it explicitly. But it is still a domain decision: someone claimed a single worker owns this work. Thread confinement fits only when the domain names that owner. If ownership is whatever thread happened to pick the work up, the domain has not named an owner, and the thread-local asserts one nobody decided. That is the finding: the domain knowledge is unwritten.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain assign this work to a single owner for its whole duration — one clerk, one case — or is the “ownership” only whatever thread happened to pick the work up?

If yes → applicable. Thread confinement is the code catching up to the knowledge; the confined state is the domain’s own case ownership.
If no → inapplicable. The confinement asserts an owner the domain never named. Name it, or pass the state explicitly.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#ThreadConfinement #ThreadLocal #Concurrency #DesignPatterns #DomainDrivenDesign #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Value Object
A Value Object is a small immutable type that code compares by field values, not by identity.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this thing is defined by its attributes and has no identity is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “a €10 note is any €10 note,” “an address is whatever its fields say,” or “two measurements of 5 kg are the same measurement,” then equality-by-value is a domain rule, not a convenience. A Value Object is that rule made executable: immutable, interchangeable, replaceable wholesale.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain treats the concept as a measure, a quantity, a description — something with no “which one is it?” question. A Value Object closes the gap: it prevents the concept from being tracked by identity, which would let two domain-equal instances be distinguished by accident. Immutability is the domain’s own “a value doesn’t change; you get a new one” rule, and validation in the constructor is the domain’s own “a value cannot exist in an invalid state” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The concept has real identity the domain tracks over time — this customer, this order, this account — even when every attribute changes. Forcing it into a Value Object erases the “which one is it?” question the domain asks constantly. Conversely, wrapping every string and number in a Value Object because immutability is fashionable is still a decision, but it signals “the domain distinguishes these” when the domain never named a distinction. That is the gap — the distinction is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert ask “which one is it?” about this thing — or only “what is it?” If equality of attributes settles the matter, it’s a value.

If yes (identity matters) → inapplicable. Model an Entity; identity is the domain’s own question.
If no (attributes settle it) → applicable. The Value Object is the code catching up to the knowledge.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #ValueObject #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Entity
An Entity is a type whose instances code tracks by an identity separate from their fields.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this thing remains itself while everything about it changes is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “the customer who moves house and changes her name is still the same customer,” then identity over time is a domain rule, not a database convenience. An Entity is that rule made executable: identity that persists through state changes, and a lifecycle the domain tracks.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain distinguishes this instance from that one by identity, not by attributes, and tracks each through birth, change, and closure. An Entity closes the gap: it prevents the thing from being copied or compared by fields, which would let the domain lose track of which customer is which. Equality by identity is the domain’s own “same customer even after moving” rule; the lifecycle methods are the domain’s own “what may happen to it, and when” rules.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “entity” has no identity the domain cares about — it is a measure, a description, a quantity, where attribute equality settles every question. Assigning it an ID invents a “which one is it?” question the domain never asks, and forces the code to maintain identity maps for things that are interchangeable. The ID signals “the domain tracks this through time” when the domain only reads its value.








TipThe faithfulness test



Does the domain track this thing through time as “the same thing” — same customer, same order, same account — even as its attributes change?

If yes → applicable. The Entity is the code catching up to the knowledge; identity is the domain’s own thread.
If no → inapplicable. Model a Value Object; inventing identity fabricates a domain question.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Entity #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Aggregate
An Aggregate is a group of objects that code loads, changes, and saves as one unit through a single root.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that these things change together, and that this rule must hold at every moment, is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “an order’s total can never disagree with its lines,” or “a reservation may not exceed the room’s capacity,” then the invariant is a business rule and the boundary around it is the domain’s own consistency claim. An Aggregate is that claim made executable: one root, one transaction, invariants enforced inside.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain names a rule that must always hold, and every path that could break it is known. An Aggregate closes the gap: it funnels all change through the root, so the invariant cannot be bypassed. The boundary is the domain’s own “these change together, or not at all” rule; references by identity to other aggregates are the domain’s own “these stay independent” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. Grouping a screen’s data into one Aggregate is still a decision: someone chose that boundary. But the boundary asserts one transaction and one invariant. It fits only when the domain names the rule that must always hold inside it. If the domain allows eventual, separate change, it never named that rule, and the Aggregate’s lock asserts a consistency nobody decided. That is the gap — the invariant is unwritten, not a save-a-join trick.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert name the invariant — the rule that must always hold inside this boundary, the way a banker names “the balance always equals the sum of entries”?

If yes → applicable. The Aggregate is the code catching up to the knowledge; the boundary is the domain’s own consistency claim.
If no → inapplicable. Draw the boundary around the actual invariant — or discover there isn’t one.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Aggregate #AggregateRoot #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Repository
A Repository is an interface that gives code collection-like access to stored domain objects.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the domain speaks of a collection of these things is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “all active orders are here; we add orders; we find open ones,” then the collection metaphor is the domain’s own vocabulary. A Repository is that vocabulary made executable: an in-memory-collection facade (add, find, remove) over persistence, named in domain terms.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain genuinely reasons about a set of things — “all overdue invoices,” “the customer by number” — and the queries map to expert phrases. A Repository closes the gap: it gives the domain its collection language while hiding storage, and it confines query logic to interfaces the experts can read. It prevents persistence calls from scattering through domain code, which would couple business rules to SQL.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A method that mirrors one screen, one report, or one ORM call is still a decision, but a Repository asserts that the domain speaks of collections. It fits only when an expert phrase matches the query. If no phrase matches, the Repository supplies vocabulary the domain never adopted — the collection is unwritten, not “merely technical.” Repositories over Value Objects or read-only projections add a facade with no collection semantics behind it.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can each repository method be read aloud to a domain expert as something they say — “find open orders,” “get customer by number” — rather than as a data-access operation?

If yes → applicable. The Repository is the code catching up to the knowledge; the collection is the domain’s own concept.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a DAO; name it honestly or reshape the queries around domain phrases.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Repository #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Domain Service
A Domain Service is a stateless operation that holds a domain rule belonging to no single entity.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this operation belongs to the domain yet has no natural home on a single entity is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “transferring money involves two accounts and a rule neither owns alone,” then the Domain Service is that fact made executable: a stateless operation named in domain language, placed where the domain says it lives.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain performs an action that spans several entities or needs domain knowledge no single entity should hold. A Domain Service closes the gap: it prevents the operation from being squeezed onto one entity (wrong owner) or diluted into an application helper (no domain home). Its name is the domain’s own verb — “transfer,” “allocate,” “renegotiate” — and its logic is the business rule, not orchestration.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “domain service” is where logic went because no one could decide who owned it — an entity skirted of its own behaviour. Then the service is an anemic-model accelerant: entities hold data, the service holds all rules, and the domain’s own subjects stop carrying their own knowledge. Likewise, a service that only fetches, orchestrates, or calls infrastructure is an application service wearing the wrong name.








TipThe faithfulness test



Can you name the operation in the experts’ words, and is it genuinely homeless — belonging to no single entity — rather than parked there for convenience?

If yes → applicable. The Domain Service is the code catching up to the knowledge; the verb is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Move the behaviour to the entity that owns it, or rename the service to what it really is.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #DomainService #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Domain Event
A Domain Event is a message that records something meaningful that happened in the domain.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the business talks about this occurrence — that it has a name, a time, and consequences — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “when an order is placed, fulfilment and invoicing both react,” then “OrderPlaced” is a domain fact, not a messaging artefact. A Domain Event is that fact made executable: something that happened, named in the experts’ words, with the past tense the experts use.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain recognises the occurrence as a milestone: experts refer to it, reports count it, other parts of the business respond to it. A Domain Event closes the gap: it prevents the occurrence from being a side effect buried in a method, and it lets reacting parts subscribe without the placer knowing them. The event name is the domain’s own vocabulary; the timestamp is the domain’s own “when it happened.”








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A table change such as “OrderSaved,” “FieldChanged,” or “RowUpdated” is still a decision, and publishing it asserts a named occurrence. It fits only when the experts name the moment and its consequences. If the experts do not, the Domain Event asserts a milestone nobody decided and forces consumers to reconstruct meaning the producer should have named. That is the gap — the occurrence is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Would a domain expert use this occurrence in a sentence — “the order was placed, so we…” — with the same name and the same consequences?

If yes → applicable. The Domain Event is the code catching up to the knowledge; the milestone is the domain’s own fact.
If no → inapplicable. It’s a change notification; name the integration honestly instead of borrowing domain dress.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #DomainEvent #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Factory
A Factory is a construct that wraps the code that creates an object.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that creating this thing involves rules — what must be true for it to exist at all — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “an order cannot exist without a customer and at least one line,” or “a policy is created through quotation, not directly,” then the creation rules are domain invariants. A Factory is that fact made executable: the domain’s own birth rules, stated once, at the birthplace.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The domain has creation rules the experts could state — required companions, initial state, eligibility. A Factory closes the gap: it prevents half-born objects from existing, which would push invariant checks into every method that touches the thing afterwards. Creation through the factory is the domain’s own “it may only come into existence this way” rule; a complex constructor argument list is often the factory’s knowledge looking for a name.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. Creating an object is still a decision, and a Factory asserts that creation follows a rule. It fits only when the experts can state the conditions under which the thing may come into existence. If the domain attaches no conditions to creation, the Factory claims governance nobody decided. That is the gap — the creation rule is unwritten, not “merely technical.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Can a domain expert state the conditions under which this thing may come into existence — and would violating them be a domain error, not a null-pointer?

If yes → applicable. The Factory is the code catching up to the knowledge; the birth rules are the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Construct directly; the ceremony invents governance the domain never claimed.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Factory #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Specification
A Specification is a rule object that code can check and combine with other rules.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that this predicate is a named business rule — one the experts evaluate, discuss, and sometimes change — is domain knowledge. If your domain model crystallises that “eligibility for the discount” is a thing the business defines, audits, and redefines, then the rule is a domain concept in its own right. A Specification is that fact made executable: a first-class, nameable, combinable rule object.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The experts name the rule, apply it in several places, or change its terms without changing the surrounding process. A Specification closes the gap: it prevents the rule from being re-implemented in a validation here, a where-clause there, and a report query somewhere else — three copies drifting apart. The specification’s name is the domain’s own phrase (“OverdueForRenewal”), and combining specifications mirrors how the experts combine the rules.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



There is no knowledge-free half of this split. A predicate such as “id != null” or “createdAfter(threshold)” is still a decision, and a Specification asserts that the rule is named policy. It fits only when the experts have a phrase for the rule and own it. If the experts never pronounced it, the Specification claims a policy nobody decided. That is the gap — the rule is unwritten, not “merely plumbing.”








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the experts have a phrase for this rule, and would they recognise their policy when they read the specification’s name?

If yes → applicable. The Specification is the code catching up to the knowledge; the rule is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep it as a plain predicate; the wrapper fabricates policy.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #Specification #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Bounded Context
A Bounded Context is a boundary inside which one model and one set of terms apply.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that the same word means different things to different parts of the business is domain knowledge. If your organisation crystallises that “a ‘product’ to sales is a SKU with margin; to logistics it is a box with weight; to support it is a warranty scope,” then one shared model is a falsehood, and the boundary between the meanings is the domain’s own division. A Bounded Context is that division made executable: inside this boundary, each term has exactly one meaning.






ImportantWhen the domain mandates it (cohesion-increasing)



The business genuinely divides — distinct vocabularies, distinct rules, distinct teams — and the split is discoverable in how experts talk past each other. A Bounded Context closes the gap: it prevents a single “unified” model from being stretched across conflicting meanings, which forces every term into nullable, optional, “sometimes it means” contortions. The context border is the domain’s own “here, this word means this” rule.








WarningWhen the domain doesn’t (cohesion-reducing)



The “contexts” are team territories or microservice quotas, drawn where the vocabulary is actually shared. Splitting one coherent model into several contexts adds translation layers between meanings that never diverged, and every context boundary the domain doesn’t recognise becomes a mapping tax. The boundary signals “the words differ here” when only the org chart does.








TipThe faithfulness test



Do the experts themselves divide — does “order” or “customer” actually mean different things across these groups, with different rules attached?

If yes → applicable. The Bounded Context is the code catching up to the knowledge; the border is the domain’s own.
If no → inapplicable. Keep one model; the extra contexts invent translation the vocabulary doesn’t need.
If you can’t answer → unclear. You haven’t found the pattern wrong; you’ve found incomplete domain knowledge.




#DDD #BoundedContext #DomainDrivenDesign #DesignPatterns #DomainKnowledge #SoftwareArchitecture #Coupling #Cohesion

title: Patterns & Constructs as Knowledge-Gap Indicators
text:
Case study: Ubiquitous Language
A Ubiquitous Language is the shared vocabulary that both domain experts and code use.

The domain knowledge gap it signals
The fact that a term has an agreed meaning between experts and code is itself the completeness-check.
