title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text: Change drivers are the engine of the whole theory. Everything the Independent Variation Principle prescribes follows from the set of change drivers and the way elements are assigned to them.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
1 What a change driver is
A change driver is a discrete, identifiable source of variation that can cause elements to require modification. It is an external condition in the operating domain: when it activates, part of the system must change.
The tax legislation is a change driver. When it changes, every element that embodies tax knowledge must change. A payment-routing standard is a change driver. The target platform is a change driver. A security classification is a change driver.
At the leaf level, a change driver is identical to a coupling dimension: both name a dimension along which elements vary together.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
section: 2 Change drivers are discovered, not chosen
text:
2 Change drivers are discovered, not chosen
This is the load-bearing fact about change drivers. The set CC is a fact about the domain, not a design choice. The analyst discovers which external conditions force the system to change; the designer does not invent them.
Change drivers are external and fixed by the domain. No design move adds, removes, or transmutes a driver. A change driver exists because the domain’s causal structure produces it, not because a designer decides it should exist.
This is why the theory is a diagnostic instrument rather than a recipe: it tells you to read the change structure off the domain, not to impose it.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
3 The assignment function
The change-driver assignment Γ:E→𝒫(C)\Gamma : E \to \mathcal{P}(C) maps each element to the set of change drivers that force it to change.

An element with |Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1 responds to exactly one change driver. Such an element is pure.
An element with |Γ(e)|>1|\Gamma(e)| > 1 responds to several. It is composite.
A composite element is irreducibly composite when no proper subset of its driver set can achieve its purpose — it genuinely needs all of them. Adapters and translators are typical examples: a module that must both follow the domain’s rule and satisfy a foreign interface is irreducibly multi-driver.

The assignment is read from the domain’s causal structure. Whether an element is pure or composite is not a label the designer attaches; it follows from which external conditions actually force the element to change.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
4 Driver independence
Two change drivers are independent when their knowledge slices do not overlap and activating one does not logically force the other. Driver independence is a well-formedness condition on the driver set, not a hypothesis the theory requires. If two drivers are mutually coupled — each activation forces the other — they do not individuate two distinct sources of change and are correctly treated as one.

title: Change Drivers and Assignment
text:
5 Driver omission and refinement
The granularity at which you read the driver set is a modelling choice. You may split one change driver into finer ones, or merge several into one coarser driver. The structural results of the theory are invariant under this refinement: a finer grain yields a richer CC with no loss of structural validity.
Omitting a driver — failing to record a genuine source of change — is a different matter. It coarsens the optimal partition and leaves that change uncontained. Driver omission is the failure mode the theory warns against: if a real change driver is missing from CC, the modules built from the incomplete set will not contain the changes that driver produces.
The taxonomy of change drivers and the discovery tests used here are developed in the published paper on the change-driver taxonomy [1], and the question of what counts as the source of a change driver is examined in the paper on whether a change driver is an actor or a document [2]. The formal account of the assignment function and of driver independence is part of the Independent Variation Principle paper [3].

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
IVP prescribes one module structure: the Γ-equivalence partition. This page explains that object — what the equivalence relation is, what properties its classes have, and how multi-driver elements fit.
The principle itself — its one-sentence statement and the four conditions — is stated on the structural formulation page. Here we work with the object the principle produces.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
1 The equivalence relation
Define the relation Γ̃\tilde{\Gamma} on the element set EE by:
e1∼Γe2⇔Γ(e1)=Γ(e2) e_1 \sim_\Gamma e_2 \iff \Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) 
Two elements are change-driver-equivalent when they are assigned the same set of change drivers. This relation is an equivalence relation: it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Therefore it partitions the element set into equivalence classes.
The Γ-equivalence partition 𝒫Γ=E/Γ̃\mathcal{P}_\Gamma = E / \tilde{\Gamma} is the set of these classes. Each class collects exactly the elements that respond to the same change drivers.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
2 Purity and completeness
A module drawn from this partition has two properties.

Purity. The module contains no element from outside its Γ-equivalence class. Every element in the module is Γ-equivalent to every other. When a change driver activates, every element affected lives in this module — and nothing unrelated lives here.
Completeness. The module contains every element of its Γ-equivalence class. Nothing that should be here has been placed elsewhere. When a change driver activates, no element that must change is scattered across other modules.

Purity is the module-level form of Separation (IVP-3): no foreign elements. Completeness is the module-level form of Unification (IVP-4): no missing elements. A module that is both pure and complete is maximally cohesive with respect to the change-driver rule. It is the unit that contains exactly the elements a change driver forces to change together, and nothing else. The formal account of purity and completeness as correctness relative to a partitioning rule is given in the published paper on the nature of cohesion [1], and the change-driver-assignment instantiation of the schema is developed in the paper on causal cohesion [2].

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
text:
3 Multi-driver elements
Not every element is pure. An adapter that must satisfy both the domain’s rule and a foreign interface has |Γ(e)|>1|\Gamma(e)| > 1. Its driver set is irreducible: it genuinely needs all of its drivers.
An element is single-driver or multi-driver. The word “impure” applies to a module, not an element: a module is impure when it groups elements that are not Γ-equivalent. A module containing a multi-driver element is necessarily impure, because that element answers to drivers its pure neighbours do not. The adapter is well-designed; the impurity it forces on its module is necessary, not a mistake.

title: The Γ-Equivalence Partition
section: 4 The partition is what IVP produces
text:
4 The partition is what IVP produces
Because IVP prescribes exactly this partition, the partition theorem is the result that the compliant structure is unique — the structure is determined once Γ\Gamma is read off the domain.

title: The Partition Theorem
text: The four conditions of IVP do more than describe what a compliant module looks like. They determine the module structure uniquely.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
1 The claim
A modularization that satisfies all four IVP conditions must be the Γ-equivalence partition — unique up to coarsening ties.
Two elements with the same change-driver assignment must co-reside (Unification), and two elements with different assignments must not co-reside (Separation). These two constraints together fix which elements belong together: exactly the Γ-equivalence classes, and nothing else.
There is no latitude in a compliant structure. Once you have read the change-driver assignment Γ\Gamma off the domain, the partition is determined.

title: The Partition Theorem
section: 2 Why this is not a design choice
text:
2 Why this is not a design choice
This is the force of the result. Classical modularization advice often treats “how to cut modules” as a judgement call, one of many defensible choices. The partition theorem says that under the change-management criterion, it is not a choice. If your goal is to contain change — to make the module that must change together and nothing else — then the Γ-equivalence partition is the answer, and it is the only answer.
This is what makes IVP diagnostic rather than suggestive. Given the domain, it reads off the structure the domain requires.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
3 Up to coarsening ties
The phrase “up to coarsening ties” records one genuine freedom. Within a single Γ-equivalence class, all elements are identical with respect to change: they answer to the same drivers. You may therefore subdivide a class into smaller modules, or keep it as one, without violating any condition. The subdivision is free for readability, team structure, or packaging — it does not change the change-containment behaviour.
What is not free is merging across classes or splitting within a class so that elements respond to different drivers are mixed. The partition’s boundaries between classes are forced; its internal subdivision is not.

title: The Partition Theorem
text:
4 Where the proof lives
The derivation that the Γ-equivalence partition is the unique cost-optimal structure is proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], which gives a counting argument on the element–change-driver incidence graph showing that grouping elements by their change-driver sets minimizes change propagation cost. The cost-minimisation of the partition is further developed in the paper on cohesion and change propagation [2] and the paper on minimizing change propagation and maintenance cost [3].

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
The Independent Variation Principle is stated over a model of a software system. This model names every object the theory needs to reason about change. It is called the software system tuple.
The tuple is written S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma). Each entry is one ingredient of the model.
The first five ingredients are inputs. They describe the system and its environment as the analysis finds them. The sixth, Γ\Gamma, is the pivot: it is the map the whole principle operates on.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
1 What the tuple is for
The tuple gives the theory a fixed vocabulary. When the site says “a change driver,” “an element,” or “the coupling relation,” it means exactly the object named in the tuple. The tuple does not describe a new kind of system. It describes any software system in terms that make its structure under change visible.
The tuple is defined and discussed in the formal papers. Here we explain what each entry means and why the tuple is built this way. The software system tuple S=(F,κF,E,Coupling,C,Γ)S = (F, \kappa_F, E, \text{Coupling}, C, \Gamma) is the model the Independent Variation Principle is stated over, as defined in the published paper on the principle [1]. The role of the causal domain knowledge κF\kappa_F in the model is developed in the paper on the nature of cohesion [2].

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
2 Elements respond to change drivers
The central modelling move is Γ\Gamma: every element is assigned the set of change drivers whose activation would force it to be modified. A computeTax() function is assigned the tax-legislation driver, because when the tax rate changes, the function must change. A sanitizeInput() function is assigned the sanitization-policy driver.
The assignment is not arbitrary. It is read from the domain: which external conditions, if they activate, force this element to change. Whether an element responds to one driver or several is a property of the domain’s causal structure, not a choice the designer makes.

title: The Software System Tuple
text:
3 Two sets must be distinguished
Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is the set of change drivers that force element ee to change. The module driver set Γ(M)\Gamma(M) of a module M⊆EM \subseteq E is the union of the driver sets of its elements.
These are different objects. Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is a set of drivers for a single element. Γ(M)\Gamma(M) is a set of drivers for a group of elements. Keeping them separate matters when the theory reasons about how elements group into modules.

title: Software Clustering
text:
Software clustering is the problem of recovering or prescribing the modular structure of a software system. For three decades it was studied as an optimization problem over a dependency graph. IVP reframes it: the difficulty of the problem is not an intrinsic feature of modularisation, but a consequence of doing it without a semantic criterion.
This page explains what IVP concludes about software clustering — why the traditional problem is hard, how IVP dissolves that hardness, and what the shift costs.

title: Software Clustering
text:
1 The traditional problem is NP-complete
Classical software clustering treats modularisation as an optimization problem: given a dependency graph, find the partition of elements that maximises cohesion and minimises coupling.
Mitchell and Mancoridis established in 2006 that this problem is NP-complete [1]. The field responded with metaheuristic search — hill-climbing, genetic algorithms, weighted graph partitioning — each searching for structurally good partitions that, in the worst case, cannot be found exactly in polynomial time.
The hardness is real, but it characterises the difficulty of partitioning without a semantic criterion, not an inherent difficulty of modularisation itself. Without knowing why elements change together, the optimiser cannot distinguish a well-motivated partition from a coincidental one. It must search exponentially many groupings, with no basis for preferring one structurally plausible partition over another.

title: Software Clustering
text:
2 What “cohesion” means in clustering
Classical clustering does not define cohesion by intent. It defines it operationally, as the internal connectivity of a cluster.
Given the dependency graph and a candidate partition, count for each module the edges inside it (cohesion) and the edges that cross its boundary (coupling). Every objective in the field is built on those two counts:

Modularisation quality (MQ). The cluster factor CF(M) = μ / (μ + ½·ε) combines the counts, and MQ averages it over the modules. TurboMQ weights edges by shared source file for multi-file systems. [2]
Modularity. The Newman–Girvan objective replaces the raw internal count with the excess of internal edge mass over a degree-preserving null model. [3] Optimising it is strongly NP-complete. [4]
Pattern-based clustering. ACDC recognises a subsystem as a body that dominates a cluster, then adopts orphans by connectivity — no scalar, but the same criterion of internal connectivity. [5]
Association-matrix clustering. Similarity is computed from shared data or calls, and cohesion is the sum of intra-cluster similarities. [6] [7]
Within-cluster compactness. Tools that borrow a data-clustering objective use the within-cluster sum of squares directly.

Cohesion and coupling therefore read the same graph. They differ only in which edges they count. A survey of the cohesion-metrics literature reaches the same conclusion from the metric side: cohesion metrics and coupling metrics examine the same graph and differ only in which partition of the edge set they report. [8]

title: Software Clustering
text:
3 IVP supplies the missing criterion
IVP provides the semantic criterion the traditional problem lacks.
Every element is governed by one or more change drivers: external conditions that, when they change, require the element to be modified. The change-driver assignment Γ:E→𝒫(C)\Gamma : E \to \mathcal{P}(C) maps each element to its set of governing drivers. The IVP partition 𝒫Γ=E/Γ̃\mathcal{P}_\Gamma = E / \tilde{\Gamma} — grouping elements with identical driver assignments — is the modularisation that minimises both module-touch count per driver activation and within-module contamination cost.

title: Software Clustering
text:
4 Given Γ, clustering is polynomial
Once Γ\Gamma is in hand, no search is needed. Each element already carries its own module membership in Γ(e)\Gamma(e): two elements belong to the same module precisely when they share the same driver-assignment set. The bound O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}) falls out of the mechanics of that grouping, not from any deep theorem — you can count the operations yourself.
Deriving the cost, step by step, using the six-step application procedure:

Identify the elements (step 1). The analysis has n=|E|n = |E| elements to place. Every element appears once in the pass.
Map drivers to elements (step 3). Each element ee carries its assignment set Γ(e)\Gamma(e), of size |Γ(e)|≤dmax|\Gamma(e)| \le d_{\max}. Set equality does not depend on the order of its members, so each element needs a canonical form before it can serve as a grouping key.
Canonicalise each element’s key (step 5, preparation). Sorting the drivers inside each set makes every element’s key unambiguous: {a,b}\{a, b\} becomes the same key as {b,a}\{b, a\}. Sorting one set of size at most dmaxd_{\max} costs at most dmaxlog⁡dmaxd_{\max} \log d_{\max} operations. Across all nn elements this is O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}).
Group by identical key (step 5, main pass). Elements that share a driver-assignment set produce the same canonical key and therefore hash to the same bucket. Inserting one element costs O(dmax)O(d_{\max}) — hashing the set and comparing it against the keys of existing buckets. Across all nn elements this is O(n⋅dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max}).
Read off the modules. Each bucket is one equivalence class — one module. The number of modules is the number of distinct keys, never more than nn. Emitting them costs O(n)O(n).

Step 3 dominates the total: hashing (step 4) is O(n⋅dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max}) and read-out (step 5) is O(n)O(n), while sorting is the only step carrying a log⁡dmax\log d_{\max} factor, so it sets the rate. So the whole pass is
O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax) O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}) 
When dmaxd_{\max} is bounded by a constant — the practical case, where no element answers to more than a handful of drivers — each element’s work is one small sort and one hash, so step 3 costs O(n)O(n) and the whole pass simplifies to O(n)O(n).
The result is deterministic. Every module in the IVP partition satisfies maximal causal cohesion Hcausal(M)=(1,1)H_\text{causal}(M) = (1, 1), and no other partition achieves (1,1)(1, 1) for all modules.
The same problem is strongly NP-complete over the dependency graph alone and polynomial when the driver assignment is supplied. The complexity class tracks the availability of the semantic criterion.

title: Software Clustering
text:
5 Clustering is not IVP
The output of clustering and the output of IVP share a shape: both partition the elements into modules. The relation that defines the partition differs, and the relation is the content.

Clustering partitions by graph connectivity (or by co-change similarity). Elements go together when they connect.
IVP partitions by Γ-equality. Elements go together when they share the same change drivers.

When dependencies track drivers, the two relations induce the same partition, and clustering acts as a search for the IVP partition. When they diverge, they diverge in both directions. An element that responds to two drivers is adjacent to both driver groups; a connectivity objective keeps it with one of them, while IVP isolates it. Two renderers for the same format that never call each other carry no edge between them; a connectivity objective separates them, while IVP joins them. Neither error is visible from the dependency graph, because both are defined relative to a Γ the graph does not carry.
This is why IVP does not derive from clustering, and does not replace it as a search method. IVP supplies the criterion the clustering objective lacks; clustering supplies a heuristic that approximates it when the criterion is not yet known. The clustering objective scores a partition by the same quantity it optimises — internal edge density — so it cannot say whether the partition is right. IVP is the independent criterion that the cohesion survey found missing from the literature. [8]
One clustering signal samples a different relation and is worth distinguishing, though it is not a better-measured one. Co-change groups elements that historical commits modified together. [9] A call edge records a standing interaction that a change may never exercise; a co-change records an actual modification, so co-change bears on the same question a change driver answers — what varies together — where connectivity does not. That is an alignment of modality, not of accuracy. Co-change fires both when a shared condition forces two elements to change and when a change to one element propagates to a dependent element, and it also fires on commit batching and on refactoring churn. Its error runs in both directions, and its size is not measurable from the co-change data alone. Co-change is a different proxy, not an established better one.
The confound has a direction. Shared-driver pairs co-change symmetrically; change propagation is one-directional, from the element depended upon to the element that depends on it. The directed conditional frequencies therefore carry more than a symmetric co-change count — but only as a filter that rules pairs out. Symmetry is necessary for driver-equivalence, not sufficient (mutual dependencies and commit batching produce it for the wrong reason), and asymmetry alone cannot separate genuine propagation from one element carrying every driver of the other.

title: Software Clustering
text:
6 The cohesion-coupling tension dissolves
The classical imperative — “maximise cohesion, minimise coupling” — treats the two as a trade-off to be balanced with weights. Under IVP, the trade-off was an artifact of optimising without a criterion.
Once every module achieves maximal causal cohesion, the coupling that modularisation can eliminate is eliminated by the same construction that maximises cohesion. The normative decomposition simultaneously maximises cohesion and minimises avoidable coupling — one optimum, not two. The weights encoded a problem that a principled criterion removes rather than solves.

title: Software Clustering
section: 7 The hard part shifts to driver identification
text:
7 The hard part shifts to driver identification
The polynomial result is conditional on Γ\Gamma being known. The complexity of the modularisation problem depends on what information is available:

Γ\Gamma fully known — polynomial: O(n⋅dmaxlog⁡dmax)O(n \cdot d_{\max} \log d_{\max}).
Γ\Gamma partially known — a mix: polynomial for the assigned elements, the traditional hard case for the rest.
Γ\Gamma entirely unknown — the NP-complete traditional case.

The polynomial advantage is therefore proportional to the completeness of the driver analysis. The hard part shifts from combinatorial search to driver identification — an epistemic problem that domain analysis must address.
The shift is an improvement, not a cost-shifting trick. Driver identification yields reusable knowledge about the domain. Partition search yields a configuration that is discarded on every requirements change.

title: Software Clustering
section: 8 Structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator
text:
8 Structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator
When change drivers resist identification, structural clustering does not vanish — it changes role. It is demoted from design criterion to hypothesis generator.
Two reasons drive identification difficulty:

Epistemic. The change drivers exist and are well-defined, but the analyst cannot see them — missing domain expertise, absent artifacts, an inherited system with no design records. The drivers are there to be found.
Structural. The domain itself resists a clean decomposition — dense driver overlap, single-authority greenfield systems, rapidly changing driver sets. No sharp partition exists to recover.

Structural clustering helps with the first and not the second. In the epistemic case, dependency density and co-change history carry indirect evidence about the hidden driver structure and can be mined for it. A cluster the algorithm produces is a question worth asking: these elements are structurally close — is there an external condition whose activation would require all of them to change together? In the structural case, the underdetermination is real: no method recovers a sharp partition, because none exists.

title: Software Clustering
text:
9 Scope and limitations
The polynomial result holds when Γ\Gamma is known. The IVP advantage narrows in three cases:

Single-authority greenfield systems — all elements governed by a single driver; the partition is one module, and the analysis is trivial.
Systems with dense driver overlap — many elements with large, overlapping driver sets; the module count is genuinely large because the domain’s change structure is entangled.
Systems in rapid-change domains — driver assignments change frequently; the partition must be recomputed, and while each update is polynomial, the cumulative cost may be non-trivial.

Driver-equivalence does not put every element in its own module. Two elements share a module precisely when they share a driver assignment, and in any real system many elements do. The number of modules is the number of distinct driver-assignment sets, not the number of elements.

title: Software Clustering
text:
10 Where the proofs live
The claim that the Γ-equivalence partition is the unique partition achieving maximal causal cohesion for all modules, and that the cohesion-coupling tension dissolves, follows from the partition result proved in the published paper on the Independent Variation Principle [10], with the causal cohesion metric developed in the paper on causal cohesion [11] and the cost-minimum of the partition in the paper on change propagation and maintenance cost [12].

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
“Favor composition over inheritance” is one of the most cited design guidelines in software engineering. It is tempting to read this as a rule IVP prescribes. It is not.
The Independent Variation Principle (IVP) is precise about what it governs and what it leaves open. This post uses a payment-processing example to show what IVP actually tells us about inheritance and composition — and, just as importantly, what it does not.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 1 What IVP governs — and what it does not
text:
1 What IVP governs — and what it does not
IVP’s normative content is a module partition, not a mechanism choice [1]. Given a system’s elements EE and its set of change drivers CC, IVP assigns each element ee a set of change drivers Γ(e)\Gamma(e) — the change drivers whose state changes create a modification requirement for ee — and prescribes, in its structural formulation [1]:

Admissibility — every element has at least one change driver: ∀e∈E,|Γ(e)|≥1\forall e \in E,\ |\Gamma(e)| \geq 1.
Element Form — every element is either pure (|Γ(e)|=1|\Gamma(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite: no proper subset of its driver set can achieve its purpose, and no decomposition into sub-elements with strictly smaller driver sets jointly preserves that purpose.
Separation — elements assigned different sets of change drivers reside in different modules: Γ(e1)≠Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)≠M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) \neq \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) \neq M(e_2).
Unification — elements assigned the same set of change drivers reside in the same module: Γ(e1)=Γ(e2)⇒M(e1)=M(e2)\Gamma(e_1) = \Gamma(e_2) \Rightarrow M(e_1) = M(e_2).

Equivalently, the modules of an IVP-compliant system are the Γ\Gamma-equivalence classes of EE [1]. The first two clauses are the ones the composition-vs-inheritance discussion must not skip. Admissibility says every element answers to some change driver. Element Form ties the assignment to purpose and to the domain knowledge the element embodies: Γ(e)\Gamma(e) is not an arbitrary label — ee embodies the knowledge governed by its drivers, so the assignment is grounded in what the element exists to realize [2]. Separation and Unification then say how those grounded assignments group elements into modules.
Inheritance and composition are both such mechanisms. The theory treats inheritance — class B extends A — as a structural dependency: a relation observable directly in the artifact, like a function call or an import. IVP does not have a “composition directive” and an “inheritance directive.” What it does have is a coupling criterion, and that is where the real guidance lies.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 2 What IVP mandates: its own minimal coupling
text:
2 What IVP mandates: its own minimal coupling
IVP’s coupling criterion follows from its rule [1]. The partition induced by Γ\Gamma-equivalence is fixed by the change drivers; the coupling that survives a compliant partition is IVP’s minimal coupling — the necessary coupling: essential same-Γ\Gamma coupling inside a module, plus the essential cross-Γ\Gamma coupling between modules that is the irreducible cost of communication between Γ\Gamma-classes.
One thing IVP’s minimal coupling forbids:

Accidental coupling — coupling not required by any domain artifact. Two elements are coupled when one depends on something the other defines or maintains; that dependency is essential when a domain artifact (a statute, contract, standard, specification) requires it, and accidental when no domain artifact mandates it — a framework convention, a language limitation, a deployment detail.

The accidental coupling IVP is most concerned with is cross-Γ\Gamma accidental coupling — accidental coupling that connects elements assigned different sets of change drivers.
IVP also leaves no room for accidental coupling between elements that should be apart. If two elements with different change-driver sets sit in the same module and are accidentally coupled, the module is impure: the partition has co-located elements that Separation would keep in different modules, and the system does not faithfully embody the domain’s change structure [1]. IVP’s Separation directive eliminates this case by construction — cross-Γ\Gamma elements are never co-located in a compliant partition. The only accidental coupling that can remain inside a module is the same-Γ\Gamma kind — a concrete reference where an abstraction would do — and that is a code-quality defect, not a failure to embody the domain.
Because the coupling verdict is relative to the chosen rule, it is not a property of the code in the abstract — it is a property of the code under a given partition. IVP’s verdict is IVP’s because IVP picks Γ\Gamma-equivalence as its modularization rule. A different rule would classify the same dependencies differently.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 3 The payment example: what IVP diagnoses

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
section: 4 Why composition avoids that specific defect

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
5 What IVP does not say
IVP does not endorse “prefer composition over inheritance” as a universal rule. Three specific caveats:
Inheritance is not forbidden. Where the two sides genuinely share the same change driver — so IVP assigns them the same Γ\Gamma and the same module — the coupling inheritance creates is essential, not accidental, and IVP is satisfied. The composition example itself uses this: CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment implement PaymentMethod, an “is-a” relationship to an abstraction that genuinely shares the payment-method change driver. That inheritance is IVP-compliant. What the example removes is inheritance across the two change drivers — subclassing a base that pulls in infrastructure the payment-method domain does not mandate. A geometric-shape hierarchy is IVP-compliant if all its elements are Γ\Gamma-equivalent, so that every change modifying one also creates a modification requirement for the others. A framework’s intentional extension points are IVP-compliant only when the extension and the base are same-Γ\Gamma; a low activation frequency does not by itself make them compliant. The defect is coupling different change drivers, not using inheritance.
Composition can violate IVP too. Composition that couples elements assigned different sets of change drivers across a module boundary is just as much cross-Γ\Gamma accidental coupling. Mechanism alone does not determine compliance; the change-driver assignment Γ\Gamma does.
The verdict is rule-relative. “The hierarchy couples independent change drivers” is an IVP-specific diagnosis. It follows from choosing Γ\Gamma-equivalence as the modularization rule. Another rule would partition the elements differently and classify the same edges differently. IVP’s answer is the answer given its choice of rule, not a mechanism-independent fact.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
6 The takeaway
IVP does not tell you to reach for composition and avoid inheritance. It tells you something more useful: start with the domain. Ask what the domain actually prescribes: what are the change drivers, and what does each element’s specification require it to embody and depend on? The change drivers determine the partition; then couple elements only where the domain requires the dependency, and never make an element embody knowledge its causal domain does not mandate. When you evaluate a design, ask not “inheritance or composition?” but “what does the structure of the causal domain knowledge dictate, and does this mechanism add coupling the domain never had?”
In the payment example, inheritance happens to manufacture accidental embodiment and cross-driver accidental coupling — through the knowledge the extends edge forces the subclass to carry — and composition happens to avoid it. That is why the classical guideline points the right way in this example. But IVP explains the reason: the best structure is derived directly from the structure of the causal domain knowledge, and the mechanism is faithful exactly when it adds no coupling the domain did not already decide.

title: Inheritance vs Composition: What the Independent Variation Principle Actually Tells Us
text:
7 Learn More
IVP formalizes the module partition a system’s change drivers prescribe and the coupling a compliant partition tolerates — giving a precise, decidable answer where classical heuristics rely on intuition. The formal development — the module partition and the coupling-floor argument — is proved in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1], with the change-driver partition and purity/completeness accounted for in Causal Cohesion [3] and the cohesion-as-correctness framework in On the Nature of Cohesion [2].
This site’s overview sections — IVP (software) and Software design — present the theory and its applications in more depth, and the language coupling analysis applies the coupling lens across 65 programming languages.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
Hexagonal architecture — Ports and Adapters — puts an application core at the centre and surrounds it with ports and adapters. A port is an interface the core defines; an adapter is the mechanism that fits it — HTTP, a message queue, a database, a payment rail. The core does not know the adapters; the adapters know the ports. Cockburn’s stated goals are that the application can run with no user interface and no database, for testing, and that mechanisms can be swapped [1].
Cockburn is explicit that the hexagon is a drawing convention — the shape is “not a hexagon because the number six is important,” but to leave room to draw the ports around the edge; and what a port is “is largely a matter of taste” [1]. So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It does, openly. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for onion architecture, clean architecture, and layered architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Hexagonal treats the core and the integration mechanisms as two disjoint change-driver sets, with a port between them.
The core’s change drivers are disjoint from the adapters’.
A change driver reaches across the port — a persisted entity’s field, whose state and mapping carry the same assignment. The port then splits one class.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
2 The claim
The core holds the application’s rules. The ports are the interfaces it defines for what it needs. The adapters are the mechanisms that implement the ports: a web controller on one side, a repository on the other. Dependency direction is the point: the core does not import an adapter; the adapter imports the port.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 3 Hexagonal’s axis is core versus mechanism
text:
3 Hexagonal’s axis is core versus mechanism
Hexagonal’s axis is a structural split: core domain versus integration mechanism. It is not a frequency ordering or a policy ordering; it is a claim that the core’s elements and the mechanism’s elements are two kinds.
Cockburn’s justification is engineering: test the core without a database or a user interface, and swap mechanisms without touching the core. Those are goals, not domain knowledge. IVP groups by which change activates an element. Core-versus-mechanism is a proxy for that: the core’s change drivers differ from the adapters’ when the domain separates them, and only then [2]. So the axis can coincide with the partition. It does not determine it.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 4 The ports are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The ports are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as a core with ports and adapters. Analysis names rules, entities, processes, events, and decisions. Cockburn derives the inside from the outside and places the ports from the use-case context; but a use-case set names operations, not ports. The port — the interface, and the indirection it carries — appears when a designer lays out code; it is an encoding. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 5 The core is not independent of the mechanism
text:
5 The core is not independent of the mechanism
Hexagonal’s strongest claim is that the core is independent of the mechanisms. That is a claim about the direction of reference. Hexagonal exists to isolate change, so the coupling at issue here is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, if recording a new domain fact is taken as one change driver covering the field, the column, and the wire field, then a persisted entity’s state and its mapping carry the same change-driver assignment. Hexagonal puts the entity type in the core and its mapping in an adapter. The port boundary therefore runs through one Γ-equivalence class. It separates the entity type from its mapping and splits that class — a Unit Completeness failure. It is exactly the failure the core-is-independent claim is meant to prevent. The core is not quiescent: under the framework’s reading, it is coupled to the very mechanism the port was meant to hold away.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 6 What hexagonal embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What hexagonal embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The dependency direction — the core owns the port, the adapter implements it — is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Dependency inversion changes placement only; it adds, removes, and transmutes no change driver. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Where it aligns, the rule adds no structure; where it does not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The ports and adapters are a claim about the cut. The port, the adapter, and the core/mechanism boundary are not in the analysis; they are concepts the designer adds.

A representation is unavoidable; what is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A port is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the boundary groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if it splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a boundary that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of hexagonal, arrives at the partition. She may isolate the core from the mechanism because that is a natural impulse, but the port-and-adapter scheme, and the inversion it carries, are a taught pattern.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Hexagonal fails wherever the port straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the persisted entity, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [2]. Judged by that standard, the core/mechanism cut is correct where no class straddles it and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For a persisted entity, it is not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
section: 9 When hexagonal is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When hexagonal is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [3]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So hexagonal answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Hexagonal does no harm only where its port boundary coincides with that decomposition. Where it does not, every change crosses a boundary the domain did not set: a class split across the boundary scatters one change, and a boundary that groups non-equivalent elements couples what the domain keeps apart.
Two caveats bound the claim. The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost: the partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states, unconditional only in the pure, disjoint change-driver case [4]; whether the metric matches real economic cost is empirical. And the theory does not discover the rule: identifying the domain conditions and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [3]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.
Beneficial, here, means only that hexagonal does no harm: its port boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own. Outside the band, hexagonal is harmful wherever its boundary does not coincide with the partition.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [3].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Hexagonal can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in a port checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the port diagram looks the same.
Hexagonal is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
11 Verdict
Hexagonal architecture is a chosen encoding, and its ports and adapters are invented concepts wherever they do not coincide with the partition. It is not a domain-mandated decomposition.

Its boundary embodies the domain’s knowledge only where it coincides with the partition; elsewhere it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
Its core-is-independent claim is false for the persisted entity: under the framework’s reading, the state and its mapping are one class, and the port boundary splits it.
Its organising axis — core versus mechanism — is a proxy, not the change-driver structure; dependency inversion changes placement only.
It does no harm only where its boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful wherever it does not. Even in the good case, hexagonal adds no decomposition value, and placement is not faithful embodiment.

When read as a prescription rather than read from the domain, hexagonal supplies no domain knowledge and no domain-grounded reason to choose it.

title: Hexagonal Architecture
text:
12 Summary

Hexagonal architecture puts a core behind ports and adapters, with the core owning the interfaces and the adapters implementing them. Its stated axis is core versus mechanism.
IVP groups by change driver, not by core versus mechanism. The axis is a proxy; dependency inversion changes placement only.
The ports and adapters appear in no analysis artifact; a use-case set names operations, not ports.
The core is not independent of the mechanism: under the framework’s reading, a persisted entity’s state and mapping carry the same change-driver assignment, so the port boundary splits one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Where the boundary coincides with the partition, hexagonal adds nothing; where it does not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: hexagonal’s ports and adapters are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Hexagonal does no harm only where its boundary coincides with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where it does not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare onion architecture, clean architecture, and layered architecture.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
Layered architecture — the classic horizontal, or “N-tier,” style — divides the system into horizontal layers by technical role: presentation, application or business logic, and persistence or data access. Each layer calls the layer beneath it; the call graph descends. A common discipline forbids skipping a layer: the presentation layer reaches the database only through the business layer.
The style has no single author. It is the default arrangement of a great many systems, taught as the natural way to separate a user interface from business logic from storage. So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It is the commonest one. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for onion architecture, clean architecture, and hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Layered Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Layers group elements by technical role: presentation, business logic, persistence.
Each change is confined to one layer.
A single change driver crosses layers — a rule edit touching presentation, logic, and persistence.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
2 The claim
The layers are technical roles: presentation (controllers, views), application (coordinating logic), business logic, and persistence (repositories, data access). Each layer depends on the layer below it. The claim is that a change to a technical concern stays within its layer: a change to the interface touches presentation, a change to storage touches persistence.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
3 Layers divide by technical role
Layering’s axis is technical role. Elements are grouped by what they technically are — a controller, a service, a repository — not by what they change for. The rule that fixes the depth is a direction claim: each layer calls the one below.
IVP does not group by technical role; it groups by which change activates an element. Technical role and change-driver class are different axes [1]. A business rule and its persistence code may share a change driver while sitting in different layers; a controller and a repository may share nothing. So layering’s stated axis — presentation versus logic versus storage — is a proxy. It can coincide with the partition, when a domain’s change drivers happen to be technical; it does not determine it.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 4 The layers are not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The layers are not in the domain’s analysis
No business analysis or functional analysis organises knowledge as presentation, business logic, and persistence. Analysis names capabilities, processes, rules, entities, and decisions. It does not name “the controller layer” or “the data-access layer.” Those categories appear when a designer lays out code; they are a technical encoding. Absence from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 5 A layer is not independently replaceable
text:
5 A layer is not independently replaceable
Layering’s strongest claim is replaceability: swap the database layer, or the presentation layer, and the others stand. That is a claim about the direction of reference. Layering exists to isolate change — a technical change stays in its layer — so the coupling at issue is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, a single business-rule change commonly drives the controller, the service, and the repository together: the rule is edited, its endpoint changes, its stored form changes. Then those elements carry the same change-driver assignment, and the layer boundaries run through one Γ-equivalence class. Each boundary that separates them splits a class — a Unit Completeness failure. The rule is scattered across layers, and the change must cross every boundary between them. Replaceability holds for the layer’s mechanism; it does not hold for the rule.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 6 What layering embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What layering embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The descending dependency rule is a claim about direction, not about the cut. Direction is domain-determined only where the domain itself orders the elements: where one element’s requirement is chosen to satisfy another’s. Layering’s rule points every dependency down, whether or not the domain orders them that way. Where they align, the rule adds no structure; where they do not, it asserts a direction the domain does not have.
The layers are a claim about the cut. Presentation, business logic, persistence: the stratification is not in the analysis.

A representation is unavoidable. What is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A layer is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the layer groups elements with different change-driver assignments, it invents a unity; if its boundary splits elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a layer that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class. Layers rarely so coincide, because a domain’s rules do not divide by technical role.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [1]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality. Layering’s layers are that deviation: the business layer usually holds rules with several distinct change drivers, and its boundary separates each rule from the persistence code that shares the rule’s change driver.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of layering, arrives at the partition. She may separate concerns — interface, logic, storage — because that is a natural impulse, but the strict layer discipline, each layer calling only the one below, is a convention. She groups by what changes together, not by what an element technically is.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof, that a structure is a convention and not knowledge. Layering fails wherever a layer straddles a Γ-equivalence class — the ordinary business-rule feature, for example. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account
IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment: elements with the same assignment belong together. A module is pure when all its elements share one change-driver assignment set [1]. Judged by that standard, layering’s layers are correct where no class straddles them and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped.
For the ordinary feature, they are not correct; off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

title: Layered Architecture
section: 9 When layering is beneficial, and when it is harmful
text:
9 When layering is beneficial, and when it is harmful
The theory is not maintenance-only. Each concern the system must respect — logical structure, security, deployment, platform, a latency budget — is, once modelled as knowledge governed by change drivers, a partitioning rule over the same element set. IVP is one such principle, and not the only one: grouping by the full change-driver set (Γ-equivalence) is the common refinement of the concerns’ rules, correct under every one at once [2]. The claim is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists. So layering answers to one decomposition, not one per concern.
Layering does no harm only where its layers coincide with that decomposition. Where they do not, every change crosses a boundary the domain did not set: a class split across layers scatters one change, and a layer that groups non-equivalent elements couples what the domain keeps apart.
Two caveats bound the claim. The cost model is separate, and it models maintenance cost: the partition minimises total maintenance cost under the coefficient condition the model states, unconditional only in the pure, disjoint change-driver case [3]; whether the metric matches real economic cost is empirical. And the theory does not discover the rule: identifying the domain conditions and building the partition is a separate domain-analysis task [2]. A concern left out of the model is a requirements gap, not a cohesion judgement.
Beneficial, here, means only that layering does no harm: its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition. It still adds no decomposition of its own. Outside the band, layering is harmful wherever its layers do not coincide with the partition.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
10 Beyond placement: faithful embodiment
The theory separates three properties: placement — the right knowledge in the right modules — which is what cohesion measures; faithful embodiment — each piece realised as it requires; and dependency parsimony — the dependencies are the ones the purpose requires. The three are independent [2].
Correctness is the second alone. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter. So cohesion governs the cost of achieving and maintaining correctness — the scope to read and the radius to change — not whether it holds. A module can be placed exactly right and still compute a rule with the wrong formula.
Layering can clear placement and fail this. Nothing in a layer checks whether the code realises the knowledge it carries, and the layer diagram looks the same.
Layering is fully sound only when it clears every bar: its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition, and the code realises the domain’s knowledge faithfully. Alignment without embodiment is a system placed correctly and still wrong about its domain.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
11 Verdict
Layered architecture is a chosen encoding, and its layers are invented concepts wherever they do not coincide with the partition. It is not a domain-mandated decomposition.

Its layers embody the domain’s knowledge only where they coincide with the partition; elsewhere they invent structure the domain did not mandate.
Its replaceability claim is false for the business rule: under the framework’s reading, the rule and its persistence code carry the same change-driver assignment, and the layer boundaries split that class.
Its organising axis — technical role — is a proxy, not the change-driver structure.
It does no harm only where its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful wherever they do not. Even in the good case, layering adds no decomposition value, and placement is not faithful embodiment.

When read as a prescription rather than read from the domain, layering supplies no domain knowledge and no domain-grounded reason to choose it.

title: Layered Architecture
text:
12 Summary

Layered architecture divides the system into horizontal layers by technical role, each calling the one below. Its stated axis is technical role.
IVP does not group by technical role; it groups by change driver. The role axis is a proxy.
The layers — presentation, business logic, persistence — appear in no analysis artifact.
A layer is not independently replaceable: under the framework’s reading, a rule and its persistence code carry the same change-driver assignment, so the layer boundaries split one class (a Unit Completeness failure).
Where the layers coincide with the partition, layering adds nothing; where they do not, it invents structure the domain did not mandate.
The strongest defensible claim: layering’s layers are invented concepts except where they coincide with the partition. Its decomposition value is the partition, which one can obtain without it.
Layering does no harm only where its layers coincide with the change-driver decomposition; it is harmful where they do not. Placement is not faithful embodiment.
IVP is one modularising principle among those the system’s concerns induce; Γ-equivalence is the common refinement of them. The theory is a re-description, not a proof that no other kind of principle exists.

Compare vertical slice architecture, which cuts the other way, and hexagonal architecture.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
Vertical slice architecture organises code by feature or use case. Each slice runs end to end for one operation — request, validation, business rules, persistence — and slices do not share layers. There is no horizontal business layer; each slice holds what its operation needs. Bogard presents it as a response to the cross-layer editing that layering forces for a single feature [1].
So the question is not whether it admits to being a design. It does. The question is which parts of it embody the domain’s knowledge and which parts it invents.
This page applies the same test used for layered architecture, onion architecture, and hexagonal architecture: does the domain’s change-driver structure mandate the cut?

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
1 At a glance








Underlying principle
Succeeds when
Fails when




Slices group elements end to end by feature or use case.
Each feature carries its own change driver and no rule crosses features.
A cross-cutting change driver (tax, audit, authorisation) reaches every slice.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
2 The claim
A slice is a feature. “Place order,” “issue refund,” “cancel subscription”: each is a slice, cut end to end through request handling, rules, and storage. The claim is that a feature change stays inside its slice. Slices do not depend on one another.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 3 Slices divide by feature or use case
text:
3 Slices divide by feature or use case
Slicing’s axis is the feature or use case. Elements are grouped by which operation they serve.
This axis is closer to the domain than the rings of onion or clean, because an analyst names operations. Where a use case is a change-driver class, the slice coincides with the partition. The axis fails when a change driver spans features. IVP groups by which change activates an element; a rule that applies to every order — currency handling, tax, authorisation, audit — is one change driver, and it reaches every slice that processes an order [2]. So the feature axis is a proxy. It can coincide with the partition, when each feature carries its own change driver; it does not determine it.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 4 The slice is not in the domain’s analysis
text:
4 The slice is not in the domain’s analysis
A business analysis names use cases, processes, and capabilities. It does not organise knowledge as slices of code that each own a request handler and a persistence path. The use case is in the analysis; the slice is the code that encodes it. The end-to-end code unit — the thing that bundles one operation’s request, rules, and storage — appears when a designer lays out code; it is an encoding. This is the distinction the style blurs: the axis is domain-near, the code form is not. Absence of the code form from the analysis is evidence, not the test; the test is coincidence with the partition.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 5 A feature is not independent of the others
text:
5 A feature is not independent of the others
Vertical slicing’s strongest claim is that each feature changes independently. That is a claim about change. A slice exists to contain a feature’s change, so the coupling at issue is change coupling.
Under the framework’s reading, a cross-cutting rule drives every slice together: change the tax rule, and every slice that computes tax changes. Then the shared change driver reaches across slices, and each slice holds its feature change driver plus the shared rule’s change driver — two assignment sets where the slice wanted one. Each slice that must carry the shared rule becomes impure, and the shared rule’s class is scattered across slices — a Unit Completeness failure. The feature is independent only when no change driver crosses slices. That is the style’s hidden hypothesis: that the feature is the whole of its elements’ change story.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 6 What vertical slicing embodies, and what it invents
text:
6 What vertical slicing embodies, and what it invents
Two parts are worth separating.

The slice boundary is a claim about the cut. When its axis — the use case — is a change-driver class, the cut is domain-near: the business names the operation, and the slice follows it. That is the closest any style on this site comes to the partition, because the analyst already thinks in operations.
The assumption that the feature is the only change driver is the invention. A slice asserts that its feature is the whole of its elements’ change story. Where a cross-cutting change driver exists, the assertion is false, and the slice invents a unity — a feature boundary the domain does not have.

The general criterion applies. A representation is unavoidable; what is not unavoidable is inventing a concept — a named kind, boundary, or category — that the knowledge does not contain. A slice is such an invention exactly when it does not coincide with a change-driver class. If the slice groups elements with different change-driver assignments — its feature’s change driver plus a shared rule’s — it invents a unity; if its boundary separates elements with the same assignment, it invents a division. Only a slice that coincides with a Γ-equivalence class is not an invention, and then it is a redundant name for a real class.
By IVP’s foundational claim, the change-driver partition is the domain’s only organising knowledge [2]. Faithfulness admits no concept that does not correspond to a Γ-equivalence class; any structure beyond the partition is deviation, and deviation is the accidentality.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
section: 7 The split is not the style
text:
7 The split is not the style
The proof is in the artifacts. Grouping by change driver yields the partition; an engineer who embeds the domain faithfully, and who has never heard of vertical slices, arrives at the partition. She groups by what changes together. A slice per operation follows only where the operation is itself a change-driver class — which the analyst’s use cases sometimes are and sometimes are not.
Non-spontaneity is evidence, not proof. The slice’s axis is domain-near, so vertical slicing is the style most likely to coincide with the partition — and the one whose failure is most instructive where a cross-cutting change driver breaks the coincidence. The encoding is the designer’s, the partition is the domain’s.

title: Vertical Slice Architecture
text:
8 The IVP account

Judged by that standard, a slice is correct where no class straddles it and no two non-equivalent elements are grouped — that is, where its feature is the sole change driver of its elements.
Where a cross-cutting rule is present, it is not correct: the shared change driver makes each affected slice impure and scatters the shared rule’s class across slices — a Unit Completeness failure. Off the partition, the decomposition is wrong under the change-driver criterion.

text:

title: MATLAB (R2026a)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 39/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 61/100
Core Coupling Analysis: MATLAB’s matrix operations decouple iteration from computation by operating on entire matrices at once. Toolboxes decouple domain-specific functionality (signal processing, control systems, image processing) from the core language. The global workspace couples all variables into a single shared namespace. Arrays are 1-indexed, coupling code to a convention that differs from most other languages. Scripts pollute the namespace since all variables created in a script remain in the caller’s workspace. A script file’s primary function is tied to its filename (local functions in scripts are a modern addition), coupling source organization to the filesystem. Cell arrays and structs provide weak structural typing.
Platform & Ecosystem: MATLAB is excellent for numerical computation, signal processing, and control systems engineering. The commercial license couples projects to MathWorks’ pricing. Simulink provides graphical modeling of dynamic systems. The toolbox ecosystem is huge but entirely proprietary. The learning curve is moderate. GNU Octave provides an open-source alternative with high compatibility. Performance is good for matrix operations. The platform’s proprietary nature creates vendor lock-in.

title: R (4.5)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 47/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 50/100
Core Coupling Analysis: R’s vectorized operations decouple iteration from computation by operating on entire vectors at once. Data frames serve as the central abstraction for structured data. Functions are first-class values. The global environment couples the namespace by default. Non-standard evaluation (NSE) couples macro-like argument capture to the calling context, creating action-at-a-distance. Copy-on-modify semantics protect against accidental mutation but increase memory usage. Dynamic typing defers all coupling detection to runtime.
Platform & Ecosystem: R is the standard for statistics and data science. It has a massive package ecosystem through CRAN. RStudio provides an excellent IDE. R is slower than Python for many tasks but is improving. It is a perfect domain fit for statistical computing. The learning curve is steep due to quirks like the <- assignment operator, factor types, and non-standard evaluation. R is memory-intensive. Security risks include eval and other dynamic code execution features.

title: SQL (ANSI SQL:2023)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 85/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 80/100
Core Coupling Analysis: SQL’s declarative query model separates the specification of what data to retrieve from the procedural how of accessing it. The schema separates data structure from queries that consume it. Views decouple presentation logic from the underlying tables. Stored procedures, however, couple application logic to the database engine. Triggers create implicit coupling by executing side effects automatically in response to data changes. Vendor-specific SQL syntax couples queries to a particular database management system. Normalization decouples data redundancy by structuring tables to eliminate duplication.
Platform & Ecosystem: SQL is the universal standard for data querying and manipulation. Every major database system uses SQL in some form. Fragmentation persists across MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server, though ANSI SQL standards reduce this. Performance is excellent because decades of query optimization research deliver efficient execution plans. The learning curve is gentle for basic queries but steep for query optimization and complex joins. SQL injection remains a major security risk because queries are constructed as strings rather than parameterized by default.

title: D (2.112)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 61/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 92/100
Core Coupling Analysis: D is a systems language designed as a successor to C++, offering optional garbage collection alongside manual memory management. Its templates are more readable than C++ templates, avoiding the notorious angle-bracket verbosity. D’s module system decouples compilation units more cleanly than C++ headers, eliminating the need for include guards. UFCS (Universal Function Call Syntax) allows method-call syntax on any type without requiring the method to be defined inside the type, decoupling syntax from definition site. Contract programming with in, out, and invariant blocks separates preconditions, postconditions, and invariants from implementation logic. The @safe, @trusted, and @system attributes separate memory-safety guarantees at the function level. CTFE (Compile-Time Function Execution) decouples metaprogramming from runtime overhead by allowing arbitrary functions to execute during compilation. BetterC mode supports embedded and no-GC environments. D supports multiple paradigms: imperative, object-oriented, functional, and metaprogramming.
Platform & Ecosystem: D follows a design philosophy summarized as “Better C++”: it provides C++-level performance and low-level control while simplifying the language with cleaner templates, a proper module system, no preprocessor, and both garbage collected and manual memory management options. Its ecosystem is smaller than Rust or C++ and its adoption remains niche rather than mainstream. Performance is excellent because D compiles to native code; the reference compiler dmd uses its own Digital-Mars backend, while the alternative compilers ldc (LLVM) and gdc (GCC) provide LLVM- and GCC-based backends. BetterC mode targets embedded systems and no-garbage-collection environments. The learning curve is moderate for developers familiar with C++. Tooling is improving, with dub as the standard package manager. The syntax is cleaner than C++ while providing similar expressive power. D is a good fit for game development, and the vibe.d framework supports web development. Corporate backing is weak, and the community is small but dedicated.

title: JavaScript (ES2025)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ No static types: All coupling deferred to runtime
✅ Prototypes decouple: Can modify behavior without inheritance
⚠️ Duck typing: Structural at runtime, but no safety
❌ Type coercion couples: Implicit conversions hide intent

Object Construction:

✅ Object literals: Simple construction without classes
⚠️ Prototypes flexible: Can change after construction
❌ new keyword confusing: this binding couples to call context
⚠️ Factory functions decouple: Can avoid new entirely

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Generational GC (implementation dependent)
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: V8, SpiderMonkey, etc. have different characteristics
❌ Closure captures create leaks: Easy to accidentally hold references
❌ Event listener leaks common: Forgotten listeners prevent collection
❌ DOM circular references: Event handlers can create uncollectable cycles
⚠️ WeakMap/WeakRef help: Can create weak references, but not automatic

Error Handling:

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking
❌ Promise rejection unchecked: .catch() optional
⚠️ Result types possible: Libraries exist but uncommon
❌ Callbacks couple error/success: (err, result) mixes concerns

Concurrency:

✅ Event loop implicit: Single-threaded simplifies
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions
❌ Promise errors untracked: Rejection type unknown
⚠️ Web Workers separate: Explicit message passing, but manual

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Global scope couples: window, globalThis everywhere
❌ Module side effects: Import order matters
❌ this binding couples: Context depends on call site
❌ Undefined/null confusion: Two absence types couple
❌ Prototype pollution: Can modify built-in prototypes globally

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Dynamic Typing vs. Predictability: All coupling deferred to runtime, no compile-time detection
Flexibility vs. Correctness: Can modify anything at runtime, couples correctness to discipline
Type Coercion: Implicit conversions couple values to contexts ("5" + 3 === "53", "5" - 3 === 2)
This Binding: Function context couples to call site (.call(), .apply(), .bind() required)
Callback Hell vs. Promises vs. Async/Await: Three async paradigms couple code to era written
Module Systems: CommonJS vs. ES6 modules couples code to environment (Node vs. browser)
Prototype Chain: Inheritance couples objects to prototype chain modifications

Core Coupling Score: 28/100

Type System & Abstraction:

⚠️ Type declarations (PHP 7+): Gradual typing, improving
⚠️ Interfaces decouple: Can program to interfaces
❌ Weak typing historically: Type juggling couples
⚠️ Traits: Multiple inheritance-like, can couple

Object Construction:

⚠️ Constructors can have side effects: No enforcement
❌ No immutability by default: Everything mutable
⚠️ Dependency injection available: Frameworks support it
❌ Global state tempting: $_GET, $_POST, $_SESSION couple

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Reference counting: Immediate deallocation when references drop to zero
✅ Cycle collector: Detects and breaks circular references
✅ Request-scoped by default: Each request has isolated memory, cleared after request
⚠️ Destructors timing predictable: __destruct runs when refcount hits zero
❌ Long-running processes leak: Traditional PHP has no long-lived processes, but Swoole/ReactPHP do
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free in pure PHP
⚠️ Extensions can leak: C extensions may have memory issues

Error Handling:

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking
⚠️ Error vs Exception confusion: Two error mechanisms couple
❌ @ operator suppresses errors: Hides coupling
⚠️ Modern frameworks handle better: Laravel/Symfony impose discipline

Concurrency:

❌ Shared-nothing by default: Each request is separate process
✅ Fibers (PHP 8.1): Built-in cooperative concurrency — enables async I/O without external extensions
⚠️ No built-in async event loop: Fibers need a framework (ReactPHP, Swoole) for full async; however Revolt/Amp provide fiber-based event loops
❌ Global state couples across requests: Sessions, databases
⚠️ Request-per-process prevents some coupling: But wastes resources

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Superglobals couple: $_GET, $_POST, $_SESSION, $_SERVER everywhere
❌ Inconsistent stdlib: strpos vs str_replace couples to memorization
❌ Type juggling couples: Implicit conversions hide intent
❌ Global namespace historically: Modern namespaces help
⚠️ Magic methods can hide coupling: __get, __call obscure behavior
