title: Ruby (4.0)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ Duck typing: No compile-time type checking, coupling invisible
✅ Pattern matching (3.0+): case/in provides exhaustive structural matching
✅ Mixins: Include modules for behavior without inheritance
⚠️ Open classes: Can modify any class, creates action-at-a-distance coupling
⚠️ RBS type signatures: External type system (.rbs files) — static checking via Steep/Sorbet, not built into runtime
✅ Blocks/Procs/Lambdas: First-class functions decouple behavior

Object Construction:

✅ initialize separate from new: Construction logic decoupled
✅ Data.define (3.2+): Immutable value objects like records/kotlin data classes
⚠️ Class methods for factories: Common pattern but not enforced
❌ No validation enforcement: Constructor invariants not checked

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection: Automatic, no manual management
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, couples performance to runtime (improved by YJIT’s reduced allocation rate)
✅ No manual deallocation: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ YJIT reduces GC pressure: Faster execution means fewer long-lived allocations

Error Handling:

❌ Unchecked exceptions: raise doesn’t appear in signatures
❌ Broad rescue: rescue without type catches everything
✅ Pattern matching with => operator (3.0+): Can destructure error objects structurally
❌ Silent failures: Methods often return nil instead of raising

Concurrency:

❌ Global VM Lock (GVL): Like Python’s GIL, couples threads to single core
✅ Fibers + Fiber Scheduler (3.0+): Cooperative concurrency with io_uring support for async I/O
✅ M:N thread scheduler (3.3+, experimental → progressing): Lightweight userspace threads
⚠️ Ractors: Actor-like concurrency (3.0+), still evolving
❌ Shared mutable state: No protection, race conditions easy

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Monkey patching: Can modify any class anywhere, global coupling
❌ Global variables: $global creates pervasive coupling
❌ Class variables: @@var shared across all instances, couples classes
❌ Method_missing: Dynamic dispatch hides coupling, runtime failures
❌ Open classes: Modification anywhere affects everywhere

text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 55/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 65/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Scratch uses visual blocks to represent code, decoupling programming syntax from logic so beginners can focus on computational thinking rather than syntax errors. The event-driven model decouples triggers (green flag, key press, message received) from the actions they invoke. Sprites couple behavior to visual objects, making each sprite a self-contained unit. Global variables couple the namespace since all sprites can potentially read and write any variable. Broadcasts couple events globally — any sprite can listen for any broadcast. The absence of types defers all coupling detection to runtime, though the constrained environment limits the damage.
Platform & Ecosystem: Scratch is excellent for education, designed for children and beginners learning programming concepts. It is a visual programming environment, not a text-based language. It is very limited for real-world applications beyond educational use. Scratch has massive adoption in K-12 education worldwide. The learning curve is effectively zero because the interface is drag-and-drop. It is not used in production environments. Security is provided by the sandboxed runtime environment. Scratch is developed by the MIT Media Lab.

title: Erlang (OTP 29)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 69/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 76/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Actor model decouples processes by design — no shared memory, message passing only. “Let it crash” philosophy decouples error handling from business logic via OTP (Open Telecom Platform) supervision trees. Pattern matching on binaries and messages exhaustively separates cases. Immutable data by default avoids mutation coupling. Hot code swapping decouples deployment from runtime, allowing upgrades without restarting the system. Dynamic typing couples correctness to runtime, mitigated by Dialyzer, a static analysis tool that detects type inconsistencies. No null: atoms serve as named constants instead. Per-process GC isolates memory collection — pauses affect one process at a time rather than the entire system, avoiding global stop-the-world pauses. The BEAM virtual machine provides preemptive scheduling, so one slow process cannot block others. Main weakness: dynamic typing, and distribution across nodes requires explicit design effort.
Platform & Ecosystem: Designed for telecom at Ericsson in 1986, Erlang excels at distributed, fault-tolerant systems and powers WhatsApp, RabbitMQ, and Discord. OTP provides battle-tested patterns for supervision, state management, and hot code reloading. The BEAM VM has over 30 years of maturity. The ecosystem includes Hex.pm for packages, rebar3 and mix for builds, and growing tooling. Elixir’s ecosystem is accessible via Erlang interop. Performance is excellent for I/O-bound workloads but weak for CPU-bound computation. The actor concurrency model is widely regarded as the gold standard. The syntax is Prolog-derived and unfamiliar to most developers. The learning curve is steep, combining functional programming, the actor model, and OTP.

text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 58/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 61/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Solidity is a statically typed, ECMAScript-syntax language for writing smart contracts that run on the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). Its coupling profile is tightly constrained by its domain. Contracts are the unit of encapsulation, and the language supports inheritance, including multiple inheritance with C3 linearization. It has complex member variables (hierarchical mappings and structs) and a type-safe ABI for multiple functions per contract. But coupling is pervasive and domain-specific: the blockchain context injects globals like msg.sender into every contract, coupling logic to the calling account. require/revert/errors make failure explicit but are not a general exception system. The EVM is single-threaded with gas accounting, so there is no concurrency in the usual sense and execution is tightly coupled to gas limits. Solidity has been criticized for being error-prone and for lacking constructs to handle blockchain-specific concerns, and its Turing-completeness means arbitrary-property verification cannot be automated decidably.
Platform & Ecosystem: Solidity is the primary language for Ethereum and other EVM-compatible blockchains, so it has a substantial young ecosystem (Foundry, Hardhat, Truffle). But it is niche, young, and carries significant security risk — it was partly blamed for The DAO hack (2016), and the smart-contract domain is rife with reentrancy and other vulnerabilities that are hard to reason about. Performance is poor in general-computing terms (EVM is slow and gas-metered). The language evolves actively (0.8.x releases), and static typing helps, but the tooling and security story remain immature relative to general-purpose languages. It is the right tool only for on-chain smart contracts; outside that domain it has no value.

The learning curve is gentle, building on decades of BASIC heritage. VB.NET has full access to the .NET ecosystem. A clear migration path to C# exists. Modern VB.NET is substantially better than VB6. Microsoft is deprecating VB.NET as a first-class language.

text: Analysis against C# 13 (.NET 9). C# 12/13 add primary constructors, collection expressions, params collections, and lock type.

title: C# (13)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Interfaces + extension methods: Can add behavior without coupling to classes
✅ Generics with constraints: Better than Java (no erasure, value type generics)
✅ LINQ separates iteration from logic: Query syntax decouples data operations
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Can couple via class hierarchies
✅ Nullable reference types (C# 8+): Separates nullable from non-nullable
✅ File-scoped types (C# 11): file access modifier restricts visibility to a source file, tightening encapsulation

Object Construction:

✅ Object initializers decouple: new Person { Name = "Alice", Age = 30 }
✅ Records (C# 9+) are immutable: Value semantics prevent coupling
✅ Primary constructors (C# 12): Reduce construction boilerplate on class/struct
✅ Collection expressions (C# 12): [1, 2, 3] unified syntax decouples creation from collection type
⚠️ Constructors can have side effects: No enforcement of pure construction
✅ DI built into ASP.NET Core: Framework-level construction decoupling

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ .NET GC decouples memory: Generational GC (gen0, gen1, gen2, LOH)
✅ No manual memory management for managed code: Safe by default
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Server/workstation GC modes, background GC helps
✅ IDisposable pattern for resources: Deterministic cleanup via using statement
⚠️ Finalizers couple cleanup to GC: Non-deterministic timing
⚠️ Stack-allocated structs: Value types avoid GC but couple to stack lifetime
✅ Span reduces allocations: Stack-based memory without GC pressure

Error Handling:

❌ Unchecked exceptions: No throws clause, errors hidden
⚠️ Result types uncommon: Libraries exist (LanguageExt) but not idiomatic
⚠️ Nullable pattern helps: ?. operator reduces null coupling

Concurrency:

✅ Async/await excellent: Best async syntax in mainstream languages
✅ Task separates async: Clear distinction from sync code
✅ Lock type (C# 13): Dedicated System.Threading.Lock with pattern-based using scoping — decouples synchronization from object casting
❌ Can still use threads with shared state: Traditional coupling available
✅ Immutable collections available: System.Collections.Immutable, FrozenSet/FrozenDictionary (C# 12+) prevent concurrent coupling with zero overhead

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Null still exists alongside nullable types: Migration incomplete
❌ Static state couples: Singleton patterns common
❌ Properties can have side effects: obj.Prop might do anything
⚠️ .NET runtime allows reflection: Can break encapsulation

text: Analysis against Go 1.26 (February 2026). Generics have been stable since 1.18 (March 2022) — over 4 years of production use. Go 1.24 added generic type aliases; Go 1.26 adds further generic and runtime improvements.

title: Go (1.26)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Implicit interfaces radical decoupling: No declaration of implementation, duck typing at compile time
✅ Composition over inheritance: No inheritance, only struct embedding
✅ Small interfaces: Convention is single-method interfaces (io.Reader, io.Writer)
✅ Generics (stable since 1.18): Type parameters eliminate interface{} casts — slices.Sort, maps.Clone, cmp.Or are type-safe (note: sync.Map remains a non-generic any-keyed type)
✅ Range-over-func (1.23): Custom iteration patterns via iter.Seq[T] decouple iteration protocol from data structure
⚠️ No higher-kinded types: Generics are first-order type parameters only
✅ min/max/clear builtins (1.21): Built-in operations eliminate unnecessary function coupling

Object Construction:

✅ Zero values make sense: Default initialization doesn’t couple to constructors
✅ Constructors are conventions: NewX() functions, not special syntax
⚠️ Can couple to package-level state: init() functions run at import

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Concurrent mark-sweep GC with sub-millisecond pause targets
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ Escape analysis optimizes: Stack allocation when possible, decouples from explicit allocation
✅ Profile-guided optimization (1.22+): Compiler uses runtime profiles to optimize, decoupling performance from manual tuning
⚠️ Defer couples cleanup to function exit: Not immediate, but predictable
✅ Simple memory model: No complex ownership rules

Error Handling:

✅ Explicit error returns: func foo() (Result, error) makes errors visible
❌ No error composition: Can’t map/flatMap errors natively
❌ if err != nil boilerplate: Error handling doesn’t compose
⚠️ Panic exists but rare: Explicit, but not in type system
⚠️ errors.Join (1.20): Can combine multiple errors, improving composition slightly

Concurrency:

✅ Goroutines separate concurrency: Lightweight, easy to spawn
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples
✅ Select decouples multiplexing: Wait on multiple channels independently
✅ Structured logging (slog, 1.21): Decouples logging concerns from application logic
⚠️ Can share memory: Mutexes allow traditional coupling, but discouraged

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Nil everywhere: nil pointers, nil interfaces couple code to nil checks (no sum types to replace nil)
❌ Global package state: Package-level variables couple to initialization order
❌ Error handling doesn’t compose: Repetitive if err != nil; generics enable Result types but not idiomatic
⚠️ Interfaces can be nil with non-nil value: (nil, *T) couples interface semantics

Core Coupling Score: 58/100 (Go 1.26 — mature generics, range-over-func, slog)

Goroutines and channels separate concurrency from shared-memory synchronization. Generics, stable for over three years, eliminate interface{} casts. Range-over-func enables custom iteration without coupling to built-in loop constructs. Main strength: simplicity prevents complex coupling from emerging. Main weakness: nil is still everywhere, error handling does not compose, and the language has no sum types or pattern matching.

✅ Predictable: Deallocation timing known

✅ Do-try-catch: Explicit error handling, checked at call site
✅ Result<T, E> available: For functional-style composable error handling
⚠️ Failable initializers: init? returns nil instead of throwing
⚠️ Force unwrap: ! bypasses safety, couples to runtime crash
✅ Guard statements: Early exit decouples validation from logic

Concurrency:

✅ Swift Concurrency (async/await): Built-in, structured concurrency
✅ Actors: Data race prevention via isolation
✅ Sendable protocol + strict concurrency checking (Swift 6, on by default): Compile-time thread safety with full enforcement
✅ Task-based: Decouples concurrent operations

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Value vs Reference: Structs vs Classes creates identity coupling decisions
ARC vs Manual: Retain cycles require weak/unowned discipline
Swift vs Objective-C: Interop couples to legacy patterns
Protocol Extensions: Default implementations can create hidden coupling

⚠️ Classes allow inheritance: Can create coupling hierarchies
✅ Protocol-oriented programming: Composition over inheritance

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Automatic Reference Counting (ARC): Deterministic, no GC pauses
⚠️ Retain cycles possible: Weak/unowned references needed for graphs
✅ Value types: No reference counting for structs
✅ Predictable: Deallocation timing known
⚠️ Objective-C interop: Can introduce manual memory management

Error Handling:

✅ Typed throws (Swift 6): throws(MyError) makes error types explicit in signatures — a major coupling improvement over untyped throws
✅ Do-try-catch: Explicit error handling, checked at call site
✅ Result<T, E> available: For functional-style composable error handling
⚠️ Failable initializers: init? returns nil instead of throwing
⚠️ Force unwrap: ! bypasses safety, couples to runtime crash
✅ Guard statements: Early exit decouples validation from logic

Concurrency:

✅ Swift Concurrency (async/await): Built-in, structured concurrency
✅ Actors: Data race prevention via isolation
✅ Sendable protocol + strict concurrency checking (Swift 6, on by default): Compile-time thread safety with full enforcement
✅ Task-based: Decouples concurrent operations
⚠️ Grand Central Dispatch (GCD): Legacy API still available, manual

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Force unwrap (!): Bypasses type safety, couples to runtime crashes
❌ Implicitly unwrapped optionals: String! hides nil possibility
❌ Objective-C interop: Can bypass Swift safety guarantees
❌ Dynamic dispatch overhead: Protocol witness tables couple performance

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Value vs Reference: Structs vs Classes creates identity coupling decisions
ARC vs Manual: Retain cycles require weak/unowned discipline
Swift vs Objective-C: Interop couples to legacy patterns
Protocol Extensions: Default implementations can create hidden coupling

title: The Objective Coupling Scoring Model: Full Mechanism Data for 65 Languages
text:
Companion to: The Great Language Smackdown: 65 Languages Through the Coupling Lens

The main article ranks 65 languages by language-imposed coupling. This companion publishes the complete per-language mechanism-presence data behind every score, so any reader can reproduce any number from first principles — no trust required.
The coupling analysis this model operationalizes — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the derivation of a modularisation directive from coupling — is developed in the published coupling papers [1], [2].
Analysis date: June 2026. All languages are assessed against the version shown.


The model is a capped-sum-per-dimension inventory:

A fixed mechanism inventory, each mechanism with a fixed weight.
For each language, every mechanism is marked present or absent (a factual determination).
Within each of the six Core dimensions (and eight Meta dimensions), the present weights are summed and clamped to at most −15.
Score = 100 − Σ(capped per-dimension contributions).

The cap equals the High weight (−15), so a dimension never costs more than one severe mechanism. This keeps scores bounded (minimum Core = 10), monotone (adding a mechanism never helps), and discriminative (no collapse to zero).


Because the model is a fixed-inventory capped-sum-per-dimension model, the bands follow directly from the mechanism weights:

90+: No dimension contains a severe (High) mechanism, and at most one dimension reaches even −8. Near the irreducible floor.
75–89: No dimension reaches −15; a small number of moderate (−8) mechanisms spread across dimensions.
60–74: At least one dimension caps at −15 (a severe mechanism), or several dimensions carry moderate mechanisms.
45–59: Two or three dimensions cap at −15, or one severe mechanism plus several moderate across other dimensions.
Below 45: Three or more dimensions cap at −15 — the language’s design trades separation of concerns for other goals (simplicity, flexibility, ubiquity, or direct hardware access).




The dimension sub-scores shown in the main article’s comparison matrices are the per-dimension contribution: 100 minus the capped sum of the present mechanisms in that dimension only. They are not independent scores — they are the building blocks of the composite, so a language’s Core score always equals 100 minus the sum of its six capped per-dimension contributions.

title: C shell (csh 8.2 / tcsh)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 57/100
Core Coupling Analysis: The C shell, created by Bill Joy in 1978, introduced a built-in expression grammar (borrowed from C) and a strong set of interactive features. But for scripting it scores among the lowest for coupling separation. Everything is words or strings with no type system. All shell variables are global by default, coupling the namespace. The language has no functions; aliases and script recursion are used as workarounds. The parser is ad hoc rather than recursive, so it cannot pipe between control structures (e.g., piping a foreach into grep fails) and produces cryptic errors. The syntax is inconsistent — set, setenv, and alias do the same thing but with different rules, and blocks terminate with endif, endsw, and end needlessly differently. Variable, command, and history substitution create implicit dependencies on execution context. Its strengths are interactive (history !!, aliases, tilde notation, directory stack, job control, path hashing), not separation of concerns.
Platform & Ecosystem: The C shell introduced many interactive innovations later copied by other shells (history, aliases, tilde notation, filename completion, job control). But it has never been popular for scripting, and the POSIX committee favored KornShell for both interactive and scripting use. The original csh has been frozen since 1993 (version 8.2); tcsh is the maintained successor and is what csh usually points to on macOS and many Linux systems. The implementation is criticized for its ad-hoc parser, missing features, and poor error messages (e.g., “0: Event not found.”). It remains on BSD, Linux, and macOS for interactive use and legacy scripts, but Bash and PowerShell are far better choices for scripting.

title: Ksh (kSH 93u+)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 68/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Ksh sits between Bash and classic sh in capability. Ksh93 supports associative arrays and provides better string manipulation than standard sh. Coprocesses enable inter-process communication. Floating-point arithmetic is supported, unlike in Bash. However, global variables are still the default everywhere. Functions are more capable than in standard sh. Ksh is POSIX-compliant with vendor extensions.
Platform & Ecosystem: Ksh has historical importance and directly influenced Bash’s design. The ksh93 version is the most advanced implementation. Ksh was used in commercial Unix systems like AIX and Solaris. Adoption is declining as Bash dominates Linux. Performance is competitive with other shells. Licensing was historically an issue but Ksh is now open source. The learning curve is moderate. Its ecosystem is smaller than Bash or Zsh.

title: Sh (POSIX.1-2024)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 57/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Sh implements the minimal POSIX shell specification. It has no arrays and no associative arrays. Everything is a string. Functions are minimal, and the original specification had no local variables. Testing uses [ rather than [[. Sh is the most portable but least powerful shell. Global namespace pollution is unavoidable because all variables are global by default.
Platform & Ecosystem: Sh offers maximum portability, guaranteed on all Unix and Linux systems. Dash is commonly used as the /bin/sh implementation. Sh is minimalist by design. Scripts written for sh run everywhere POSIX is supported. Performance is fast due to minimal feature overhead. Sh has no interactive features. The learning curve is gentle because there are few features to learn. It is used for boot scripts and system scripts where portability is critical.

title: C (C23)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Structs separate data: Pure data, no methods
✅ Function pointers enable polymorphism: Can pass behavior as data
❌ No encapsulation: Everything is public
❌ No generics: Void pointers couple to type casting
✅ No inheritance: Can’t create coupled hierarchies

Object Construction:

✅ Explicit memory management: Allocation separate from initialization
✅ Designated initializers: Can initialize specific fields
❌ No constructors: Manual initialization couples to usage
❌ Global state common: Static variables couple modules

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Manual control enables precise memory strategy: Can separate memory management from logic
✅ Explicit allocation/deallocation: malloc/free make lifetime visible
❌ No safety: use-after-free, double-free, memory leaks all possible
❌ No RAII: Must manually track and free resources
✅ Predictable: No GC pauses, deterministic performance
❌ Pointer arithmetic couples to memory layout: Buffer overruns couple to hardware
✅ Custom allocators: Can decouple allocation strategy (arena, pool, etc.)
❌ Undefined behavior on errors: Memory safety violations are UB

Error Handling:

✅ Explicit error codes: Return values make errors visible
❌ No enforcement: Can ignore return values
❌ errno couples: Global error state couples functions
❌ NULL everywhere: Pointer errors couple all code

Concurrency:

❌ pthreads manual: All synchronization explicit
❌ Shared mutable state default: No protection
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No prevention
⚠️ Explicit is predictable: At least coupling is visible

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Pointers couple to memory layout: No abstraction over memory
❌ Header files couple: Includes create compilation dependencies
❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope
❌ No namespaces: Global namespace pollution
❌ Undefined behavior: Buffer overruns, null derefs

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Power vs. Safety: Complete control couples to complete responsibility for safety
Simplicity vs. Safety: No abstractions means manual discipline required to control coupling
Performance vs. Correctness: Optimization couples to unsafe patterns (buffer tricks, pointer arithmetic)
Portability vs. Platform Access: Platform-specific code couples to hardware/OS
Manual Memory Management: Must couple resource acquisition to every usage site
Undefined Behavior Everywhere: Memory errors couple entire program to runtime environment
Header Dependencies: Changes to one header couple to all files that include it (transitively)

Core Coupling Score: 25/100

Verdict: C provides no coupling prevention mechanisms but also imposes few forced coupling constructs — the language itself is neutral. With discipline, developers can separate concerns through function pointers, explicit error codes, and manual memory management. Without discipline, globals, macros, and undefined behavior couple everything. Main insight: coupling in C is entirely up to the programmer. The same language can produce extremely low or extremely high coupling depending on how it is used.

title: F# (9)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Discriminated unions separate cases: Like Haskell ADTs
✅ Type providers decouple data access from code: SQL, JSON, etc. accessed via types generated from schemas
⚠️ OOP interop allows inheritance coupling: Can use C# classes with inheritance, coupling subclasses to base classes

Object Construction:

✅ Immutable records by default: Construction doesn’t couple to mutation
✅ With-copy syntax decouples updates: { person with Age = 30 } doesn’t modify original
⚠️ Can use .NET constructors with side effects: Interop allows coupled construction

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ .NET GC decouples memory: Generational GC handles deallocation
✅ Immutability simplifies GC: Fewer mutable references, cleaner collection
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Non-deterministic pauses, though .NET GC is mature
⚠️ Can use IDisposable from .NET: Manual resource management via use keyword couples cleanup
✅ Garbage collection handles closures: Captured references are traced by the .NET GC, not by reference counting

Error Handling:

✅ Result type separates success/failure: Result<'T, 'Error> makes errors explicit
⚠️ Can throw .NET exceptions: Interop allows unchecked exceptions
✅ Railway-oriented programming pattern: The community embraces this functional error-handling style where success and failure paths are composed like parallel railroad tracks using Result types

Concurrency:

✅ Async workflows decouple async from sync: async { } blocks separate concerns
✅ MailboxProcessor for actors: Message passing decouples concurrent operations
⚠️ .NET threads allow shared mutable state: Interop permits coupling

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ .NET interop is double-edged: Allows violations via C# patterns
❌ Mutable cells exist: Can create ref cells, coupling to mutable state
❌ Nulls from .NET: Nullable references from C# libraries reintroduce null-checking coupling

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Functional Purity vs. .NET Interop: Can’t enforce purity when calling C# code
Type Safety vs. Practical Libraries: .NET libraries use null, exceptions, mutation—F# must accommodate
Railway-Oriented Programming vs. Exceptions: Community promotes Result types but .NET uses exceptions
Immutability by Default vs. Performance: Persistent data structures slower than .NET mutable collections
FP Culture vs. OOP Platform: F# encourages FP but runs on OOP-first platform

title: PureScript (0.15)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ All Haskell benefits plus algebraic effects: Effect system separates different effect types (unlike Haskell’s monolithic IO)
✅ Row polymorphism for extensible records: Can decouple from exact record shape
✅ Type classes with functional dependencies: More precise abstraction control

Object Construction:

✅ Same as Haskell: ADTs, smart constructors, no global state

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ JavaScript GC decouples memory: Compiles to JS, inherits JS GC
✅ Immutability simplifies: No cyclic mutable references
⚠️ JavaScript GC pauses: Non-deterministic, inherited from JS runtime
✅ No space leaks from laziness: Strict evaluation by default (unlike Haskell)
⚠️ JS interop can create leaks: Foreign JS code may hold references

Error Handling:

✅ Effect system makes errors explicit by type: Effect (console :: CONSOLE, exception :: EXCEPTION) Unit shows exactly what can fail
✅ Explicit exception handling: No hidden runtime exceptions

Concurrency:

✅ Aff monad for async: Separates async coordination from sync logic
✅ Effect tracking prevents coupling: Can’t accidentally do async in sync code

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ JavaScript FFI can bypass type safety: Interop creates coupling holes
❌ Small ecosystem means reinventing wheels: Couples you to specific libraries

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Type Safety vs. JavaScript Interop: FFI boundary loses all guarantees, couples to JS runtime behavior
Effect Granularity vs. Complexity: Fine-grained effect tracking increases cognitive load
Compile Target Constraints: Must fit JavaScript semantics, can’t have true parallelism
Ecosystem Size vs. Quality: Small community means fewer libraries but tighter coupling to available ones

title: Cohesion
text: The cohesion series reworks one of the oldest concepts in software design. Its core conclusions are developed across this set of pages.

title: Cohesion
text:
1 Where cohesion sits
Cohesion and coupling are the two classical “quality” measures of modular structure. The cohesion series gives cohesion a principled definition: correctness relative to a partitioning rule [1]. The coupling page does the same for coupling — and shows that within any single dimension, coupling is a consequence of cohesion, not an independent objective.
Cohesion is distinct from IVP, though the two are related. IVP groups elements by change-driver assignment. Cohesion is the more general measure of correctness relative to any partitioning rule. The change-driver rule is one instance of that general idea — the instance IVP is built on.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
The cohesion survey [1] reviews every metric in the literature that carries a “cohesion” label: 24 metrics, from LCOM1 (1994) to MOGA (2010). Its finding is stark: every one of them measures a structural property of the code — shared fields, call connections, dependency edges, execution traces — and none measures cohesion itself. The proliferation is itself a symptom: the field has never agreed on what cohesion is, so each metric chose a different structural graph to stand in for the concept.
This page summarizes what each metric actually measures. For the series’ positive account — cohesion as correctness relative to a partitioning rule — see core conclusions.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
1 Measuring cohesion by its absence
The best-known family is literally named for a lack: LCOM stands for Lack of Cohesion in Methods. Higher LCOM means less cohesion. This is not a polarity quirk that a sign change would fix. An LCOM variant counts something structural — method pairs that do not share fields, connected components that are absent — and negating the score yields only the negation of the proxy, not cohesion.
There is a deeper confusion beneath the naming. Every LCOM variant operates on the method–attribute access graph: the raw input is a coupling relation. LCOM counts pairs for which that coupling does not hold and reports the count as cohesion. By its own data, the LCOM family is a family of coupling metrics that have been called cohesion metrics since their origin.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
text:
3 Why this matters
The metrics differ in which coupling relation they extract, which transformation they apply, and which normalisation they prefer. They do not differ in what they measure: all measure coupling and report it as cohesion.
This has three practical consequences, developed in the survey:

The cohesion–coupling tradeoff is an artifact of measurement convention. Cohesion metrics count internal edges and coupling metrics count cross-boundary edges of the same graph. Designers balancing the two are balancing one dependency relation against itself under two labels.
A high score can mask a mess. When elements that belong apart happen to share many fields or call each other, LCOM, TCC, and LCC all report high cohesion. Structurally cohesive modules receive a quality signal the metric cannot support.
LCOM-triggered refactoring can reward the wrong direction. Standard heuristics treat LCOM thresholds as extract-class triggers. But LCOM detects structural clustering, not principled misgrouping.

None of this makes the metrics useless. Correlation with fault-proneness and maintenance effort has been reported across multiple studies, so structural scores work as screening heuristics and change predictors. The limitation is interpretative: the score measures coupling density, and domain knowledge about grouping conditions is needed to say more.

title: Cohesion Metrics: What Each One Actually Measures
section: 4 Where the series goes from here
text:
4 Where the series goes from here
The survey establishes the negative result: no structural metric measures principled cohesion. Later papers in the cohesion series give cohesion a positive definition — correctness relative to a partitioning rule — and derive a metric from the reason elements change rather than from the footprint of their co-location. See core conclusions and knowledge embodiment.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
Under a single partitioning rule, a module can deviate in exactly two ways: it can hold elements that do not belong, or it can be missing elements that do. These defects are independent — a module can have either, both, or neither — and they demand opposite repairs. That structure forces the answer to a natural question: how many numbers must a cohesion metric report?
This page proves that the answer is two. One axis cannot distinguish the two failure modes; two axes can; and no third axis adds anything for this purpose. The pair — purity and completeness — is the minimal adequate output for a rule.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
1 One rule, two opposite defects
Fix a partitioning rule PP [1] and assess a module MM against the class CC it should realize.

Impurity. MM contains an element outside CC. The remedy is to remove it — to split.
Incompleteness. Some element of CC lies outside MM. The remedy is to add it — to merge.

Write the two axes as
purity(M)=|M∩C||M|,completeness(M)=|M∩C||C|.
\text{purity}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|M|},
\qquad
\text{completeness}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|C|}.

Both lie in [0,1][0,1]. The two defects are independent in the strict sense: all four combinations occur.

The two failure modes point in opposite directions. Merely knowing that “cohesion is low” is therefore of no help: the correct action could be to split or to merge, and the two actions are opposites.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
2 One axis is not enough

Proposition (dimensional necessity). Let s(M)=g(purity(M),completeness(M))s(M) = g(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) be any scalar that factors through the pair. (a) If gg is symmetric, there are two modules of opposite defect whose scores are exactly equal. (b) If gg is continuous and strictly increasing in each argument, the two defect classes are indistinguishable to any finite precision, and no threshold on the score separates them.

Proof. Fix a rule with a class CC of size 44, and four foreign elements x1,…,x4x_1,\dots,x_4 from another class.

M1=C∪{x1,…,x4}M_1 = C \cup \{x_1,\dots,x_4\} has purity=4/8=1/2\text{purity} = 4/8 = 1/2 and completeness=4/4=1\text{completeness} = 4/4 = 1: impure but complete.
M2={a,b}M_2 = \{a,b\} for a,b∈Ca,b \in C has purity=2/2=1\text{purity} = 2/2 = 1 and completeness=2/4=1/2\text{completeness} = 2/4 = 1/2: pure but incomplete.

Both are realizable in one system.
(a) A symmetric gg gives s(M1)=g(1/2,1)=g(1,1/2)=s(M2)s(M_1) = g(1/2, 1) = g(1, 1/2) = s(M_2) — exactly equal scores for opposite defects. The geometric mean pc\sqrt{pc} scores both at 1/21/\sqrt{2}; so does the arithmetic mean, and every other symmetric aggregate.
(b) The impure-but-complete modules trace the curve B1={(p,1):0<p<1}B_1 = \{(p,1) : 0<p<1\}; the pure-but-incomplete modules trace B2={(1,c):0<c<1}B_2 = \{(1,c) : 0<c<1\}. Strict monotonicity makes g(1,1)g(1,1) the supremum of gg on both curves; continuity makes each image g(B1)g(B_1), g(B2)g(B_2) an interval with that same supremum. Two intervals with a common supremum overlap, so some (p*,1)∈B1(p^*,1) \in B_1 and some (1,c*)∈B2(1,c^*) \in B_2 satisfy g(p*,1)=g(1,c*)g(p^*,1) = g(1,c^*). An impure-complete module and a pure-incomplete module therefore share the same score, and their images approach one another without limit as either defect shrinks. No threshold on the score line can separate “split” from “merge.” ◼\blacksquare
This is why “low cohesion” as a single graded quantity cannot guide a repair. The score is monotonically related to both faults, but it cannot tell the designer which of the two is present — the one thing the designer needs to act.
A caveat keeps the claim honest. The impossibility is for scalars that behave as measurements — symmetric, or continuous and monotone in the two axes. A pathologically discontinuous injection could in principle pack the pair into one real number, but such a function is not a score: it carries no magnitude or ordering that corresponds to defect severity, and it does not arise from the purity/completeness semantics. Every actual cohesion score — a product, a mean, a weighted sum, a distance from the ideal — is continuous and monotone, and every one of them falls to the proposition.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
3 Two axes are enough
The pair not only fails to lose information — it loses none that matters. It determines the failure mode exactly.

Proposition (sufficiency). The pair (purity(M),completeness(M))(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) determines which of the four states a module is in.

Proof. Two equivalences, immediate from the definitions.

purity(M)=1⇔|M∩C|=|M|⇔M⊆C\text{purity}(M) = 1 \iff |M \cap C| = |M| \iff M \subseteq C: no element of MM lies outside its class, i.e. MM is pure.
completeness(M)=1⇔|M∩C|=|C|⇔C⊆M\text{completeness}(M) = 1 \iff |M \cap C| = |C| \iff C \subseteq M: no member of the class lies outside MM, i.e. MM is complete.

So the pair (p,c)(p,c) reports, coordinate by coordinate, whether the module is impure (p<1p<1) and whether it is incomplete (c<1c<1) — the two booleans the remedy depends on. The four cases of the table are read off directly, and with them the correct action. ◼\blacksquare
Together the two propositions give the result: one axis is insufficient; two axes are sufficient. For a single rule, two metrics are necessary and enough.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
4 Why exactly two — not three
Two axes are the minimum, and they are also the maximum needed for the failure-mode question, because a partition admits exactly two failure modes.
The reasoning is a counting one. Relative to the class CC, each element of the module is either inside CC or outside it, and each member of CC is either inside MM or outside it. Two independent questions therefore arise — does MM hold foreign elements? and is MM missing class members? — and they are independent because all four combinations are achievable (the table above exhibits each). To determine the failure mode is to answer both booleans; two coordinates answer two independent booleans minimally. A third coordinate could describe the module more finely (which elements are foreign, how the class is scattered), but it would carry no additional information about which failure mode applies — the axis count the schema requires.
This is why a pairwise, two-axis reading is the correct working form, not a convenience: it is exactly the dimension at which the failure mode becomes visible and no further.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
5 Many rules, many pairs
A system is often assessed under several partitioning rules at once — logical structure, deployment, security, platform. Each rule is its own partition of the same element set, and each admits the same two failure modes, so each contributes its own (purity, completeness) pair. For kk rules the cohesion profile is the 2k2k-tuple of pairs [1].
The necessity argument applies rule by rule: one number cannot serve a single rule, so one number certainly cannot serve the joint requirement. And the pairs are genuinely irreducible across rules. When two rules cross-cut — neither refines the other — placement under one carries no information about placement under the other. The same physical placement can be correct under one rule and wrong under another, and a repair that improves one pair can degrade another. Each rule must be read on its own terms.
When one rule refines another, the pairs are still both needed: the coarse rule frames the fine one, and a clean finer-rule pair does not vouch for the coarser placement that contains it. The coarse pair is load-bearing and must be read first.
The general form, then: two axes per rule; 2k2k axes for kk rules. Collapsing across rules to a single scalar repeats, one level up, the error the proposition already rules out within a rule — it discards the distinction between defects that call for opposite actions.

title: Why Two Metrics Are Necessary
text:
6 Where this comes from
The two-axis structure is Condition 4 (adequate dimensionality) of the cohesion metric conditions, and the 2k2k-tuple is the cohesion profile, both developed in On the Nature of Cohesion [1]. The companion page Why cohesion has no scalar metric extends the same obstruction from diagnosis to the placement verdict: a scalar cannot decide whether an element is misplaced, and any scalar that appears to is the rule in disguise.

title: Principles
text:
Design principles and their analysis — coupling, cohesion, and related software-engineering principles.

Cohesion — cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule; the (purity, completeness) pair; the knowledge-embodiment theorem.
Coupling — coupling is access to a shared resource; coupling is a consequence of cohesion; the coupling floor.

Cohesion as correctness relative to a partitioning rule is defined in the published paper on the nature of cohesion [1]; the analysis of coupling is published in the coupling series [2].
